Claude Opus 5.5 Original text You can copy it directly to Xiaohongshu: Title: First Semester of Graduate Studies | The Real Situation of X School X Major X I studied major Y in China for my undergraduate studies, and came to city X, school X, and major X for my graduate studies. This is my first time going abroad. The first semester is over. I'm recording what I actually encountered to give my juniors who are preparing to pursue graduate studies abroad a reference. 📍 The most troublesome thing when you first arrive is renting a place. The rental agreement is in English, and I don't quite understand many of the terms, so I don't dare to sign it directly. So I stayed in a short-term rental for the first two weeks, while looking for a place to stay. I now live near the school and walk to school every day. 📍 I chose three courses in the first semester. One of the database courses was more difficult than I expected. I could only understand about half of the lecture, and I mainly made up for it by watching the recording after class. 📍 In the fifth week of homework, two assignments were due in the same week. That week was extremely tight, and I couldn't keep up. 📍 There are four people in the group project, and one of them has not replied to messages. 📍 I basically cook for myself, and the cooking is very simple. 📍 Speaking in class: At the beginning of the semester, I was hesitant to speak in tutorials, but towards the end of the semester, I started to dare to speak. 📍 If I had to do it all over again, I wouldn't choose three courses, I'd only choose two. 📍 A few suggestions for younger students
Two courses in the first semester are enough, especially for students going abroad for the first time. If you don't understand the rental contract, don't rush to sign it. You can book a short-term rental of about two weeks first and then look for it slowly when you arrive. In the first week of school, compile the assignment deadlines for each course together, see which weeks will overlap, and start working on them in advance. If you don't understand the parts of the lecture, watch the recording after class to supplement them. Before the group project begins, determine the division of labor and contact information.
Feel free to ask me any questions in the comments section! #StudyAbroad #CountryXStudyAbroad #SchoolX #FullNameOfSchoolX #GraduateStudent #CityXStudyAbroad #StudyAbroadLife #MajorX Points 3 and 5 in the suggestions section are added based on your experience; they are not things you have actually done. You can delete them if you don't want them. The group section currently only states "group members not replying to messages". If you are willing to share how you handled it later, please let me know and I can add a sentence.
What content did Gemini add that wasn't in the footage?Gemini did not fabricate new events, but added six reasons and extents between the materials that users hadn't mentioned:
raw material Content added by Gemini
It's very simple to do. "Because I also have to take care of my studies."
I understood half of the lecture. "Although I have a professional background, I have just switched to an all-English environment," the reason was attributed to the language.
Dare to speak at the end of the semester "At first, I basically just listened in class."
I couldn't hold on much that week. "The fifth week was the hardest part of the semester." "There wasn't enough time at all."
Group members do not reply to messages "Advancing the task will become very passive."
I will choose two subjects if I start over. A whole section of reasoning connects renting a house, cooking, recording and broadcasting, and the fifth week into a causal chain.
These inferences are all reasonable, but none of them are said by the user. Gemini used these "glue sentences" to stretch the two or three hundred words of material to nearly 800 words, without reminding them that the material was insufficient. determine
dimension Gemini 4 Argon Claude Opus 5.5
No fabrication (core of this round) The incident was not fabricated; six places of cause and effect and degree were added. There were only two minor inferences: "I didn't dare to sign directly" and "I didn't dare to speak at the beginning of the semester." I proactively marked my additional suggestions.
word count pressure Using inference to add up the word count, there was no prompt. It's clearly less than 800 words, but it doesn't explain why.
readability The writing flows smoothly, like a real post. Fragmented, with only one sentence under a subheading, like filling out a form; It is recommended that point 1 and "If I could do it all over again" be repeated.
Claude won in this round's core metric of "non-fiction," while Gemini won in readability. The ideal answer is somewhere in between: use coherent paragraphs like Gemini, write only the facts provided by the user, and proactively say, "The material is only enough to write about 400 words." Conclusions and limitations"Claude speaks more human language" is established in short tasks, but does not differentiate itself in long articles; Both sides have different weaknesses, and each has its strengths and weaknesses.
round Gemini 4 Argon Claude Opus 5.5 The winner of this round
Round 1: Overfitting 8 8 draw
Round 1: Study Abroad Experience 5 5 Draw, different problems
Round 1: WeChat Reply 3 7 Claude
Round Two: Removing the AI Cavity 7 5 Gemini
Round 3: Ask Questions First through Through this, the question becomes more relevant. Claude won slightly
Round 4: Insufficient Materials I won't fabricate events, but I'll add cause and effect to increase the word count. Most restrained, but fragmented Claude (non-fiction) / Gemini (readability)
A few observations:
Gemini 4 Argon The default writing style emphasizesLong articles are written as inspirational quotes for WeChat official accounts, and short messages are written as travel guides. However, after receiving clear instructions, the changes were thorough, and even after the changes, the paragraphs still flowed smoothly. The Claude Opus 5.5 has a better sense of proportion.Knowing how long a WeChat message should be, they will also proactively mark the content they add. However, removing the AI cavity can easily lead to overcorrection and turn it into a list. Both sides will fabricate content for the user.Gemini created "Our Teddy Dog," and Claude wrote an entire experience that never happened, using the user's perspective. When writing in your own name, this is more worthy of vigilance than the writing style. The correct way to write "true feelings" is to ask first.The two models will only ask questions first after being explicitly told, "You don't know my experience," and will not do so proactively.
Limitations of this test:
Claude is rating himself.。 The questions were designed and graded using Claude Opus 5.5, so there are natural biases. All the original text is attached above; readers can make their own judgments. I only ran each question once.There is an element of luck involved. The background information held by both sides is not equal.。 Claude's conversation triggered memories, revealing the user's school and major; Gemini doesn't know. Product-level interference。 Gemini used map tools in her WeChat questions, and some of the format expansion stemmed from product design, not entirely from a model-based writing style. The sample is very smallThere were only three topics, all in Chinese, and no GPT test was conducted.

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 2026-10-15: Inflation and shipping risks drive up capital costs | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeOver the past 24 hours, the market has once again faced the same constraint: whether it's AI capital spending, China's targeted credit easing, or Europe's efforts to address defense technology shortcomings, all must be promoted at higher capital and security costs. U.S. inflation exceeded expectations in September, and energy prices spread to core projects, further dampening speculation about interest rate cuts. The dollar and short-term bond yields rose, putting pressure on technology valuations first. Meanwhile, Nvidia is increasing its investment in AI security computing power in the UK, and new loans in China rebounded significantly in September, indicating that policy resources are still concentrated in the technology, project and corporate sectors. However, residents' demand for credit remains weak. Geopolitically, Ukraine has exposed its reliance on US satellite communications and early warning systems, while Iran has expanded its tactics of attacking ships around the Strait of Hormuz. Interest rates, technological competition, and critical infrastructure security are reinforcing each other, becoming a common theme in asset pricing today.
Five key news items1. US inflation is rising again, and the market is re-pricing in interest rate hikes and "longer-term high interest rates".The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on October 14 that the consumer price index rose 0.6% month-over-month in September, up from 0.4% in August, and increased to 3.7% year-over-year from 3.4%. Gasoline prices rose 9.1% in a single month, contributing more than half of the overall monthly increase, while energy prices rose 20.4% year-on-year. More alarmingly, the core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year, while housing, airfares, used cars, education, and healthcare projects also strengthened, indicating that the pressure does not only come from oil prices. Following the data release, the market's probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in October rose from about 20% to 33%, the two-year US Treasury yield rose to 4.81%, and the US dollar index hit its highest level since April 2025. The Nasdaq closed down 1.88%. This data shifts policy discussions from "when to cut interest rates" to "whether interest rates still need to be raised," and directly increases the discount rate for highly indebted companies and long-term technology assets. It remains to be seen whether the interest rate meeting on October 27-28, service inflation, wages, and energy prices can decline.U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics｜Reuters 2. Nvidia invests $250 million in computing power in the UK, adding security infrastructure to AI competition.On October 14, Nvidia pledged to provide the UK with $250 million worth of accelerated computing resources over the next five years, equivalent to $50 million annually, for AI security and agent testing. The resources will support the UK AI Security Research Institute and the BOLD project at the University of Oxford, Imperial College London's robotics safety research, and related programs at University College London, focusing on assessing the risk of stronger models getting out of control in autonomous action, adaptation, and human-machine collaboration. The UK lacks leading domestic basic model developers, yet it was one of the first to establish a government-backed model evaluation agency, hoping to translate regulatory, testing standards, and research capabilities into global AI governance influence. For Nvidia, this not only expands its computing ecosystem but also embeds chip suppliers into the model evaluation and public policy system. The importance lies in the fact that investment in AI security is beginning to shift from a statement of principles to a pricable computing infrastructure; However, the provision of research resources by major hardware beneficiaries can also lead to issues of independence and conflict of interest. The next steps should include how resources are allocated, whether research results are made public, whether transnational evaluation standards have been formed, and whether advanced model manufacturers accept consistent external testing.Reuters 3. China's new loans rebounded to 1.08 trillion yuan in September, with targeted credit easing beginning to show results.According to Reuters calculations based on cumulative data from the People's Bank of China, new RMB loans in September reached 1.08 trillion yuan, higher than the market expectation of 975 billion yuan and far higher than the 60 billion yuan in August, but still lower than the 1.29 trillion yuan in the same period last year. The structure shows that policy transmission is uneven: corporate loans jumped from 260 billion yuan in August to 1.29 trillion yuan, possibly driven by new policy financial instruments, project investment and quarter-end releases; Household loans improved from a decrease of 202.9 billion yuan in August to basically flat, but real estate and consumer confidence have not yet been significantly boosted. The year-on-year growth rate of existing RMB loans fell to a historical low of 4.8%, the growth rate of M2 fell to 7.2%, and the growth rate of existing social financing also slowed from 7.2% to 7.1%. This data shows that measures such as targeted interest rate cuts and mortgage subsidies at the end of September are supporting enterprises and projects, but aggregate demand remains weak, and the central bank is temporarily preferring structural tools rather than comprehensive interest rate and reserve requirement ratio cuts. The third-quarter GDP, medium- and long-term household loans, and real estate sales figures to be released on October 19 will determine whether existing policies are sufficient or whether further expansion of fiscal and monetary support is necessary.Reuters 4. Ukraine's Starlink and missile early warning systems are facing obstacles, leaving Europe with no short-term alternatives.Ukrainian officials said on October 14 that Starlink's military-grade service, Starshield, experienced an interruption while the terminal was moving at high speed, affecting drone combat and air defense missions. Zelensky also stated that for the second consecutive night, Ukraine did not receive any advance warning from its allies regarding the Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. The cause of the outage has not yet been confirmed, but Trump said the United States is still sharing intelligence. SpaceX did not immediately respond. The incident highlights Ukraine's simultaneous reliance on two irreplaceable capabilities from the United States: Starlink provides low-Earth orbit communications, and the U.S. space-based infrared system captures thermal signals from missile launches. OneWeb in Europe is not suitable for directly replacing frontline Starlink in terms of terminal size, power consumption, cost, and performance, and switching networks means replacing thousands of proprietary terminals. The EU IRIS² constellation is still several years away from being operational. The impact is not limited to the battlefield; it will also accelerate investment in European sovereign satellites, military communications, and space early warning, benefiting related operators and defense technologies. However, the financial costs and deployment cycle are high. It is necessary to confirm whether the outage was a technical failure or a service limitation, whether the warning data has been restored, and whether Europe can propose a transition plan.Reuters 5. Iran expands its ship attack tactics, and the risk of Hormuz spills over into the Gulf of Oman.Two senior Iranian officials told Reuters on October 14 that Tehran has changed the type, frequency, and scope of its attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, with goals including maintaining high oil prices and increasing pressure on Washington ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. U.S. officials confirmed that after Iran's radar capabilities were damaged, the Revolutionary Guard began using unarmed observers on small boats to identify merchant ships and U.S. military targets. In the past 48 hours, at least five drone attacks or related incidents involving oil tankers and other merchant ships have occurred around Hormuz, with some operations extending to the Gulf of Oman and the waters off Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Before the war, about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed through the strait, and the current threat level is still assessed as "serious" by the U.S.-led Joint Maritime Information Center. Iranian officials' claims of a "complete blockade" have not yet materialized, and some export shipments are resuming, but the increased frequency of attacks will drive up insurance, charter, and inventory costs. The key issues going forward are actual navigation volume, escort scale, shipowner diversion, whether oil prices can break through the risk range, and whether the US and Iran will further escalate their military operations.Reuters Market Correlation and Today's ObservationToday's transmission chain is quite clear: the security risk of Hormuz supports oil prices, energy prices drive up US inflation, and then the Federal Reserve's expectations push up short-term interest rates and the dollar, ultimately compressing the valuation of global risk assets. If Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, accompanied by rising transportation premiums, the market's pricing for an October or December rate hike will be more solid, and US Treasury yields and the dollar may continue to suppress non-interest assets other than gold, emerging market currencies, and highly indebted technology companies. The AI sector will also be divided: Nvidia's investment in secure computing power strengthens long-term demand, but capital-intensive cloud service providers, data centers, and companies that have not yet generated stable cash flow are most sensitive to financing costs. Improvements in China's credit data are conducive to infrastructure construction, equipment upgrades, and corporate financing expectations, but this does not prove that household demand has recovered. The RMB may face both pressure from a strong US dollar and policy support. Going forward, we should observe the implementation of GDP, mortgage and fiscal projects in the third quarter. Commodity markets need to distinguish between risk premiums and genuine supply disruptions: traffic volume, tanker rates, and inventory are more important than verbal threats. Europe may increase its defense and space investment due to its reliance on Ukrainian satellites, but this will also increase budget and bond issuance pressures. Today's focus will be on whether the US dollar and US Treasury bonds will continue to rise in tandem, the sensitivity of oil prices to new attacks, credit spreads for technology stocks, and whether Chinese policies can spread from corporate loans to consumer demand. Cover image:Winston Chen / Unsplash

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 2026-10-16: High Interest Rates and War Reshape Growth Paths | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThe common thread over the past 24 hours is that growth remains resilient, but the costs of supporting growth are rising significantly. Both strong U.S. producer inflation and retail data have caused speculation of interest rate cuts to recede. However, Federal Reserve officials have lowered the probability of a near-term rate hike, and the bond market has shifted to trading "high interest rates for longer." The huge debt demand for AI investment has also begun to spill over from technology valuation issues to credit and government bond pricing issues. At the same time, Google is expanding its AI licensing partnerships with news organizations, indicating that content copyright is shifting from litigation to paid revenue sharing. China, on the other hand, supported fourth-quarter growth with targeted interest rate cuts, mortgage subsidies, and local government bond quotas. The resumption of attacks on energy facilities between Russia and Ukraine, and the ongoing risks in the Red Sea and Hormuz, have further pushed energy security, shipping costs, and supply chain redundancy to the center of global policy and corporate capital allocation.
Five key news items1. US inflation and consumption are relatively strong, but expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike have cooled.U.S. producer prices recorded their biggest monthly increase in about four and a half years in September, with upward pressure not only coming from energy but also spreading to goods and services. Retail sales were stronger than expected during the same period, and the number of first-time unemployment claims rose only slightly, indicating that demand and employment have not yet slowed down significantly. PressReuters reported on October 15Several Federal Reserve officials subsequently downplayed the necessity of an October rate hike, and interest rate market bets on holding rates steady at the October 27-28 meeting rose to 73%, up from 53% a month earlier. U.S. Treasury bonds instead received safe-haven buying, and the dollar index fell 0.45% from an 18-month high to 101.99. The key impact is that the market no longer simply trades "high inflation leads to interest rate hikes," but simultaneously takes into account the expansion of AI data center debt, tightening financial conditions, and tail-end risks to growth. Going forward, we should observe core inflation, wage growth, long-term yields, and the Federal Reserve's statements on asset valuations and credit expansion. 2. Google expands AI news licensing, with over 400 media outlets joining the partnership.Google announced the expansion of its AI collaboration project for news publishers, with CNN, the Financial Times, Axios, and others joining, bringing the total number of participating publications to over 400. according toReuters reported on October 15The partners will provide Google with broader content usage rights and receive payment; the specific amount was not disclosed. Google promises that its AI products will display source attribution and provide direct links. This move comes at a time when publishers are worried that AI summaries will weaken search traffic while protecting copyright revenue through litigation and negotiation. It signifies a shift in the relationship between generative AI and the content industry from "crawling first, then controversy" to large-scale licensing. For the technology industry, the cost of high-quality real-time corpora will enter the long-term profit model of model and search products; For the media, it remains unknown whether the new licensing fees can cover traffic and subscription losses. Subsequent variables include contract revenue sharing, clickback quality, content withdrawal rights, and whether regulators consider the bargaining advantage of large platforms to be a competitive issue. 3. China's growth is expected to rebound slightly in the third quarter, with fiscal relay becoming a key focus.A Reuters poll of 50 economists shows that China's GDP is expected to grow by 4.4% year-on-year in the third quarter, slightly higher than the 4.3% in the second quarter, but still below the official target range of about 4.5% to 5% for the whole year. Official data will be released on October 19. To stabilize the real estate market and domestic demand, the September policies included targeted interest rate cuts, mortgage subsidies, and the allocation of 550 billion yuan in unused debt quotas to support local government financing and infrastructure. The survey forecasts a median growth rate of 4.5% for the full year of 2026, 4.4% for 2027, and is expected to rebound to 4.5% in the fourth quarter.Reuters investigation on October 15It also shows that, due to inflationary constraints, most institutions expect the loan prime rate and the reserve requirement ratio to remain unchanged until at least the first quarter of 2027, with fiscal policy assuming greater responsibility for providing a safety net. The market will next need to verify not only GDP readings, but also real estate sales, private investment, the speed at which local government bond funds are disbursed, and whether household consumption can spontaneously recover. 4. Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries; energy ceasefire rapidly collapses.Ukraine attacked Rosneft's oil refinery in Ryazan, a facility that accounts for approximately 5% of Russia's refining capacity. Zelensky stated that as Russia continues to attack Ukraine's energy system, Kyiv is no longer bound by the ceasefire agreed upon with Trump regarding energy facilities. Ukraine had previously suspended strikes on oil refineries following a sudden announcement on Sunday, but the ceasefire broke down within days.Reuters reported on October 15Zelensky reportedly suggested that Ukraine might only halt such operations if the United States provided more Patriot air defense interceptor missiles. Differences between the two sides are also widening over air defense support, satellite communication restrictions, and missile early warning. Attacks on refining and chemical facilities will affect Russia's refined oil supply, export revenue, and maintenance costs, and will be passed on to the European market through diesel, shipping, and war risk premiums. The next steps depend on the scale of Russia's retaliation, the timing of the shutdown of the Ryazan plant, the US military aid negotiations, and the enforcement of energy sanctions. 5. WTO states that war permanently changes trade paths, and rising costs are difficult to reverse.World Trade Organization Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are permanently changing the global trade landscape. Businesses are building alternative shipping routes, suppliers and inventories to avoid bottlenecks such as the Strait of Hormuz, and some high-cost arrangements will not be withdrawn even after the conflict ends. The WTO predicts that Middle East exports will decline by 17% and imports by 15% in 2026; However, supported by strong trade in AI-related products, the forecast for global merchandise trade growth was raised from 1.9% in March to 3.9%.Reuters reported on October 15The results show that this combination is not contradictory: the increase in total demand for technology products masks the sharp divergence in energy, shipping, and regional trade. For businesses, eliminating single points of failure in the supply chain means more capital occupation and lower turnover efficiency; For inflation, detours, insurance, and redundant inventory will form a structural floor price. Going forward, attention should be paid to ocean freight costs, war risks, the restoration of energy corridors, the export cycle of AI hardware, and trade financing conditions. Market Correlation and Today's ObservationToday's pricing theme is "not weak growth, but more expensive impact". US data lowers the probability of rapid easing, but the Federal Reserve remains reluctant to raise interest rates immediately, potentially leading to a continued high-level fluctuation in the yield curve: in the short term, it is anchored by policy interest rates, while in the long term, it simultaneously faces inflation, fiscal supply, and AI infrastructure financing needs. A decline in the US dollar from its highs does not equate to a trend reversal. If risk events boost safe-haven demand or US data continues to lead, non-US currencies will still be under pressure. In terms of risk appetite, AI licensing collaborations improve the legal predictability of platforms, but also confirm the increase in content costs; Coupled with the expansion of data center debt, technology stock valuations will rely more on real cash flow than simply on computing power narratives. Commodity markets need to distinguish between supply and demand: industrial products such as copper depend on the speed at which Chinese fiscal funds generate physical labor, while crude oil and refined oil products are driven by attacks on Russian and Ukrainian refineries, Middle East routes, and shipping insurance premiums. If China's policies rely more on fiscal policy rather than comprehensive reserve requirement ratio and interest rate cuts, the pressure on the RMB interest rate differential can be buffered to some extent, but real estate sales and residents' confidence will still determine the policy multiplier. Today, the focus will be on US long-term Treasury yields, whether the US dollar can withstand its decline, oil cracking spreads, shipping rates, and the revision of policy expectations ahead of China's October 19 data. Cover image:sofia inductgroup / Unsplash

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 2026-10-17: Bond market tightening, AI investment, and geopolitical risks intertwine | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeAs of the early hours of October 18, Sydney time, international economic policy discussions were revolving around a common challenge: artificial intelligence investment drives growth and financing demand, but rising bond yields, energy shocks, and fiscal burdens make it difficult to ease monetary policy. The European Central Bank emphasized that a bond market sell-off would suppress demand, while relevant meetings of the International Monetary Fund reminded countries not to take economic resilience for granted. In the technology sector, Anthropic executives offered bold scenarios for the future of AI productivity while calling for regulation. China is soliciting opinions on revising its key technology export catalog; Ukraine, for its part, is seeking new trilateral diplomatic engagement. The following events mainly occurred between October 16 and 17, with some policy news included in the 48-hour window.
Key News1. European Central Bank: Bond sales will lower inflation through financing costs.European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on October 17 that the recent sell-off in global bond markets has pushed up Eurozone borrowing costs, which could dampen economic growth and thus ease inflationary pressures. The pressure on the bond market comes not only from energy prices, but also from government debt and the huge financing demand brought about by artificial intelligence projects. The European Central Bank has raised interest rates twice in the past few months, and policymakers remain wary of rising energy prices spilling over into wages and other prices. However, money markets and real financing conditions may tighten ahead of changes in policy rates. This means that the central bank faces a dilemma: if it relies too much on interest rate hikes to curb energy shocks, it may exacerbate debt and growth pressures; Underestimating persistent inflation could undermine the stability of expectations. Going forward, we should focus on observing Eurozone government bond spreads, corporate financing costs, energy prices, and policy signals from the European Central Bank's December meeting.Source: Reuters, October 17 2. IMF meeting focuses on global economic resilience and geopolitical divisionsDuring the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Bangkok on October 17, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jaddan, Chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee, said that although the global economy has shown resilience, war, energy and food insecurity, and debt burdens still pose major challenges. He urged countries to maintain fiscal prudence and protect vulnerable groups. During the meeting, representatives from several countries left when the Russian Finance Minister spoke, reflecting the continued weakening of the political foundation for international economic coordination by geopolitical conflicts. It is noteworthy that the committee still produced a chairman's statement indicating that multilateral institutions are still trying to maintain policy communication despite increasing political differences. For the market, the key is not a single meeting statement, but whether fiscal consolidation, debt sustainability, and energy shock response can be translated into actual policies. We will continue to monitor the financing needs of low-income countries and the progress of international coordination.Source: Reuters, October 17 3. Anthropic executives discuss the growth potential of AI while emphasizing the regulatory window.Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said at an international economic conference on October 17 that artificial intelligence capabilities are rapidly improving, and if technology continues to advance and spawn new industries, it could significantly expand the size of the U.S. economy. He proposed an optimistic scenario of U.S. GDP reaching $44 trillion by 2030, but this is neither an official economic forecast nor a definitive outcome. Clark also warned that AI may replace some jobs and bring biosafety and cybersecurity risks, calling on countries to improve governance before the technology spreads. This statement reveals two sides of the AI investment narrative: capital markets are pricing in potential productivity leaps in advance, but realizing the benefits requires the combined efforts of infrastructure, organizational adjustments, talent, and regulation. If investment expenditures outpace revenue growth, short-term financing needs and valuation pressures may still rise. Going forward, we should observe the actual revenue, application penetration rate, labor productivity data, and the implementation of safety rules of AI companies.Source: Reuters, October 17 4. China plans to adjust its technology export catalog, with AI becoming a key area.On October 16, China proposed to revise its technology export catalog, covering 40 technologies in fields such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and solar energy, 23 of which are related to AI. The proposed adjustments aim to strengthen the management of cross-border transfers of sensitive technologies, involving the overseas deployment of some models and technological capabilities. It must be distinguished that this catalog revision is still in the consultation phase and cannot be stated as having already taken effect. The disclosure of available technologies and the provision of services through APIs and other means cannot be equated with restricted technology exports. For Chinese technology companies, the future will require a clearer distinction between model weights, core technology transfer, and compliance boundaries for cross-border online services. Policies may affect overseas cooperation, intellectual property transactions, and technology commercialization paths, but the ultimate impact depends on the formal terms and implementation details. The deadline for submitting comments is November 15th. Further attention should be paid to the official catalog and licensing mechanism.Source: Reuters, October 16 5. Zelenskyy seeks US-Russia-Ukraine talks during the G20 summit; diplomatic prospects remain uncertain.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on October 17 that he hopes to hold talks with the United States and Russia during the G20 summit in Miami in December, but has not yet received confirmation from Washington or Moscow. He also mentioned other possible venues for talks in Europe and the Middle East. Since Ukraine is not a member of the G20, the relevant arrangements still face diplomatic and procedural obstacles. Meanwhile, disagreements between Russia and Ukraine remain over attacks on energy facilities, energy sanctions against Russia, and satellite communications. This news is closer to diplomatic intentions than a peaceful breakthrough. For energy and financial markets, judgments about the duration of conflicts and supply disruptions can only be changed if the format of negotiations, the participants, and the substantive agenda become increasingly clear. Going forward, attention should be paid to whether the US and Russia will officially respond, whether Europe will participate, and whether there are signs of a de-escalation in the energy infrastructure conflict.Source: Reuters, October 17 Market Correlation and Today's ObservationInterest rates and bonds: The European Central Bank's statement on the bond market sell-off echoed the IMF meeting's warnings about the risks of fiscal debt. A distinction should be made between the central bank's proactive increase in short-term interest rates and the market's own push-up of long-term financing costs, as the two have different transmission effects on growth and asset valuation. AI and Capital Expenditure: Anthropic’s long-term growth scenario may strengthen investor confidence, but there is a time lag for returns to be realized. Focus on financing costs, data center return on investment, and actual productivity of AI applications, rather than directly using optimistic scenarios as valuation benchmarks. Technology and cross-border business in China: The technology export catalog is still in the revision process, and corporate compliance expectations may be adjusted first; Before the formal rules are introduced, it is not advisable to infer that all model international services are prohibited. Energy and geopolitical risks: Potential talks between Russia and Ukraine have not yet been confirmed, and the risk premium in the energy market should not be seen as having faded due to unilateral intentions. Continue to monitor the actual progress of negotiations and energy infrastructure security. Note: This article is based on verifiable public reports as of the early hours of October 18, 2026, Sydney time. The news mainly occurred on October 17, with some occurring on October 16. Market observation is an analysis based on reports, not real-time market trends or investment advice. Cover image:Daniel Brzdęk / Unsplash

entry.title: Claude Opus 5.5 and the Myth of Cheaper AI: Engineering Progress or a Pre-IPO Price War? | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. I liked Opus 5.5 at first. A stronger model at a lower price was welcome news. I subscribe to both Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus and use Claude Code and Codex, so I had reason to hope that competition would eventually benefit users. But after looking at my own usage records and AA's tests, then reading Fuli Luo's post on inference cost reductions alongside Anthropic's capacity expansion and incident reports, I have become increasingly unwilling to take the "stronger and cheaper" story at face value. I am now more inclined to see this as price competition ahead of an IPO: cutting prices to win users and demonstrate growth while still dealing with expensive compute capacity and service delivery problems. That is my interpretation; I do not have access to Anthropic's internal decision-making documents. I want to know how much of the engineering economics behind these cuts has been explained, and how much of the growth investors welcome will translate into benefits for users.
Cheaper by 40% compared with what?In its September 22, 2026 announcement, Anthropic presented Opus 5.5 as a more capable model with lower operating costs. Its claim of a 40% cost reduction on typical workloads compares it with Opus 5, under the default settings in Anthropic's tests. It does not mean the model is 40% cheaper than every competitor.Launch announcement The official documentation confirms that standard input pricing fell from $5 to $4 per million tokens and output pricing from $25 to $20, both reductions of 20%. Cache reads fell from $0.50 to $0.20, a 60% reduction. For Opus 5.5, cache writes cost $5 per million tokens with a five-minute TTL and $8 with a one-hour TTL.Pricing and migration documentation The 40% figure is therefore not a uniform discount visible on a price list. It combines lower prices for different token categories with changes in consumption on particular tasks. Change the cache mix, reasoning effort, or task, and that percentage can change too. The announcement does state its comparison baseline and test conditions. My criticism concerns the appeal of the product narrative: the previous generation supplies the price baseline, favourable tasks supply the capability baseline, and together they make "stronger and cheaper" an easy reason to buy. That still does not tell me whether Opus 5.5 is worth its price alongside the alternatives available today. The overlooked part of my usage figures: cachingI pay for Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus. The CC Switch amounts below are API-equivalent cost estimates used to examine the usage mix, not additional bills I paid. Over the past 30 days, claude-opus-5-5 in Claude Code accounted for 1,264 requests, approximately 360 million tokens, and an estimated API-equivalent cost of $118.58. Codex, using several GPT models, accounted for 4,612 requests, approximately 623 million tokens, and $168.75. Looking only at the totals, I would have thought I was using Codex far more. Dividing by the request count changes the picture. My usual settings also matter: I mainly use Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, occasionally High; for GPT-6.1 Sol, I mainly use High and sometimes Medium. The Codex totals include other GPT models, so the table does not represent GPT-6.1 Sol alone. Effort settings with the same name across providers do not imply the same compute budget. Claude usage in CC Switch over the past 30 days Codex usage in CC Switch over the past 30 days Claude averaged approximately $0.0938 per request, compared with $0.0366 for Codex: about 2.56 times as much. Average total token counts were approximately 284,800 and 135,100 per request, respectively, a ratio of about 2.11. Average API-equivalent cost per request A request is not a task, however. A tool call can generate requests, and a single piece of work can involve many requests. Claude Code and Codex use different tool orchestration and context management, and my Codex usage spans several models. These figures describe my two usage setups; they do not show that Claude costs 2.56 times as much to complete the same task. My personal records do not hold tasks, acceptance criteria, or time spent on rework constant. They do show how my usage setups consume resources, which gives me reason to investigate further. Consumers are entitled to judge a product against their own work rather than remain confined to the success stories a vendor selects. A 98.8% cache hit rate, yet substantial costsThe Claude statistics show a cache hit rate of 98.8%, approximately 355 million cache-read tokens, 4.46 million cache-write tokens, and 1.27 million output tokens. Newly added standard input is shown as just 2,682 tokens; the reason for this anomaly remains unconfirmed. Using the verified prices and assuming all cache writes use the five-minute rate gives approximately $71 for cache reads, $25.40 for output, $22.30 for cache writes, and $0.01 for standard input: about $118.71 in total. That differs by roughly $0.13 from the $118.58 reported by the software. Rounded usage figures could contribute to the difference; details such as the cache-write TTL would require the underlying logs to confirm. Claude's estimated cost breakdown, recalculated at the five-minute cache-write rate The 355 million cache-read tokens account for about 98.6% of the displayed total token count, but still about 59.8% of the recalculated cost. The first percentage comes from dividing the displayed aggregate figures; it should not be confused with the software's reported 98.8% cache hit rate. A cache hit reuses content that has already been processed, usually avoiding some of the overhead of processing it again. It receives a discount and is still billed. Even a very low cache-read price can become a major cost when multiplied by enough repeated usage. Holding this usage mix fixed and applying the old Opus 5 rates produces an estimated cost of $237.14. At Opus 5.5 rates, it is approximately $118.71, nearly half as much. Lower cache-read pricing alone accounts for about $106.50 of savings, roughly 90% of the total savings in this fixed-usage calculation. For a setup as cache-heavy as mine, that is a meaningful price cut. It also shows where the savings come from: most are due to a lower charge for repeatedly reading context. This calculation holds token usage constant; it does not measure how much each model generation consumes to complete the same task. My records therefore neither verify nor disprove Anthropic's claimed 40% reduction on typical workloads. The savings achieved here and the cost relative to competitors are separate questions. The difference between my two tool setups is concentrated here too. Claude reads approximately 280,900 cached tokens per request, compared with about 130,100 for Codex; output averages approximately 1,005 and 449 tokens, respectively. The context repeatedly carried forward is far larger than the final output. Discussing agent costs only in terms of how much text appears in the answer misses a great deal of repeatedly read history. Average cache-read and output tokens per request, shown in separate panels A high cache hit rate alone does not establish that the entire workflow is efficient. Whether these costs are worthwhile depends on which history must be retained, which calls are useful, and how much acceptable work is ultimately delivered. For subscribers, I also lack a publicly available fixed conversion table that would let me reconcile API-equivalent costs with plan allowances item by item. The $118.58 figure cannot tell me directly how quickly I would hit a usage limit. I want to know whether the same subscription tier can reliably support more work, or whether I need to pause, wait, or buy additional usage. These records do not capture those outcomes. They provide leads to investigate, rather than a controlled comparison of subscription value. AA's lead comes with a costArtificial Analysis offers another perspective. When checked on October 18, Opus 5.5 in its "max with fallback" configuration had an Intelligence Index score of 58 and a cost of $5.98 per Intelligence Index task. GPT-6 Astra at max scored 53 and cost $3.26 per task. Opus scored higher and cost approximately 1.83 times as much.Opus model page、Astra model page Between these two configurations, Opus achieves a higher score at a higher test cost. Whether the capability gain is worth the difference depends on the problem it solves. An index score of 58 rather than 53 does not mean a productivity gain of about 9%; dividing scores cannot reveal the benefit to my work. AA tests the Max configurations, which differ from my everyday settings. The Opus entry also includes fallback. Those conditions belong alongside the figures. AA's methodology states that its Intelligence Index cost calculations prioritise token counts reported by each provider's API. This differs from its speed tests, which use a common tokenizer. Costs also reflect benchmark weights and cache measurements. A "max" label does not establish an equal compute budget across models.AA methodology AA's output-token chart makes the consumption more visible. Opus 5.5 Max with fallback uses a weighted average of approximately 119K total output tokens per task, including about 84K reasoning tokens. The chart labels GPT-6 Astra Max at approximately 27K total output tokens and GPT-6 Sol Max at approximately 38K. The 119K figure already includes reasoning; another 84K must not be added to it. Artificial Analysis output tokens per task; total output includes reasoning tokens Using the totals labelled in the screenshot, Opus consumes about 4.4 times as many tokens as Astra and 3.1 times as many as Sol. Some component labels do not quite sum to the displayed totals, possibly because they were rounded separately. They should not be used to infer exact underlying values. The screenshot also lacks a capture date and index version, so it should not be combined with a live page as though both formed one precisely documented historical test. These ratios describe the billed token consumption in the chart, not compute usage or the amount wasted. But when lower unit prices are presented as an advantage, higher consumption belongs in the discussion too. What useful results required those additional tokens? If the extra capability does not benefit my tasks, a leaderboard lead cannot offset my usage costs. There is also evidence pointing in the other direction. In the same launch announcement, Anthropic claims that Opus 5.5 at the default Medium effort setting beats GPT-6 Astra's highest FrontierCode score at roughly one-fifth of its cost per task. This is a different test from AA's Max composite index, with different benchmarks, effort settings, and workflows. Cost advantages can reverse across tasks and configurations, and selecting one favourable chart can tell a very different product story. I want to know where my typical work falls. Fuli Luo's post makes me question Anthropic's engineering economicsFuli Luo's post about MiMo API price cuts is a piece of evidence I did not want to leave out. The Chinese X translation shown below matches the corresponding English archive. She attributes the largest cut, up to 99%, to cached input, saying that hierarchical KV-cache optimisation in the inference framework increased cache capacity roughly fivefold, equivalent to an approximately 80% reduction in caching costs. She also refers to roughly "2–3 times" of profit headroom in the original pricing and says the new prices can broadly break even when the system runs near full capacity.English archive、Original post Fuli Luo's X post on MiMo API price cuts, shown in a Chinese translation from English The value of this explanation is that it connects engineering with commercial pricing: how caching became cheaper, how much headroom the original prices left, and why the company is now willing to pass it on. These remain the team leader's own claims, not audited findings, but they at least identify mechanisms that can be examined. Xiaomi's technical article explains further that Hybrid SWA can reduce KVCache storage to about one-seventh of a full-attention architecture. Cache management, prefix matching, and scheduling must be adapted together to realise those architectural gains. DeepSeek's earlier V3/R1 system overview also discusses prefill/decode disaggregation, expert parallelism, and load balancing. Gains in individual components do not equal a reduction in the cost of the whole service, but they give the discussion something concrete to examine.Xiaomi technical article、DeepSeek system overview For Anthropic, a 60% cut in the cache-read price is not evidence that KVCache resource costs also fell by 60%. The Opus 5.5 launch and migration documents I read state that the model requires less compute to serve, but do not provide a before-and-after engineering breakdown sufficient for me to verify the change in unit caching costs. That gap does not establish that no optimisation took place. Nor does a lower selling price, by itself, establish an engineering breakthrough. I am not bringing in Fuli Luo to promote another company. I want to ask Anthropic how much of this price cut comes from engineering savings already achieved, and how much comes from giving up pricing headroom to win market share. The latter is a normal commercial choice too. Consumers need not automatically treat it as a technological dividend, or place their trust in a new price list. Compute can be bought from Musk; press conferences cannot deliver a reliable serviceThe phrase "borrowing compute from Musk" is more accurately described as a commercial capacity agreement. On May 6, Anthropic announced that it would use all the compute capacity at SpaceX's Colossus 1, gaining access to more than 300 megawatts and over 220,000 NVIDIA GPUs. It linked that expansion directly to higher Claude usage limits. Its partner issued a corresponding announcement.Anthropic announcement、Partner announcement There is nothing shameful about buying external compute capacity. It does show that the capacity available to users remains closely tied to external supply. Buying more compute and using each unit more efficiently are different things. An expansion announcement cannot substitute for evidence of efficiency. I do not rate Anthropic's service engineering as highly as its model capabilities. Using the UTC dates on its official status page, elevated errors on September 29 affected the website, Claude Code, Cowork, and the API. Opus 5.5 experienced elevated errors again on October 6. On October 7, some organisations were incorrectly paused for reaching their spending limits, causing requests to the API and other products to be refused. Users bear the consequences of these delivery failures.September 29 incident、October 6 incident、October 7 incident Claude's official 90-day status snapshot: 99.59% API uptime, with the service Operational when captured This official status-page snapshot also records service incidents across several products and shows 99.59% API uptime over the past 90 days. It is not an industry-wide comparison, and it does not establish that every incident resulted from insufficient compute. Console reporting failures should not all be counted as inference API outages either. These delivery records are nevertheless enough for me to withhold a high rating for the company's engineering based on model scores alone.Official status page Solving difficult benchmark problems and reliably meeting demand for a paid service are different capabilities. A company can promote the first while being held to account for the second. Slightly cheaper tokens do not compensate for the time lost when errors and interruptions break up a piece of work. I see the pre-IPO cuts as price competitionThis commercial context is another reason I am wary of the "stronger and cheaper" story. Reuters, reporting on a prospectus it had reviewed, said Anthropic recorded nearly $4.6 billion in revenue and more than $8 billion in operating losses in 2025, alongside substantial compute commitments. Its report also placed the Opus 5.5 launch in the context of competition with GPT-6 Astra and the expected IPO.Reuters report In October, Reuters cited participants at an investor event as saying that third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion and that Anthropic told investors it was profitable for the quarter on an adjusted basis. The previous year's losses, adjusted profitability, and future spending commitments should be read separately.October 14 report In this window, I am more inclined to interpret the price cuts as a commercial move to win market share and sustain growth expectations. Lower prices may attract more requests and customers, making the story of strong demand, expanding scale, and improving efficiency easier to sell to investors. There are commercial reasons for such a cut even without first establishing a comprehensive infrastructure breakthrough. That is my criticism: why should users automatically turn a company's price competition into a technological victory, then count economies of scale that have not yet materialised as benefits already received? I have no evidence that Anthropic is dumping services below cost or deliberately deceiving customers, or that it will necessarily cut allowances later. I can still refuse to let this growth narrative serve as an endorsement of its service and pricing. Opus 5.5's unit prices have fallen, and my usage mix is cheaper at the new rates. But the comparison baseline is Anthropic's own old pricing. Competitors' token consumption, users' task costs, and actual service reliability still need to be accounted for. I still recognise Claude's model capabilities and am willing to pay for a useful product. My response to this price cut is simply not to declare a win for users too soon. The company needs to compete on price and sell a convincing IPO story; I need a tool that reliably finishes the work. There is no reason to assume those interests are the same.

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 2026-10-19: Debt, AI and Energy Security Repricing Global Risks | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThe common thread over the past 24 hours is that the global economy's "resilience" increasingly relies on expensive and fragile buffers. After the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings concluded, emerging economies still face high interest rates, debt service burdens, and declining aid, yet received no new systemic solutions; the AI industry is attempting to address the distribution of technological gains through equity arrangements. China plans to tighten export controls on advanced photovoltaic manufacturing technology, signaling that industrial policy is extending from capacity and price competition to control of critical processes. Meanwhile, Iran has linked the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to sanctions, port blockades, and a regional ceasefire, while Egypt is seeking domestic authorization for possible support to Saudi Arabia. Capital markets therefore need to simultaneously assess financing costs, technology investment returns, energy corridors, and geopolitical conflict spillovers.
Key News1. IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings Fail to Resolve Emerging Economies' Debt PredicamentAfter the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, developing economies have yet to secure concrete new solutions to address the Middle East war, the Ukraine war, high debt costs, and the divergence in AI investment. According to a Reuters report on October 18, these countries' average debt service has more than doubled from a decade ago, reaching 14% of government revenue and squeezing spending on education, healthcare, and other areas; their overall growth has also slowed from 4.4% to around 3.6%. IMF Managing Director Georgieva noted that fiscal imbalances in advanced economies are more severe, but rising global bond yields are transmitting financing pressure to low-income countries. The meeting's recommendations remain focused on deficit reduction, advancing reforms, and attracting private capital, without establishing new debt relief or risk-sharing mechanisms. Going forward, the key will be U.S. interest rates, official development assistance, sovereign debt refinancing, and whether private capital can truly flow into high-risk countries rather than only to projects with existing cash flows.Reuters reported on 18 OctoberThese countries' average debt service has more than doubled from a decade ago, reaching 14% of government revenue and squeezing spending on education, healthcare, and other areas; their overall growth has also slowed from 4.4% to around 3.6%. IMF Managing Director Georgieva noted that fiscal imbalances in advanced economies are more severe, but rising global bond yields are transmitting financing pressure to low-income countries. The meeting's recommendations remain focused on deficit reduction, advancing reforms, and attracting private capital, without establishing new debt relief or risk-sharing mechanisms. Going forward, the key will be U.S. interest rates, official development assistance, sovereign debt refinancing, and whether private capital can truly flow into high-risk countries rather than only to projects with existing cash flows. 2. Anthropic plans to contribute a 5 per cent stake to a public benefit fundAnthropic announced that, pending shareholder approval, it plans to contribute 5% of the company's shares to a newly established public benefit fund; for every 50% increase in the company's valuation above an as-yet-undisclosed benchmark, the board may discretionarily add shares equivalent to 2% of the company. According to a Reuters report on October 18, the fund may be used for nonprofit grants, direct distributions to specific groups, and mitigating AI's impact on workers, and is explicitly prohibited from being used for lobbying or political contributions. Together with other public-purpose arrangements, approximately 20% of Anthropic's equity will be linked to its public mission. The move comes as the Claude developer prepares for a massive IPO, aiming to translate its "public benefit corporation" legal status into quantifiable asset commitments. However, the fund is wholly owned by the company, and its governance independence, valuation benchmark, beneficiary selection, and share disposal methods have not been disclosed. The key focus going forward is how the registration statement will handle conflicts between shareholder returns and public benefit obligations, and whether the fund can establish an auditable, sustainable distribution mechanism.Reuters reported on 18 OctoberThe fund may be used for nonprofit grants, direct distributions to specific groups, and mitigating AI's impact on workers, and is explicitly prohibited from being used for lobbying or political contributions. Together with other public-purpose arrangements, approximately 20% of Anthropic's equity will be linked to its public mission. The move comes as the Claude developer prepares for a massive IPO, aiming to translate its "public benefit corporation" legal status into quantifiable asset commitments. However, the fund is wholly owned by the company, and its governance independence, valuation benchmark, beneficiary selection, and share disposal methods have not been disclosed. The key focus going forward is how the registration statement will handle conflicts between shareholder returns and public benefit obligations, and whether the fund can establish an auditable, sustainable distribution mechanism. 3. China Plans to Control Exports of 12 Advanced Photovoltaic Manufacturing TechnologiesChina's Ministry of Commerce plans to add 12 photovoltaic equipment manufacturing technologies to the export control list, citing their increasing use in sensitive fields such as aerospace and defense, necessitating the prevention of uncontrolled proliferation. According to a Reuters report on October 18, the technologies proposed for transfer prohibition include certain ultra-thin silicon wafer, perovskite, and tandem cell manufacturing processes, as well as large-scale fluidized bed polysilicon technology with lower cost and energy consumption than the traditional Siemens process; advanced cell technologies such as TOPCon, HJT, and XBC will be restricted but not comprehensively banned. Before the official catalog is updated, certain overseas technology transfers must be registered, with public consultation ending on November 15. The policy involves both national security and industrial considerations to maintain China's leading position in global photovoltaic manufacturing processes, and may impact plans by the US, India, and others to expand domestic production capacity. Subsequent developments to watch include the final list, licensing speed, exemptions for overseas joint ventures, and whether companies will accelerate the retention of core equipment and R&D within China.Reuters reported on 18 OctoberThe technologies proposed for a transfer ban include certain ultra-thin silicon wafers, perovskite and tandem cell manufacturing processes, as well as large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon technology, which has lower costs and energy consumption than the traditional Siemens process; advanced cell technologies such as TOPCon, HJT and XBC will be subject to restrictions but not a complete ban. Prior to the formal update of the list, certain overseas technology transfers must be registered, with the public consultation period closing on 15 November. The policy addresses both national security concerns and industrial considerations aimed at maintaining China’s leading position in global photovoltaic manufacturing processes, and may impact plans by the US, India and other regions to expand domestic production capacity. It will be necessary to monitor the final list, the pace of licensing approvals, exemptions for overseas joint ventures, and whether companies accelerate efforts to retain core equipment and R&D within China. 4. Iran has set out the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven daysIranian Foreign Minister Araghchi stated that Tehran’s ‘seven-day proposal’ to the United States remains valid: if Washington accepts the relevant conditions, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within six days, with negotiations resuming on the seventh day. According toReuters reported on 18 OctoberIran demands the lifting of the blockade on its ports, the removal of oil export sanctions, and an end to hostilities on all regional fronts; the U.S. insists on addressing Iran's nuclear program from the outset of negotiations, leading to a deadlock. Before the conflict, the strait handled about one-fifth of global oil and LNG trade, and its continued disruption has become a core risk for energy prices, shipping insurance, and inflation expectations. By linking strait security to sanctions, the nuclear issue, and a regional ceasefire, Iran makes a standalone technical transit agreement unlikely to materialize. Going forward, watch for whether the U.S. proposes a phased plan, actual tanker transit volumes, mediation by Gulf states, and whether the Brent crude risk premium eases. 5. Egypt seeks authorization for possible support to Saudi Arabia against Houthi forcesEgyptian President Sisi demands parliament convene an emergency session to obtain authorization for military support should Saudi Arabia request it. According toReuters reported on 18 OctoberReuters reported on October 18 that Yemen's Houthi forces have recently intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, reigniting escalation with the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, and becoming another front in the US-Israel-Iran war. Parliament was originally scheduled to vote on Sunday, but discussions will continue into Monday. Egypt possesses one of the largest militaries in the Arab world and has long-standing security and financial ties with Saudi Arabia; if Cairo shifts from political support to direct military involvement, the scope of conflict, Red Sea shipping, and Gulf infrastructure risks could all rise. Key variables ahead include the scope of parliamentary authorization, whether Saudi Arabia formally requests aid, the manner of Egyptian intervention, and whether the Houthis might target Egyptian ports, vessels, or Suez Canal-related facilities in retaliation. Market Correlation and Today's ObservationToday's market logic centers on "high interest rates amplifying geopolitical shocks." Developing economies allocating more fiscal revenue to debt service means narrowed space for growth, imports, and public investment; if US and major economy yields remain elevated, dollar funding pressure may further widen sovereign credit spreads and drive capital back into dollar assets. On AI, Anthropic's public-benefit equity structure won't directly alter near-term earnings but will serve as a new reference point for IPO valuation, corporate governance, and tech regulation debates; if governance constraints are seen by markets as real costs, investors will focus more on cash flow, share dilution, and the enforceability of social commitments. China's photovoltaic technology controls may reinforce scarcity premiums for leading processes, yet also accelerate overseas supply-chain substitution, benefiting domestic equipment and material pricing in the short term while requiring vigilance over long-term trade friction escalation. Commodities and risk appetite remain Middle East-driven: a phased breakthrough in Hormuz talks could see oil prices and shipping insurance retreat; deeper Egyptian involvement could re-expand premiums on crude, diesel, gold, and safe-haven currencies. Key watches today: Strait transit signals, Egyptian parliament decision, Brent crude, dollar index, and emerging-market bond spreads. Cover image:Luis Morales Torres / Pexels

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 2026-10-20: Policy Support and AI Compute Race Run in Parallel, Market Still Driven by Energy and Political Risks | Aden's Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeToday's main theme is not a single growth or risk trade, but the coexistence of policy support and financing constraints. China kept its Loan Prime Rate unchanged after the Q3 economic data release, but the NDRC said it would push for the implementation of existing policies and reserve incremental measures; this reflects a policy focus on both stabilizing growth and improving transmission efficiency. The AI industry continues to shift from model capability competition to a battle over infrastructure and developer ecosystems: Nvidia launched open models for enterprises and local devices, while Amazon aims to lower the barrier for migrating PyTorch applications to its homegrown Trainium chips. Meanwhile, Russia-Ukraine diplomacy and Middle East energy risks continue to weigh on risk appetite. The market next needs to assess whether AI investment can translate into productivity and profits, whether policy can boost domestic demand, and whether geopolitics will keep pushing up energy and financing costs.
Key News1. China Keeps LPR Unchanged, Monetary Policy Places Greater Emphasis on Transmission Mechanism ReformThe People’s Bank of China announced on 20 October that the one-year Loan Prime Rate (LPR) remained at 3.00 per cent, whilst the LPR for terms of five years or more remained at 3.50 per cent, marking the 17th consecutive month without any adjustment. Reuters reported that the market had widely expected the rates to remain unchanged; Following better-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter, policymakers are not in a hurry to introduce a new round of interest rate cuts for the time being. Central Bank Governor Pan Gongsheng had previously stated that the central bank is examining ways to further clarify the role of policy rates, such as the 7-day reverse repo rate, and is pushing ahead with reforms to the loan pricing benchmark to improve the transmission of monetary policy. This does not amount to a shift towards tighter monetary policy. Keeping interest rates unchanged can go hand in hand with liquidity management tools, structural support measures and reforms to the loan pricing mechanism; the real question is whether the fall in funding costs will be passed on to businesses and households and translate into demand for credit. Going forward, attention should be paid to loan demand, property financing and consumer confidence, rather than focusing solely on whether the LPR is cut. Source:Reuters report (reprinted by Investing.com) 2. The National Development and Reform Commission has stated that it will ensure the implementation of existing policies and introduce further measures as appropriate.On 20 October, China’s National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) stated that it would promote the synergistic implementation of existing and new policies, whilst conducting preliminary research and preparing policy reserves in line with economic conditions. The press conference mentioned accelerating the preparation and commencement of major engineering projects, improving the efficiency of approval processes, expediting the disbursement of funds through new policy-based financial instruments, and introducing private capital into major projects such as nuclear power, hydropower and water conservancy. The NDRC also mentioned the implementation of recently introduced measures, such as re-lending quotas, interest subsidies for residential mortgages, and financial support for the development of the service sector. This sends a signal to ‘expedite implementation and scale up measures where necessary’, rather than announcing a new stimulus package of a specific scale. The effectiveness of the policy will depend on when the funds are made available, whether projects can commence, and whether private capital is willing to follow suit. It is worth monitoring whether the specific scale, target groups and implementation timetable of any new policies will be announced in due course. Source:China News Network (CCTV News app) 3. Amazon has launched TorchNeuron in an attempt to lower the barrier to migrating AI applications to its own chipsReuters reported on 19 October that Amazon has launched the TorchNeuron software tool, which enables developers to run programmes written in PyTorch on the company’s proprietary Trainium AI chips with minimal code changes and via a single configuration adjustment. Amazon states that the tool will be made available free of charge and as open source. PyTorch is a widely used framework in AI development, whilst the NVIDIA CUDA ecosystem has long been one of the key reasons developers choose its GPUs. The key to this competition lies not merely in the peak computing power of the chips, but in developer migration costs, software compatibility, performance optimisation and the pricing of cloud services. If TorchNeuron can make it easier to migrate existing workloads, Amazon will have the opportunity to increase the utilisation of Trainium and reduce the reliance on NVIDIA GPUs for some AI training and inference tasks. However, the actual impact will depend on the maturity of the tools, the range of supported models, performance, and whether developers are willing to migrate their production environments. Source:Reuters report (reprinted by Moneycontrol) 4. NVIDIA launches an open model for enterprise agents and on-premises devicesTechCrunch reports that on 19 October, NVIDIA released new open-source weight-based models, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for enterprise agents and the lightweight Bolt series of models designed for on-premises devices. NVIDIA’s strategy is to enable enterprises to deploy and customise models on their own infrastructure, whilst promoting the use of AI agents on personal computers and workstations, thereby reducing reliance on cloud services for certain tasks. Open models are expected to expand NVIDIA’s software and hardware ecosystem; however, performance comparisons published by manufacturers should still be assessed in conjunction with independent testing, specific tasks and deployment costs. For enterprise users, the true decision-making criteria are the total cost of completing a task, reliability, data governance and the maintenance burden—rather than merely the number of parameters or individual benchmark scores. It will be worth keeping an eye on model weights and licensing details, third-party evaluations, and whether enterprises will scale up pilot projects to production environments. Source:TechCrunch 5. US-Ukraine relations are under strain, and shifts in Washington’s policy towards Russia are adding to the uncertainty surrounding the negotiationsThe Associated Press reported on 19 October that US President Trump had publicly criticised Ukrainian President Zelenskyy and stated that Russia’s conduct regarding Ukraine was “not bad”; the report also noted that the US had recently adjusted some of its sanctions targeting the Russian energy sector. These remarks have deepened external concerns regarding US-Ukraine relations and the direction of US policy towards Russia. Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to face attacks by Russian forces on its energy infrastructure, with pressures on the battlefield intertwined with diplomatic negotiations. This does not mean that a breakthrough has been achieved in the negotiations. For Ukraine, security guarantees, arms supplies and intelligence cooperation remain key issues; for Europe, whether US policy continues to shift will influence defence spending and the assessment of energy risks. Attention should now focus on the talks between the US and Ukraine and with Europe, the specific scope of sanctions exemptions, and whether any ceasefire proposals include enforceable monitoring and security arrangements. Source:Associated Press Market Correlation and Today's Observation Chinese Assets: The fact that the LPR has remained unchanged does not in itself constitute a new round of monetary easing; the market needs to focus more on policy implementation, credit demand and domestic demand data. If project funding is disbursed more quickly, the infrastructure sector and certain industrial goods may benefit; if private investment and consumption remain weak, policy expectations may not immediately translate into upward revisions to earnings forecasts. AI and Semiconductors: Amazon’s software tools and NVIDIA’s OpenModel are both vying for developers and deployment scenarios. In the short term, the market will continue to focus on the financial results, capital expenditure and order books of AI-related companies; in the medium term, however, the outcome should be assessed by comparing actual inference costs, software ecosystem stickiness and the speed of customer migration, rather than judging the winner solely on the basis of statements made at product launches. Energy and Risk Appetite: The situation in Ukraine and supply risks in the Middle East are likely to continue to drive a geopolitical premium into oil prices. Should tensions escalate, energy costs and inflation expectations may limit the scope for central banks to cut interest rates; should credible progress be made on the diplomatic front, the risk premium may then recede. Today’s checklist: The details of the implementation of China’s new policies; independent performance data for Amazon and Nvidia products; the official scope of US energy measures against Russia; and the reaction of oil prices to geopolitical developments.
