entry.title: Daily Briefing | 21 October 2026: Attacks on Black Sea shipping, new proposals on Russia-Ukraine and the deepening integration of AI into industry | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThe main narrative over the past 24 to 48 hours has been that geopolitical risks are spreading from the battlefield to trade routes, whilst AI continues to shift from a race for models to specific industries. Commercial vessels in the Black Sea have been hit by a series of drone attacks, prompting NATO to announce an increase in reconnaissance deployments in the region; meanwhile, following his meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo, US Special Envoy Witkov plans to travel to St Petersburg to present a new ceasefire proposal to Putin, as diplomatic and military pressure mounts simultaneously. On the market front, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond remains above 5 per cent, whilst oil prices hover around US$100 per barrel; high interest rates and energy costs continue to weigh on risk appetite. At the sectoral level, OpenAI’s acquisition of Orchestra Bio, a collaborative platform for drug R&D, and the launch of ‘AI+Consumer’ measures by nine Chinese government departments both indicate that AI investment is seeking more direct avenues for revenue and demand.
Key News1. NATO has stepped up its deployment in the Black Sea, whilst attacks on merchant ships have been occurring with increasing frequencyA NATO spokesperson announced on 20 October that the organisation would deploy additional patrol aircraft and intelligence personnel to the Black Sea, as well as providing radar systems, drones and explosive ordnance disposal teams, with a focus on enhancing situational awareness through increased sensor coverage and data sharing. This comes against the backdrop of attacks by drones on several merchant vessels and chemical tankers in waters near Romania and Bulgaria since October, with reports indicating that at least 23 crew members have been killed or are missing. The attacks are widely attributed to Russia, though Moscow has denied involvement, and neither NATO nor Romania and Bulgaria have formally named Russia as the perpetrator. The EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Karras, described this as a “dangerous and unacceptable escalation” and suggested that its aim may be to undermine Ukraine’s revenue from grain exports. The implication is that, as the Black Sea serves as a vital maritime route for Ukraine’s grain and certain commodities, should the attacks continue, shipping insurance premiums, freight rates and grain prices are all likely to rise, which, combined with the situation in the Middle East, would exacerbate global pressures on food and energy supplies. Key points to watch: whether NATO will further escalate its escort operations or aerial patrols, and how the insurance market will adjust its pricing for Black Sea shipping routes. Source:Al Jazeera 2. Witkov travels to St Petersburg to present a new proposal; Russia-Ukraine talks enter a critical phaseAccording to Axios, citing US officials, US Special Envoy Witkov held talks in Oslo on 20 October with Zelenskyy, as well as leaders from Norway and Finland and representatives from the UK, France, Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO, to discuss a ‘framework agreement’ to end the war. The US stated that the talks had achieved “meaningful progress” and that it planned to meet with Putin in St Petersburg on 21 October to present an updated proposal, with Kushner participating via video link. Zelenskyy stated that, provided Russia took reciprocal action, Ukraine would be willing to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, and expressed hope that a trilateral meeting involving the US, Russia and Ukraine could be held next, although Russia had previously rejected this format. Trump had previously agreed to lift sanctions on diesel sales to Russia and had publicly pressured Zelenskyy to reach an agreement. The implications are that the progress of the negotiations will have a direct impact on European energy prices, the supply of Russian crude oil and refined petroleum products, and expectations regarding European defence spending. Key points to watch going forward include: Putin’s response to the new proposal, whether a trilateral meeting will materialise, and Ukraine’s decisions regarding strikes on oil refineries. Source:Axios 3. OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio, betting on AI to be integrated into the entire drug discovery processOn 20 October, OpenAI announced the acquisition of Orchestra Bio. The platform helps biopharmaceutical teams coordinate multi-year drug development processes: AI agents monitor research and project progress; when an issue arises at any stage (such as a failed production batch that could delay clinical trials), they automatically identify the affected tasks and timelines, and present decision-makers with a comparison of potential solutions. OpenAI will integrate Orchestra Bio’s team and technology into its Rosalind product line for the life sciences (which includes the GPT-Rosalind model and Rosalind Workbench); the value of the transaction has not been disclosed. This acquisition demonstrates that leading AI companies are shifting their focus from general-purpose models to workflows in high-value vertical sectors; the core of the competition is no longer solely about model capabilities, but rather the ability to integrate with clients’ data, processes and decision-making chains. Key areas to watch going forward include the progress made by OpenAI and its partners—such as Novo Nordisk and Moderna—in implementing these solutions, as well as the response from other AI companies in the pharmaceutical sector. Source:OpenAI 4. Nine Chinese government departments have introduced 18 measures to drive the upgrading of consumption and commerce through AIOn 19 October, the State Council Information Office held a press conference at which nine departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, jointly unveiled guiding principles on promoting consumption and commercial development through artificial intelligence. The document comprises 18 measures covering the integration of AI into product design, manufacturing and marketing, the consumption of smart devices and robots; service scenarios such as healthcare and smart elderly care; intelligent warehousing and autonomous delivery; as well as commercial smart entities in the areas of shopping, operations and logistics. The guidelines also provide support in the areas of standards, digital infrastructure and financing. Yuan Xiaoming, Assistant Minister of Commerce, stated that this move aims to address the urgent need to boost consumption. The press conference revealed that total retail sales of consumer goods for the first three quarters of this year amounted to approximately 37 trillion yuan, representing a year-on-year increase of 1.1 per cent, whilst retail sales of services grew by approximately 5 per cent. Meanwhile, sales of smart glasses on major platforms rose by 110 per cent year-on-year. (This item is a news update from within the last 48 hours.) The policy does not set any quantitative targets; rather, it serves as a general guideline. With the growth rate of goods consumption at only around 1 per cent, domestic demand remains relatively weak, and the policy aims to create additional demand through AI and new types of devices. Key points to watch going forward include: local implementing regulations; whether the policy will be linked to trade-in schemes or consumption subsidies; and whether retail figures will improve in the fourth quarter. Source:State Council Information Office / SCIO 5. US Treasury yields are hovering at high levels, oil prices are approaching US$100, and the earnings season is now underwayOn 20 October, US new housing starts for September fell by 5.2 per cent month-on-month; the weaker-than-expected figures caused the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds to dip slightly to around 5.09 per cent, though it remained within the high range seen since 2002. WTI crude oil briefly surpassed US$100 per barrel that day following attacks on Saudi Arabia and Gulf shipping routes; oil futures indicated that the market expects prices to remain around US$88 in seven months’ time, significantly higher than the forecast of approximately US$75 in July. According to Benzinga, the CME FedWatch tool indicates that the market estimates an approximately 85 per cent probability that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged in October. Reuters reported that Iranian officials have stated Tehran intends to delay negotiations with the US to prevent President Trump from achieving a diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the 3 November mid-term elections. In terms of financial results, SpaceX’s third-quarter revenue and profits exceeded expectations, whilst Netflix’s revenue fell slightly short of forecasts, causing its share price to drop by around 6 per cent in pre-market trading; Meta, Tesla, Lam Research, Texas Instruments and IBM are due to report their results on 21 October. Key points to watch: whether the AI capital expenditure guidance from major tech companies can support valuations, and whether oil prices and yields will continue to rise in tandem. Source:Charles Schwab、Benzinga Market Correlation and Today's ObservationSeveral news stories today point to the same constraint: high funding costs, rising energy and shipping risks, and the need for AI investments to demonstrate revenue more quickly. Shipping attacks in the Black Sea and the Middle East are driving up oil prices, freight rates and food price risks; when combined with US Treasury yields exceeding 5 per cent, this will continue to weigh on highly valued assets. Should substantive progress be made in the Russia-Ukraine negotiations, this could ease pressure on European energy and refined oil prices; however, the details of any proposed solution and Russia’s stance remain unclear at present. On the AI front, OpenAI’s entry into drug R&D workflows and China’s use of AI to stimulate consumption indicate that the market will focus more on the commercial implementation of AI rather than mere investment in computing power; this will also serve as the yardstick for assessing this week’s earnings reports from tech giants. Checklist:
Putin’s response to Vitkov’s new proposal, and whether a trilateral meeting will take place Black Sea shipping insurance rates, wheat prices and further NATO deployments Whether WTI can hold steady at $100, and whether the yield on 10-year US Treasuries will return to above 5.1 per cent AI capital expenditure and revenue guidance in the financial reports of Meta, Tesla, IBM and others Local implementation guidelines for China’s ‘AI+Consumer’ measures and fourth-quarter retail figures
Cover image:Bent Van Aeken / Unsplash

entry.title: The Synchronisation of the Wave of Protests Across Europe: How Interest Rate Cycles and the Cost-of-Living Crisis Are Fuelling a Wave of Transnational Protests | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Around 17 October 2026, large-scale street protests erupted almost simultaneously in several countries, including France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium, with a partial curfew imposed in certain areas of Paris. Was this simultaneous wave of protests across multiple countries the result of ‘contagion’ via social media, or did everyone receive the same bill? This article examines the September inflation figures for each country, the European Central Bank’s interest rate hikes and fiscal space, to analyse the common causes of this wave of protests, the cases of Spain and France, and possible scenarios for how the situation might unfold this winter.
The data in this article is current as at 20 October 2026; the probabilities of the scenarios are analytical estimates and do not constitute investment advice. NOTES Key Findings Macroeconomic factors share a high degree of commonality: This wave of cross-border protests did not erupt by chance, but stems from a common broader context. The conflict in the Middle East (escalating tensions between the US and Iran, and the prolonged blockage of the Strait of Hormuz) has pushed Brent crude oil prices to around US$110 (US$110.48 as at 20 October), compounded by the European Central Bank (ECB) resuming interest rate hikes, the pressures from energy, transport and the cost of living all converged simultaneously across many European countries at the end of the third quarter of 2026. The weighting of ‘shared triggers’ far exceeds that of ‘emotional contagion’: Social media has certainly accelerated the cross-border replication of protest forms such as roadblocks, night-time standoffs and student walkouts; however, the timing of people taking to the streets in various countries closely aligns with the surge in consumer price index (CPI) figures in September, and the underlying driver remains the economic burden. The ‘asymmetric structure’ of ‘soaring energy prices and stable core inflation’: Core inflation in France stands at just 1.5%, Core inflation in the eurozone stood at just 2.5%… in stark contrast to the widespread inflation of 2022. The cost-of-living squeeze is concentrated on essential expenses such as fuel for commuting, winter heating and rent, directly affecting young people with limited financial reserves; this is the economic rationale behind students taking the lead in this round of protests. The European Central Bank is caught in a ‘policy mismatch’: On 10 September, the ECB raised interest rates by 25 basis points (deposit rate 2.50%(the first such increase since 2023), with the market pricing in the possibility of a further rise in December. Interest rate rises do not increase oil supply; rather, they push up the cost of mortgages (the overall cost of new housing loans 3.54%), corporate lending (3.80%) and the cost of servicing government debt; all three transmission channels are supported by official ECB data. Situational Judgement: Base-case scenario (probability approximately 50%) are intermittent protests that have become a regular feature of weekends during the winter months; they are unlikely to topple the government in the short term; the escalation and spread resulting from deteriorating geopolitical conditions, and the natural subsiding of tensions brought about by geopolitical détente, each have their own course. 25% the possibility that...
Data Gaps and Confidence LevelsSome data cannot be obtained directly; the data gaps, alternative approaches and levels of confidence are as follows:
Missing items Details Impact on the analysis Alternative Methods and Cross-Validation Confidence level
The Wikipedia article on ‘2026 European unrest’ Unable to retrieve the full entry in real time It is not possible to verify, on a country-by-country basis, the start times of the protests in each city and the subsequent events Cross-referenced with reports from The Guardian (10–18), CNN (10–19) and CNBC (10–20) Chinese
Figures on casualties and arrests A lack of standardised, real-time and publicly available policing statistics across countries It is not possible to quantify precisely the total number of participants in the cross-border demonstrations or the scale of the arrests Focus solely on describing widespread phenomena, whilst citing official control measures such as local curfews —
2011 / 2019 Original Documents on the Protest Wave Unable to access the full text of the academic database directly The system framework is unable to annotate the page numbers of monographs individually Drawing on recognised analytical frameworks in the study of social movements (research by Tufekci, Ortiz and others on the repertoire of struggle and online diffusion) Chinese
EU Housing Breakdown Data Eurostat’s rent index and house price-to-income ratio are not directly available The section on the housing crisis is primarily qualitative in nature, with some countries lacking detailed figures. Based on data from the Spanish National Institute of Statistics (INE) by category (housing and utilities: +7.2 per cent) and publicly available reports on holiday rentals; no unverified figures have been included. Low / Qualitative
Time series of government budget deficits in selected countries Data from non-core countries, such as Austria, where the budget deficit in 2026 exceeded 4 per cent of GDP The assessment of fiscal tightening pressures relies in part on reports relayed by the international financial press Based primarily on verifiable financial indicators such as French government bond yields (at a 24-year high) and Spanish long-term government bonds Chinese
I. Factual Background: The Spatio-Temporal Alignment of the Wave of Protests and Macroeconomic Data1.1 Timeline and Scope of the ProtestsBased on a summary of The Guardian’s explanatory piece of 18 October, and reports by CNN on 19 October and CNBC on 20 October:
Outbreak nodes: Around 17 October 2026, large-scale street demonstrations broke out simultaneously in several major European economies, with the situation rapidly escalating into riots in some areas. Areas affected: France is at the epicentre of this unrest, with partial curfews already in place in some districts of Paris; coordinated protests have emerged in Belgium, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Albania and other countries. Group characteristics: Secondary school pupils and university students have become a significant force on the streets in France and southern Europe, calling for measures to curb the cost of living, halt rent rises, improve school facilities and oppose cuts to public spending.
1.2 Comparison of inflation figures across countriesData source: Eurostat and national statistical offices, cross-checked by TradingEconomics; data as at September 2026.
Country / Region September CPI year-on-year August (previous figure) Core inflation / Key energy sub-components Billing Characteristics
Spain 4.9% 4.3% Year-on-year figures for the transport sub-sector +10.5%(Of which diesel in August, year-on-year) +30.3%); housing and public utilities, year-on-year +7.2% The CPI was the highest among the five samples, with transport and housing costs showing a marked deterioration
Italy 4.2% 3.2% Inflation jumped by 1.0 percentage points in a single month A rebound in fixed expenditure on energy and food
The eurozone as a whole 3.8% 3.2% Energy breakdown year-on-year +18.9%(a new high since January 2023); core inflation stood at just 2.5% Typical inflation driven by external energy factors
France (HICP) 3.4% 2.6% Energy breakdown year-on-year +21.3%, petroleum products +36.2%；Core inflation stands at just 1.5 per cent Domestic demand is sluggish, and the impact of imported oil prices is severe
Germany 3.3% 2.9% A general, moderate upward trend Industrial energy consumption is under pressure, whilst protests have been slow to emerge
Inflation figures for major European countries in September 2026, compared with energy and key sub-categories Figure 1France and Spain, where protests first broke out, are precisely the countries experiencing the most severe and rapid surge in energy inflation; core inflation in both countries remains relatively stable, with pressure concentrated on energy and essential household bills. Key insights: France and Spain, where protests broke out earliest and were most intense, happened to be the countries that experienced the sharpest surge in inflation and the largest increases in the energy sub-index between August and September (France’s HICP rose from 2.6 per cent to 3.4 per cent, whilst Spain’s rose from 4.3 per cent to 4.9 per cent). It should be noted that this observation is based on only two of the five countries in the sample and constitutes evidence that is ‘consistent with the mechanism’, rather than a rigorous statistical test; whilst the rise in energy prices in Germany was relatively moderate, protests also spread there, suggesting that, in addition to common triggers, local factors are also at play in each country. Households’ perception of inflation often stems from their monthly fuel, electricity and water bills, and the timing of the protests aligns with the time lag in these bill shocks. 1.3 The European Central Bank and the Sovereign Debt Crisis Monetary policy: The European Central Bank on 10 September 2026A 25-basis-point interest rate rise was announced, bringing the main refinancing rate to 2.65%, the interest rate on the deposit facility has risen to 2.50%This marks the first interest rate rise since 2023 (following eight consecutive rate cuts between June 2024 and June 2025). The minutes of the monetary policy meeting published on 8 October acknowledged upward risks to inflation but, constrained by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, deliberately avoided providing guidance on the medium-term interest rate path. The interest rate derivatives market has already begun to price in a further rate rise in December. Widening sovereign debt spreads: The yield on 10-year French government bonds is approaching Highest level in 24 years, the fiscal deficit widened further between January and August 2026; yields on Spanish 10-year government bonds hovered at their highest levels since 2013. The fiscal manoeuvre room of both peripheral and core European countries is constrained by capital markets.
II. Why does ‘synchronisation’ occur: the three-tier mechanism of protest wavesResearch into the 2011 Arab Spring, the 15-M movement in Spain, the Occupy Wall Street movement, and the wave of protests that swept across numerous countries in 2019 indicates that the formation of transnational protest waves depends on the coupling of several structural levels:
Level Mechanism Key elements
First floor Common macro-level triggers (fuel, leading to simultaneous outbreaks) The conflict in the Middle East has kept Brent crude trading at the upper end of the US$100–110 range, with energy bills hitting everyone equally; the European Central Bank has raised interest rates, leading to a general tightening of borrowing and debt-servicing costs
Second floor The Transnational Replication of Forms of Resistance (Accelerator) Social media rapidly disseminated images and tactics relating to roadblocks, localised curfews and student rallies; young people across various countries developed a sense of collective efficacy, feeling that ‘neighbouring countries are also protesting’.
Third floor Political and Fiscal Vacuum (Amplifier) Party divisions and a weak coalition government towards the end of Macron’s term; high government bond yields have left no room for energy subsidies, making it difficult for the government both to foot the bill and to crack down firmly.
A three-tier mechanism operates in a top-down manner: shared bills foster a widespread sense of deprivation, social media provides a means of mobilisation, and the political vacuum allows the protests to persist and continue. The Three-Tiered Drivers and Transmission Mechanisms of the Wave of Transnational Protests in Europe Figure 2Common macroeconomic factors (oil prices and interest rates) provide the underlying fuel, social media offers a replicable form of protest, and fiscal and political vacuums leave society without a safety net.
Level 1: Common macro-level factors (primary drivers)The 2011 crisis was triggered by the collapse of sovereign credit in certain southern European countries and had a distinctly country-specific character; by 2026, however, Europe will be facing a highly homogeneous form of ‘import-driven energy inflation’. The price premiums resulting from disruptions to crude oil and liquefied natural gas supplies caused by blockades of the Strait of Hormuz have fallen almost indiscriminately on every household in the eurozone. This shared financial burden explains why several countries reacted in unison in mid-October. Level Two: The transnational replication of forms of protest (social media as a catalyst)The protests across different countries have been remarkably uniform in form: student walkouts, blocking ring roads, setting fire to roadblocks, and guerrilla-style confrontations with riot police. Driven by algorithmic recommendations and short-form videos, the protest tactics and slogans of one city can be adopted by young people in neighbouring countries within 48 hours. Social media has not only reduced the information costs of transnational mobilisation but also provided psychological support in the form of the reassurance that ‘protests elsewhere have already been recognised’. Third layer: Political vacuum and depletion of fiscal space (amplifier)France is undergoing a period of political realignment towards the end of Macron’s term, with the traditional establishment’s grip on power waning; several southern European countries are also hampered by fragile coalition governments. Unlike in 2011, government bond yields in major countries are now very high, and governments are unable to ‘buy stability’ by issuing large-scale bonds to fund full energy subsidies. Lacking the resources for compromise and fearful that heavy-handed suppression might trigger a political backlash, the standoff on the streets has thus reached an impasse.
Note: This article concludes that the current wave of protests is ‘primarily driven by common causes, with cross-border transmission playing a secondary role’. If the spread were primarily driven by social media, the time lag between outbreaks in different countries would typically be eliminated within a matter of days; however, this round of protests has unfolded in waves since 17 October, closely aligned with the timing of CPI data releases and the start of the heating season in various countries. III. The Politicisation of the Housing Crisis: SpainSpain is a prime example for observing ‘how the rising cost of living translates into issues of social class’:
The combined pressure of rising prices and rents: Spain’s CPI for September stood at 4.9 per cent, the highest of the five countries surveyed; the housing and utilities sub-index rose year-on-year 7.2%, with diesel prices rising year-on-year 30.3%。 The conflict between the commercialisation of tourism and the housing shortage: In August 2026, Spain welcomed a record number of international visitors, whilst short-term holiday rentals (such as Airbnb) in cities including Barcelona and Madrid continued to crowd out long-term rental properties. Tenants’ rights organisations have successfully elevated the issue of ‘unaffordable rent’ from a personal financial hardship to a social movement opposing gentrification and the institutional capital monopoly on housing. As data on the house price-to-income ratio and the monthly rent index at EU level are not directly available, this section provides only a qualitative overview and does not include any unverified figures.
IV. Student Protests and Generational Squeeze: FranceYoung students have become the driving force behind this round of protests, and the factors behind this are directly linked to the underlying structure of inflation:
The billing structure is most disadvantageous to young people: This round of inflation has been driven primarily by energy (France: +21.3 per cent), transport (Spain: +10.5 per cent) and rent, whilst core inflation (France: just 1.5 per cent) has remained subdued. The younger generation, who have no assets to their name and lack tools to protect against inflation, see the majority of their expenditure concentrated on essential costs such as commuting, shared utility bills and cheap takeaway meals; as a result, they are far more severely affected than middle-aged and older people who own property. Decentralised methods of mobilisation: Compared with the ‘May 1968’ protests or the 2006 campaign against the First Employment Contract (CPE), these student demonstrations represent a decentralised, ‘network-based’ mobilisation, with no coordination by traditional trade union leaders. The government is facing a governance impasse with no clear negotiating counterpart, and the imposition of a partial curfew in Paris also reflects the diminishing effectiveness of traditional law-and-order measures.
V. The Double Squeeze of Energy Bills and Interest RatesThis section explains the following:The energy crisis and central bank interest rate rises are putting pressure on the European real economy from two directions simultaneously. 5.1 Input-side energy shocksThe eurozone’s energy sub-index rose year-on-year 18.9%, with the energy sub-index in France reaching as high as 21.3%. Europe’s structural vulnerability, stemming from its heavy reliance on fossil fuel imports, has once again been laid bare against the backdrop of turmoil in the Middle East. The blockage of the Strait of Hormuz has now lasted for approximately seven months; although crude oil shipping volumes have partially resumed, shortages of refined petroleum products (particularly diesel and jet fuel) remain severe, directly driving up diesel prices in Spain by 30.3 per cent and petroleum product prices in France by 36.2 per cent. Key price movements and timeline of geopolitical events for Brent crude oil in the second half of 2026 Figure 3With the Strait of Hormuz blocked for around seven months, shortages of refined oil products such as diesel have continued to drive up inflation in Europe. 5.2 Three channels through which the ECB’s interest rate rises are transmittedAccording to the European Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Interest Rate Statistics (ECB MIR, published on 2 September 2026, covering July data) and financial market data, the policy rate (deposit facility rate of 2.50 per cent) is being transmitted to the real economy along three main channels:
Conduction pathways Interest rate levels Transmission mechanisms and impacts Data sources
Base policy rate 2.50%(Interest rates on deposit facilities) On 10 September, interest rates were raised by 25 basis points to tighten overall liquidity; the market still expects a further rate rise in December European Central Bank Interest Rate Decision
Channel 1: Newly granted mortgages 3.54% Increasing the monthly mortgage repayments for new-build properties and the repayment burden of existing variable-rate mortgages is exacerbating the housing affordability crisis ECB Banking Interest Rate Statistics (July data)
Channel 2: Loans to non-financial enterprises 3.80% Increasing the cost of financing for companies’ working capital and investments, thereby limiting scope for pay rises ECB Banking Interest Rate Statistics (July data)
Channel 3: Micro-enterprises and sole traders 4.29% Self-employed individuals and micro and small enterprises bear the highest risk premium and have the weakest buffers ECB Banking Interest Rate Statistics (July data)
Government debt servicing a near 24-year high With yields on 10-year French government bonds remaining high and the budget deficit widening, the Treasury is finding it difficult to provide large-scale funding for a comprehensive price-cap subsidy scheme. Benchmark yields on the French government bond market
The transmission of the European Central Bank’s policy interest rates to the real economy and financing costs Figure 4The policy interest rate rose to 2.50 per cent, driving up mortgage rates (3.54 per cent) and small business loan rates (4.29 per cent) across the board. 5.3 Monetary Policy Mismatch and the Stagflation DilemmaInterest rate rises fail to curb sea freight rates and tanker war risk premiums (Brent crude, 20 October) US$110.48). In the face of a supply shock, monetary policy can only curb demand; it cannot increase supply. I wrote inFederal Reserve Interest Rate Hikes and Oil PricesThe ‘failure of policy instruments in the face of supply shocks’ discussed in the article also holds true in Europe, where dependence on energy imports is even higher, making the situation there even more precarious. VI. Austerity Pressures and Political Capitalisation (Outlook) The ‘Austerity 2.0’ standoff with the trade unions: As the European Union has re-tightened the deficit thresholds under the Stability and Growth Pact (with Austria’s budget deficit, for example, already exceeding 4 per cent of GDP), countries face strict constraints when drawing up their budgets this winter, forcing them to cut education spending and postpone pay rises in the public sector. The winter protests by trade unions and public-sector employees are likely to converge with student demonstrations. The political gains of the far right and populist forces: Experience in Europe suggests that the social anger fuelled by street protests typically translates into votes after 6–12 months. Far-right opposition parties are exploiting the cost-of-living crisis and anti-austerity sentiment to attack the establishment government. As opinion polls remain volatile, this article offers only a tracking outlook and refrains from drawing political conclusions.
VII. Scenario Analysis and Forward-Looking IndicatorsNote: The probabilities are analytical estimates based on macroeconomic variables and political constraints; they are not definitive forecasts.
Scenario Pathways to Development Probability Trigger conditions Market and Social Implications
A: Base-case scenario Intermittent and persistent during winter Approximately 50 per cent Brent crude is fluctuating within the $100–$110 range;The ECB raised interest rates by 25 basis points in December, but its statement adopted a wait-and-see stance;France and Spain have only introduced small-scale, targeted relief measures, with no large-scale, universal subsidies;The demonstrations did not escalate into an indefinite, cross-sector strike The protests have developed into regular weekend demonstrations, causing localised disturbances;The current government is under pressure, but is unlikely to collapse in the short term;The euro and European sovereign debt continue to trade at a moderate political risk discount
B: Worsening circumstances Escalation of protests and transnational spread Approximately 25 per cent The Strait of Hormuz has once again been subject to an armed blockade, with oil prices soaring to over $115;Confrontations between the police and the public in key cities have escalated, resulting in serious casualties;Joint strike by transport, energy and school trade unions;The austerity budget was rammed through Parliament, fuelling a backlash The protests have spread to more countries in Central and Northern Europe;France faces a crisis over a vote of no confidence in the government or early general elections;European bond spreads widened involuntarily, causing European share markets to fall
C: Mitigating circumstances Geopolitical Tensions Easing and Gradually Abating Approximately 25 per cent A ceasefire framework has been agreed in the Middle East, and oil prices have fallen back below US$90;Demand for heating peaks in the latter half of winter, and the base effect in energy prices causes inflation to ease;The government has allocated special funds to provide rent subsidies to young people and tenants;The ECB’s December decision sent a clear signal of a pause As the bitter cold and the cost-of-living crisis eased, the street protests naturally subsided;The political crisis has been temporarily resolved;Public sentiment is shifting towards the next election cycle
Three Possible Scenarios for the Evolution of the Wave of Protests in Europe and Key Indicators to Monitor Figure 5The baseline scenario (50 per cent) is that the protests will evolve into intermittent demonstrations that become a regular feature of weekends during the winter; key factors to watch are the trend in oil prices, the ECB’s December monetary policy guidance and the negotiations over the French budget. Tracking and Falsification ChecklistWhen assessing the direction of the wave of protests, the three most telling indicators are:
International oil prices: If Brent crude falls back below US$90, the energy-import-driven logic will rapidly weaken, and the probability of Scenario C will rise significantly; if it breaks through US$115, the risk associated with Scenario B will surge. ECB December decision: If the ECB were to pause its rate rises under pressure from stagflation and adopt a neutral stance, expectations of a further tightening of financial conditions would cool significantly. Budget deliberations in the French National Assembly: Keep an eye on the vote on public expenditure and energy taxes in the 2027 Budget. If the government invokes constitutional provisions to force the bill through, leading to the collapse of the Cabinet, the political crisis will rapidly spill over into the economy.

entry.title: Fed Rate Hikes and Oil Prices: Why This ‘Stagflation’ Has Left the Fed in a Bind | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. This article was written on 21 October 2026; the data is current as at 20 October 2026. The dates of the two Federal Reserve meetings mentioned in the article—27–28 October and 8–9 December—are subject to the calendar in effect at the time of publication. NOTES Soaring oil prices, virtually stagnant employment, and a Federal Reserve that is still raising interest ratesLet’s look at three things first. Firstly: Brent crude is currently trading at US$109 per barrel. Following military action against Iran by the US and Israel at the start of the year, oil prices have risen steadily; in September, US petrol prices rose by 34.2 per cent year-on-year. Secondly: US non-farm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September. By comparison, the figure for August was 133,000. The unemployment rate, meanwhile, rose to 4.2 per cent. Thirdly: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates just last month, bringing the federal funds rate to 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent, and the market is still betting on another hike in December, with the probability having been priced in at as high as 94 per cent at its peak. With these three things happening at the same time, something just doesn’t seem quite right. Prices are rising, jobs are becoming scarcer, and the central bank, far from rescuing the economy, is actually slamming on the brakes? If you find this unreasonable, congratulations—your intuition has picked up on a genuine contradiction. This article explains exactly why this contradiction exists, why the Federal Reserve finds itself in a bind, and how it relates to your and my mortgage, petrol costs and savings.
What actually happened: a concise list of factsLet’s start by looking at the key figures (see the end of the article for data sources):
Indicators Latest value Previous figure Notes
CPI year-on-year (September) 3.7% 3.4% Of these, energy rose by 20.4 per cent and petrol by 34.2 per cent
Core CPI (September) 2.6% — Excluding energy and food, the figures are actually quite moderate
PPI (September) 6.3% — Producer prices are rising even more sharply
Non-farm payrolls (September) +29,000 +133,000 Unemployment rate: 4.2 per cent; hourly wages up by just 3.0 per cent year-on-year
Federal Funds Rate 3.75%–4.00% 3.50%–3.75% Interest rates were raised by 25 basis points on 16 September, with the decision passed unanimously (12–0).
10-year US Treasury yield 5.11% — An increase of approximately 113 basis points over the course of a year
Brent crude oil US$109.3 — Oil prices remain high following the attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz
Comparison of year-on-year changes in various price and cost components in the US, September 2026 Figure 1The sharpest rise was seen in the oil price chain, whilst food and core inflation remained virtually unchanged—a classic sign of a supply shock. This table actually tells a story: price rises are concentrated in the energy sector, whilst those that have not risen (food: 2.5 per cent; core: 2.6 per cent) are all very moderate. Why is it unreasonable, and why is it reasonable?Normal inflation is caused by ‘too much money and too few goods’: when the economy overheats, people rush to spend, and businesses, unable to recruit staff, are forced to raise wages, which in turn drives up prices. In this case, raising interest rates is effective: by increasing interest rates, consumption and investment cool down, and prices naturally fall. But not this time. Year-on-year trends in the US CPI and core CPI over the past 12 months, and the surge in energy prices in September Figure 2The overall CPI jumped to 3.7 per cent in September, whilst core inflation stood at just 2.6 per cent; the rise was almost entirely driven by energy prices. The source of this inflation is very clear: the Middle East. Since fighting broke out in late February, oil prices have been on an upward trend; in September, the energy sub-index rose by 20.4 per cent year-on-year, with petrol up 34.2 per cent, leading to a 6.3 per cent rise in the PPI (Producer Price Index). By contrast, core inflation—excluding energy and food—stood at just 2.6 per cent, whilst food inflation was only 2.5 per cent. In other words, the domestic US price system itself is not overheating; it is imported energy that is driving up the overall figures. Demand is actually cooling further. In September, only 29,000 new jobs were created, the unemployment rate rose to 4.2 per cent, and hourly wage growth stood at just 3.0 per cent – none of which are characteristics of an overheating economy. Consumption does indeed show resilience, but the quality of this resilience is questionable: in August, personal disposable income grew by just 0.3 per cent, whilst consumer spending rose by 0.9 per cent; the extra spending came from savings, with the savings rate having fallen to 4.1 per cent. Consumption propped up by existing savings cannot be considered a sign of truly robust demand. This explains that ‘irrationality’: the current inflation is supply-shock driven; the Middle East holds the reins on oil prices, and no matter how aggressively the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, it cannot conjure up a single oil tanker. The tools and the problem to be solved are simply not a good match. Schematic diagram illustrating the transmission mechanism between supply shocks and interest rate hike cycles Figure 3The chain of transmission of supply shocks: interest rate rises can curb demand, but they cannot control oil tankers. So why is the Federal Reserve still raising rates? Because what it really fears is not the current CPI figures, but inflation expectations. Once businesses and households come to believe that ‘prices will keep rising’, wage and pricing behaviour will follow suit, at which point inflation will truly become uncontrollable. Therefore, the purpose of raising interest rates is not to suppress oil prices, but to signal to the market that the central bank is not standing idly by and that the 2 per cent target remains in place. This is a gamble that oil prices will fall of their own accord, whilst using interest rates to keep inflation expectations in check. Incidentally, here is an intriguing detail: the resolution passed on 16 September was adopted unanimously by a vote of 12–0, with the statement noting that ‘employment growth is in line with the labour force’. However, with non-farm payrolls at just 29,000 and the unemployment rate rising to 4.2 per cent, there is a clear disconnect between this statement and the figures. How should this be interpreted? One possibility is that the new Chairman, Warsh, deliberately downplayed the weakening in the labour market to leave room for continued tightening; another is that the single-month non-farm payrolls figure was affected by ‘noise’ such as statistical adjustments and changes in the labour force base due to immigration, and that actual employment conditions were not as poor as the surface figures suggested. There is currently no conclusive evidence to support either interpretation; next month’s employment report (to be released on 6 November) will provide further clues. What does this mean for ordinary people?No matter how impressive the macroeconomic figures may seem, they ultimately come down to the bill. Mortgage rates: 7.5 per cent, and still rising. According to MBA statistics (as reported by the media), the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate reached 7.50 per cent in the week of 9 October, marking the eighth consecutive week of increases and a cumulative rise of approximately 141 basis points since the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. Historically, the long-term average for 30-year mortgage rates is 6.08 per cent, having fallen to a low of 2.85 per cent at the end of 2020. A rough calculation shows that for a 30-year mortgage of US$400,000, if the interest rate rises from 3 per cent to 7.5 per cent, the monthly repayment would increase from approximately US$1,686 to US$2,796. The extra US$1,110 or so represents the real cost borne by homebuyers in recent years. Homebuyers are naturally voting with their feet: mortgage applications have fallen for six consecutive weeks, and applications to purchase a home dropped by a further 4 per cent last week. Comparison of monthly repayments for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage of US$400,000 in the US Figure 4For the same property and the same loan amount, the monthly repayment is $1,110 higher. Petrol prices: The bill at the petrol station is the most obvious indicator. Petrol prices are up 34.2 per cent year-on-year, representing a fixed monthly additional outlay for commuters. With the autumn and winter heating season fast approaching, heating fuel prices have risen by 74.2 per cent year-on-year, meaning heating costs will be significantly higher this winter. Savings: A savings rate of 4.1 per cent means the financial cushion is very thin. Consumption is still growing, but this is being fuelled by the drawing down of savings. Should oil prices rise again, or should the labour market continue to weaken, it is this consumption—which is being sustained by people’s savings—that will be the first to contract. Car loans and credit cards: As I have not been able to verify the latest interest rate figures for these two items from a reliable source, I shall not quote any specific figures. However, the general trend can be reasonably inferred: as they are linked to the benchmark interest rate and banks’ funding costs, they will only rise, not fall, during an upward cycle in interest rates. My assessment: The market may have overestimated the likelihood of a rate rise in DecemberCurrent market pricing suggests an approximately 83 per cent probability of no rate change at the 27–28 October meeting, whilst the probability of a rate rise at the 8–9 December meeting fluctuates between 75 per cent and 94 per cent. The prevailing view is that the Bank will ‘wait and see’ in October and raise rates once more in December. I take a different view:I believe the probability of a rate rise in December has been overestimated; the scenario of ‘no change in either October or December’ (which I put at around 35 per cent) is more likely than the market is pricing in. There are three reasons: Firstly, the structural driver of inflation is oil prices, not demand. Provided the situation in the Middle East does not deteriorate further, the base effect on oil prices is likely to subside of its own accord in the fourth quarter, at which point the CPI will fall, and the Federal Reserve will have no need to raise rates further. Secondly, employment figures are deteriorating. If the 29,000 new jobs represent a trend rather than a blip, continuing to raise interest rates would be like placing another weight on an already fragile labour market. At the IMF Annual Meeting in Bangkok, Warsh offered no indication regarding the October meeting, stating only that ‘higher-than-expected inflation has not altered the assessment of the economy’ – a remark that seemed more intended to leave room for manoeuvre than to signal forthcoming action. Thirdly, the marginal effect of interest rate rises does not, in any case, affect oil prices; an additional 25 basis points would offer virtually no direct benefit to CPI; on the contrary, it would further push up the 10-year government bond yield—which has already reached 5.11 per cent—and mortgage rates—which stand at 7.5 per cent—causing immediate damage to the housing sector. What evidence would overturn my assessment? Two things: firstly, the employment report on 6 November showed that the labour market is regaining strength (with job creation returning to over 100,000), indicating that the demand side is genuinely overheating; secondly, the CPI figures for 10 November showed that inflation, excluding energy, has also begun to rise (with the month-on-month core rate rising consecutively), indicating that the oil price shock has already spilled over into wage and service pricing behaviour. Should either of these two events occur, I will shift my stance to support a rate rise in December. Conversely, if rates are indeed raised in December, please bear in mind that this is a move intended to ‘stabilise expectations’ and does not mean that inflation has genuinely spiralled out of control; this can be verified by examining the core components of the next CPI figure. The knock-on effects on the markets, and on the Australian dollar and the renminbiThe bond market has already priced in these expectations of ‘higher for longer’: 10-year US Treasuries are yielding 5.11 per cent, whilst 30-year bonds are yielding 5.43 per cent (Trading Economics, 20 October 2026). US equities are hovering near historic highs, but technology shares are falling: the Nasdaq has dropped by 3.7 per cent over the past month, and the market is beginning to re-evaluate the highly leveraged financing of AI data centres (the sharp fall in CoreWeave’s bonds is a sign of this). The US Dollar Index stands at 101.7 and the price of gold at US$4,125, both reflecting the same macroeconomic narrative. A quick note for readers in Australia and those following the renminbi: whilst the Federal Reserve is tightening monetary policy, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has also been raising interest rates this year (the cash rate has now reached 4.60 per cent). With both central banks tightening simultaneously, the renminbi faces interest rate differential pressure against both currencies, and the short-term depreciation pressure is greater than I had anticipated inThe previous analysis of the RBA and the AUD/CNY exchange rateIt is stated more broadly in the text; however, if the Federal Reserve were to begin cutting interest rates in 2027 due to a deterioration in the labour market, the Australian dollar’s interest rate differential advantage would also narrow ahead of schedule. Whilst the mechanism has changed, the medium-term directional conclusion that the Australian dollar will remain ‘relatively weak’ remains unchanged for the time being, though the trigger point may be brought forward. ConclusionThe most ironic aspect of this round of ‘stagflation’ is that whilst Washington holds no sway over inflation or employment, it is the hand that presses the button to raise interest rates. All the Federal Reserve can do is stabilise expectations and then wait for oil prices. If they fall, there will be a soft landing; if not, another rate hike will be necessary in December, and every ounce of that stagflation will ultimately land on the bills of ordinary households, from monthly mortgage repayments to petrol station receipts. 6 November and 10 November: two dates, two sets of figures, which essentially seal the fate of the first season of this story. Data sources and notes Federal Reserve decision of 16 September (interest rate raised to 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent, passed 12–0):federalreserve.gov CPI series (CPIAUCSL, BLS raw data obtained via FRED):fred.stlouisfed.org; Unemployment rate time series:fred.stlouisfed.org. High confidence Non-farm payrolls +29,000: Trading Economics, citing the BLS (tradingeconomics.com), within the confidence interval 30-year mortgage rate: 7.50 per cent: MBA statistics, as cited by Trading Economics (tradingeconomics.com） 10-year yield 5.11 per cent, US Dollar Index, oil prices, gold prices: Trading Economics (data as at 20 October 2026) The scenario probabilities are estimates made by the author based on open market pricing and fundamental analysis; they are provided for reference only and do not constitute investment advice.
Cover image:Jan Zakelj / Pexels

entry.title: Australian Interest Rate Hikes and the AUD/CNY Exchange Rate: The RBA’s 2026 Tightening Cycle and AUD/CNY Scenario Analysis | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. In 2026, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) raised the cash rate from 3.60 per cent to 4.60 per cent, returning it to its highest level since 2011. How will this round of monetary tightening affect Australian households, businesses and tenants? With the interest rate differential between China and Australia now standing at 3.6 percentage points, where is the AUD/CNY exchange rate headed? This article brings together an analysis of the RBA’s rate-hiking cycle, macroeconomic and social impacts, global interest rate differentials and multi-scenario analysis of the AUD/CNY exchange rate, concluding with recommended timeframes for currency exchange and key indicators to monitor.
This article is based on personal research and analysis; the data is current as at 20 October 2026. The probabilities of the scenarios are based on subjective judgement and do not constitute any investment or foreign exchange advice. NOTES Key Findings Nature of the interest rate hike cycle: The RBA raised interest rates by a cumulative 100 basis points during 2026 (with the cash rate rising from 3.60 per cent to 4.60 per cent, the most recent increase taking place on 30 September 2026); the primary focus of this round of rate rises was to ‘curb inflation’ rather than to ‘prevent overheating’ . The RBA has maintained a hawkish stance, and the market has already priced in a further increase of approximately 15 basis points by the end of the year, followed by a further increase of approximately 30 basis points in the first half of 2027. Economic and Social Polarisation: The economic landscape is showing a rare ‘scissor gap’: Mortgage repayments account for around 10 per cent of household disposable income, and consumption is gradually slowing; house prices have fallen by 1.6 per cent from their March peak (with investor loans leading the decline); however, on the corporate side, driven by AI and data centre construction, private investment has bucked the trend and grown by over 10 per cent. Highly uneven distribution of social pressure: The pressure is concentrated onNew borrowers with high leveragewithLow-income tenants; the unemployment rate rose from 3.5 per cent to 4.6 per cent (a five-year high, including the impact of adjustments to the statistical methodology).
Global Interest Rates and Yield Spreads: On 17 September 2026, the Federal Reserve also raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent, thereby disproving the assumption that the RBA was the ‘sole hawk’. The spread on the 10-year long end of the yield curve is extremely wide: the Australian 10-year bond (5.23 per cent–5.26 per cent) is significantly higher than the Chinese 10-year bond (1.64 per cent), with the China–Australia spread at approximately +3.6pp; the 10-year yield spread between China and the US is approximately +3.5pp(US 10-year Treasury bonds: 5.11 per cent–5.12 per cent). Policy rates: RBA 4.60% vs China’s 1-year LPR 3.0% (spread +1.6 percentage points). The long-end yield spread is supporting the Australian dollar, but this has already been fully priced into the current exchange rate.
AUD/CNY Scenario Analysis: The AUD/CNY exchange rate currently stands at approximately 4.6647 (RBA official figure, 20 October 2026), constrained by the interest rate differential between China and Australia, the moderate appreciation of the renminbi against the US dollar (USD/CNY 6.6861) and the counter-trend decline in iron ore prices. Short-term (3–6 months) benchmark range: 4.50–4.75 (probability 52 per cent), with a slight bias towards weakness; Probability of a downtrend: 28 per cent; probability of an uptrend: 20 per cent. Medium-term (1–2 years) benchmark range: 4.40–4.80 (50 per cent probability), with a tendency towards weakness amidst volatility; The key turning point will be when the RBA’s interest rates peak and begin to fall in 2027.
Currency exchange guide: There is currently no clear one-way trend. The conditions for buying Australian dollars (for study abroad, rent and living expenses) are gradually improving, and converting them back into renminbi is relatively favourable in the short term; keep a close eye on the CPI figures at the end of October, the RBA’s decision in December and the trend in iron ore prices.
Data Sources and Confidence LevelsThis article endeavours to distinguish between official primary data, derived calculations and secondary aggregated data. As some institutional websites cannot be accessed directly due to network conditions or dynamic rendering, the sources and reliability of the various data sets are as follows:
Data categories Indicators and Values Date of collection Sources and Methods Confidence level Limitations and Alternatives
Australian Government Baseline Cash rate 4.60 per cent, Commodity Price Index (+15.5 per cent), AUD/CNY (4.6647) 2026-09~10 RBA official website (Resolution Statements, Monetary Policy Statements (SMP), daily exchange rates) High Official first-hand data, cross-checked and verified as accurate
US official baseline Federal Funds Rate (3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent), USD/CNY (6.6861), Broad US Dollar Index (121.40) 2026-10-19 Federal Reserve Open Market Operations (OMO) page, H.10 statistical bulletin High Official statistics; cross-validation results are consistent
US / Australian 10-year government bonds 10-year US Treasuries (5.11%–5.12%), 10-year Australian government bonds (5.23%–5.26%) 2026-10-20 Cross-check using TradingEconomics and CountryEconomy; verified against FRED OECD September monthly figure (5.283 per cent) High Cross-verification from multiple sources
China 10-year government bond 1.64 per cent (reports from 10–15 state 1.67 per cent) 2026-10-20 TradingEconomics Interbank Quotes (Aggregated Source) Chinese The dynamically loaded data on the China Bond official website cannot be retrieved; this series is not available on FRED or the OECD; the China-US yield spread of 352 basis points reported by TE has been cross-checked.
China’s policy interest rates 1-year LPR: 3.0 per cent (unchanged for 17 consecutive months) 2026-10 Third-party financial round-up / Historical series Chinese Data from the People’s Bank of China’s official website and CFETS cannot be obtained directly; this is based on historical time series data.
Iron ore Prices ‘defy the trend and fall’ 2026-10-01 RBA Commodity Price Index Report: Qualitative Comments Chinese Platts: 62 per cent; specific levels for DCE and SGX swaps were not obtained; the RBA’s qualitative conclusion was used.
US Dollar Index Trading flat, slightly weaker 2026-10-16 Federal Reserve Broad Dollar Index Chinese Replace the DXY with the Federal Reserve’s official index
I. A Review of the RBA’s 2026 Interest Rate Hike Cycle1.1 The path of rising cash ratesIn 2026, the RBA reversed the cycle of interest rate cuts seen in 2025 (three cuts totalling 75 basis points to 3.60 per cent in 2025) and raised interest rates cumulatively during the year. 100bp, with the cash rate surpassing the peak of the previous tightening cycle (4.35 per cent from November 2023 to 2024) to reach its highest level since 2011. Changes to the RBA cash rate in 2026(Source:RBA Official Interest Rate Records）：
Effective date of the resolution Magnitude of change Interest rate following the change Voting results Policy Stance
2026-02-04 +25bp 3.85% Unanimously adopted Resuming monetary tightening to address labour market resilience and a resurgence in prices
2026-03-18 +25bp 4.10% Unanimously adopted Curbing the stickiness of core inflation
2026-05-06 +25bp 4.35% Unanimously adopted Matching previous highs, reinforcing the tightening of financial conditions
2026-06-17 Unchanged 4.35% Unanimously adopted Examining the lag effects of monetary tightening
2026-08-12 Unchanged 4.35% Unanimously adopted August SMP figures released, pointing to upside risks to inflation
2026-09-30 +25bp 4.60% Unanimously adopted Breaking through the previous high signals that “interest rates will be raised further if necessary”
1.2 Policy rationale: curbing inflation, rather than preventing overheatingPursuant to the announcement of the Board resolution dated 29 September 2026 (MR-26-27), this round of contraction is driven by a combination of external supply shocks and domestic structural rigidities:
External inflation: Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continue to escalate, with global energy and shipping prices significantly higher than the RBA’s previous forecasts. Technological demands drive up costs: Global AI computing power and infrastructure development have driven up the prices of technology hardware, electricity infrastructure and specialist equipment. Domestic production capacity bottlenecks: The labour supply and construction capacity have long been in a delicate balance. Official statement: Although the previous interest rate rises have led to a marked slowdown in economic activity, trimmed-mean inflation remains well above the 2 per cent–3 per cent target range; the Board considers that ‘the risks of inaction far outweigh the risks of tightening’.
1.3 Macroeconomic Expectations and Market PricingBased on the RBA’s August Monetary Policy Statement (SMP) and Minutes of the Board Meeting of 29 September：
Inflation: Year-on-year overall CPI for the quarter ending June 2026 3.9%, Trimmed Mean CPI year-on-year 3.6%. The RBA forecasts that inflation will not peak until Early 2028 only then will it return to the 2.5 per cent benchmark. Growth and Employment: GDP growth is expected to slow to by the end of 2026 1.4%; the unemployment rate is forecast to rise to in 2028 4.8%。 Market pricing: As of October 2026, interest rate derivatives had already factored in the September rate rise and priced it in A further increase of approximately 15 basis points by the end of 2026、A further increase of approximately 30 basis points in the first half of 2027。
II. The Impact of Interest Rate Rises on the Australian EconomyThe transmission of interest rate rises is characterised by a multi-track pattern, with ‘households under pressure, businesses resilient and external demand showing mixed trends’. 2.1 Household finances: the debt burden is approaching its peak High debt-servicing ratios: The total amount of scheduled principal and interest repayments has risen to approximately 10%, approaching its peak since 2024. Consumer spending is slowing but remains resilient: Growth in retail sales continues to slow. However, since the start of 2024, real per capita disposable income has shown a modest recovery, and homeowners who purchased property earlier have built up substantial buffers for mortgage repayments (Offset/Redraw accounts) during the period of low interest rates. Whilst overall consumption is weaker than in previous years, it remains stronger than the levels suggested by confidence indicators.
2.2 Property: Demand under pressure, whilst supply remains inflexible Price correction: The All-Australia House Price Index has fallen cumulatively since its peak in March 2026 1.6%, slightly exceeding the RBA’s initial estimates. Credit tightening: A decline in borrowing capacity has led to a marked reduction in new housing loans, withInvestor loans led the decline… coupled with market expectations of policy changes regarding negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT). The supply-demand gap has not disappeared: The RBA has repeatedly emphasised that net migration and planning restrictions continue to underpin housing demand; whilst interest rate rises have primarily curbed purchasing power and transaction volumes, they have not eliminated the supply-demand gap.
2.3 The corporate sector: the ‘scissors effect’ resulting from AI investment In contrast to the household sector, investment by Australia’s private non-financial enterprises bucked the trend and grew year-on-yearMore than 10 per cent。 The main source of power comes fromConstruction of large-scale data centres, AI computing hubs and supporting renewable energy grids. The boom in corporate capital expenditure has largely offset the drag on GDP caused by the contraction in consumption.
2.4 Trade and Exchange Rate Transmission Currency appreciation: The Australian dollar’s trade-weighted index (TWI) has appreciated by approximately 5%(Latest: 64.7), which has helped to offset some of the imported inflation. Product differentiation: The RBA’s Commodity Price Index rose year-on-year on 1 October 15.5%(denominated in SDRs), but there are marked internal differences:Iron ore, alumina and copper ore bucked the trend and fell, whilst other commodities generally rose. The weakness in iron ore—which accounts for the largest share of exports to China—is a structural risk weighing on Australia’s terms of trade.
2.5 Resilience of the financial systemAccording to the RBA’s October 2026 Financial Stability Review (FSR),MR-26-28）：
The banking system’s capital adequacy ratio and liquidity buffer remain at prudently high levels. Mortgage arrears rates remain under control; the proportion of owner-occupiers experiencing a cash flow shortfallLess than 2 per cent… the proportion of loans with negative equity is very low, and there is currently no risk of systemic mortgage defaults.
III. Social Polarisation Resulting from Interest Rate RisesThe costs of this round of austerity have not been borne equally across society, but have instead been distributed in a markedly asymmetrical manner. 3.1 Existing property owners and new borrowers Long-standing property owners (with strong resilience): Households that purchased a property during the period of low interest rates between 2020 and 2022, or which have accumulated a substantial offset balance, have experienced a relatively minor net impact from the interest rate rises; some households have even realised a net interest gain as deposit rates have risen to between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. New borrowers (highly vulnerable): Young households that entered the property market at peak prices over the past 1–3 years, with high debt-to-income (DTI) ratios and thin savings buffers, have borne the brunt of the impact. However, RBA survey data shows that even among the lowest-income quintile of borrowers, the median savings balance is still sufficient to cover nearly a year’s worth of repayments.
3.2 Low-income tenants: the dual pressures of high inflation and high rents The RBA’s September minutes clearly state that,Low-income tenantsThey are the most vulnerable group in this current cycle of inflation and monetary tightening. They have neither property to hedge against inflation nor much return on high-interest savings; meanwhile, the shortage of housing means landlords continue to pass on their holding costs, with rents rising significantly faster than wages. RBA Governor Bullock has stated that high inflation is essentially a regressive tax; the turmoil in the Middle East is making the whole of Australia poorer, with the most vulnerable bearing the brunt of it.
3.3 The Labour Market: A Rise in the Unemployment Rate and Changes in Statistical Methodology The unemployment rate has fallen from the start of this cycle’s 3.5% Rise to 4.6%(Figures published in August). Explanation of terms: The RBA noted that the unemployment rate jumped from 4.4 per cent in June to 4.6 per cent, partly due to a technical rise resulting from the sample rotation and methodological adjustments in the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ (ABS) Labour Force Survey (LFS), which should be interpreted with caution; however, the trend towards a marginally looser labour market has been confirmed.
IV. The Global Interest Rate Environment and the China–Australia / China–US Interest Rate SpreadInterest rate differentials are a key benchmark for assessing the medium-term pricing of non-US currencies. The following data is current as at 20 October 2026. 4.1 10-year government bond yield Australia 10Y: 5.23%（TradingEconomics）/ 5.26%(CountryEconomy); the FRED OECD monthly figure for September was 5.283 per cent. (Confidence level: high) US 10-year: 5.11%（TradingEconomics）/ 5.12%(CountryEconomy); DGS10 remains above 5.10 per cent. (Confidence: High) China 10Y: 1.64%(TradingEconomics interbank quotes; its report of 15 October stated 1.67 per cent). (Confidence level: medium)
4.2 Yield Curve Structure
Dimensions of comparison US / Australian interest rates Interest rates in China Interest rate spread Scope and Sources
China-Australia Long-End (10-year government bonds) 10-year Australian government bonds: 5.23 per cent–5.26 per cent China Bond 10Y: 1.64 per cent +3.6pp 20 October 2026, dual-source verification
China–US long-term yields (10-year government bonds) 10-year US Treasury bonds: 5.11 per cent–5.12 per cent China Bond 10Y: 1.64 per cent +3.5pp Consistent with the 352 bp reported by TE
Policy interest rates in China and Australia RBA cash rate: 4.60% 1-year LPR: 3.00% +1.6pp Official resolution vs the LPR, which has remained unchanged for 17 consecutive months
Policy interest rates in China and the US Federal Funds Rate: 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent 1-year LPR: 3.00% +0.75~1.0pp 17 September 2026: Range following the interest rate rise
The long-term yield spread between China and Australia is approximately +3.6 percentage points: China’s 10-year government bonds have remained at historic lows (1.64 per cent) amid an accommodative monetary policy environment, whilst Australian government bonds have risen to over 5.23 per cent, driven by the RBA’s interest rate hikes and inflation premiums. The yield spread of approximately 360 basis points provides underlying support for the Australian dollar. The long-term interest rate differential between China and the US stands at approximately +3.5 percentage points: The yield spread between the 10-year US Treasury (5.11 per cent) and the 10-year China Bond is consistent with the 352 basis points reported by TradingEconomics on 15 October, thereby cross-validating the reliability of the long-end data. Policy interest rates: RBA 4.60% versus LPR 3.0%, spread +1.6 percentage points; Fed 3.75%–4.00% versus LPR, spread +0.75 to +1.0 percentage points.
4.3 Spillover effects of the Federal Reserve’s shift to interest rate rises Key assumptions have been refuted: The Federal Reserve on 2026-09-17 Interest rates were raised by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%(Source:Fed OMO), bringing the cycle of interest rate cuts in 2025 to an end. The meaning of ‘cross-market’: The narrative of the “RBA going it alone on a hawkish path” no longer holds water, as the global economy has returned to an environment of synchronised monetary tightening in the US and Australia. The Fed’s shift towards a hawkish stance has bolstered the US dollar (with the broad US Dollar Index stabilising around 121.40), capping the upside potential for the Australian dollar against the US dollar; however, the relatively strong US dollar is also putting pressure on the renminbi, with the two factors partially offsetting each other in the AUD/CNY exchange rate.
4.4 The marginal effect of interest rate differentials on exchange ratesThe China–Australia interest rate differential is a long-term structural factor that supports the Australian dollar and weighs on the renminbi. However, the widening of the long-end yield spread has persisted for several months, and this factorThis has already been fully priced in at the current exchange rate of around 4.6647. The interest rate differential acts more as a ‘safety net’ to prevent a sharp fall in the Australian dollar than as a new catalyst to drive the exchange rate to continue rising in a one-way direction. V. AUD/CNY Price Trends and Multi-Scenario Analysis5.1 Present Value of Exchange Rates and Cross-Validation Spot exchange rate (20 October 2026, official RBA figure): AUD/CNY = 4.6647(Over the past three days: 4.6469 → 4.6607 → 4.6647, a slight rebound) AUD/USD = 0.6984, Australian Dollar TWI = 64.7
Cross-check: The Federal Reserve’s H.10 data was released at the same time USD/CNY = 6.6861。
The theoretical figure differs by approximately 0.1 per cent from the 4.6647 published by the RBA; the data is reliable. 5.2 Key driving variables China-Australia interest rate differential (bullish for AUD/CNY, but has lost its edge): The +3.6pp spread at the long end is limiting the downside, but its marginal impact is waning. Commodities (bearish): Iron ore prices are bucking the trend and falling. As the key link between Chinese demand and Australian export revenues, this weakness is directly weighing on the Australian dollar. Renminbi exchange rate (bearish on AUD/CNY): According to the Federal Reserve’s H.10 data, the USD/CNY exchange rate fell from 6.6937 on 13 October to 6.6861 on 16 October; the renminbi’s steady appreciation against the US dollar has limited the upside potential for the AUD/CNY exchange rate. Risk premium (bearish): The spread of hostilities in the Middle East has fuelled demand for safe-haven assets; as a risk-sensitive currency, the Australian dollar is prone to coming under pressure when capital flows back into the US dollar.
5.3 Short-term scenario (3–6 months, up to April 2027)
Scenario AUD/CNY range Subjective probability Trigger Conditions and Evolutionary Pathways
Outlook: Volatile, with a slight downward bias 4.50–4.75 52% The RBA is expected to raise interest rates by a further 15–25 basis points in December or early 2027;The Federal Reserve has kept rates at 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent whilst adopting a wait-and-see approach;Iron ore prices have weakened slightly but have not collapsed;The situation in the Middle East remains at a standstill and has not triggered a widespread flight to safety;The renminbi is trading within the 6.65–6.70 range
Downward trend: The Australian dollar is weakening 4.30–4.50 28% Weak demand from China has caused iron ore prices to fall sharply;The conflict in the Middle East has escalated sharply, triggering a global ‘risk-off’ sentiment;The Federal Reserve raised interest rates more than expected;Australia’s unemployment rate has risen above 4.8 per cent, bringing the RBA’s tightening cycle to an early end
Upward trend: The Australian dollar is strengthening 4.75–4.90 20% Australia’s third-quarter CPI significantly exceeded expectations, with the RBA’s successive interest rate rises pushing the total increase past 5.0 per cent;A ceasefire has been reached in the Middle East, leading to a sharp rebound in risk appetite;China has rolled out a stimulus package that exceeded expectations, driving a sharp rebound in ferrous metals
Note: Given the dual headwinds of the renminbi’s appreciation against the US dollar and the Federal Reserve’s interest rate hikes, the probability of the AUD/CNY breaking through the 4.90 level—a scenario representing extreme strength—is very low. 5.4 Medium-term scenario (1–2 years, 2027–2028)The main focus for the medium term is:The advantage in interest rate spreads has gradually narrowed as the cycle has progressed, with a policy inflection point driving a return to the mean.
Scenario AUD/CNY range Subjective probability The Logic of Evolution
Outlook: Volatile with a downward bias 4.40–4.80 50% The RBA will reach the peak of its interest rate hikes in the first half of 2027 (at around 4.90 per cent–5.00 per cent), after which it will shift to a wait-and-see stance and begin cutting rates;The unemployment rate has risen to 4.8 per cent and GDP growth has slowed to 1.4 per cent, with the lagged effects of monetary tightening becoming apparent;Following the RBA’s policy shift, the interest rate differential has narrowed, the renminbi has strengthened moderately, and the exchange rate may settle back around 4.50
Australian dollar strengthens: holding steady at high levels 4.80–5.00 25% Inflation in Australia is proving more persistent than expected, prompting the RBA to maintain high interest rates for longer;Driven by an improved external environment coupled with policy support, commodities have seen a temporary recovery;The price remains under pressure from the 5.00 psychological level
Weakness in the Australian dollar: a sharp pullback 4.00–4.40 25% The global economy has slowed significantly;Pressure is mounting on the Australian property market and highly indebted households, forcing the RBA to cut interest rates rapidly;Iron ore has been under significant pressure over the long term
VI. Foreign Exchange Reference Points and Key Monitoring Indicators6.1 Currency Exchange Guide Need to buy Australian dollars (for tuition fees, rent, living expenses and essential expenses upon arrival in Australia): There is no need to chase higher prices. The China-Australia interest rate differential has already been fully priced in, and with the renminbi strengthening moderately against the US dollar, there is limited upside above 4.66 in the short term. Should geopolitical shocks cause the Australian dollar to pull back to 4.50–4.55… you might consider purchasing foreign currency in batches as and when required. In the medium term, the RBA’s policy shift in 2027 may result in lower currency exchange costs. Requirement to convert RMB (remittance of income from Australia, trade settlement): We are currently in a period of protection against high interest rate differentials,The 4.65–4.75 range is a relatively favourable window for foreign exchange conversion. Given that the interest rate differential advantage is likely to gradually diminish by 2027, it is not advisable to allocate assets in Australian dollars based on expectations of a one-way appreciation.
6.2 Checklist for Monitoring Key Indicators RBA Interest Rate Decision and Minutes: Pay particular attention to the wording of the resolution on 1–2 December 2026, including forward guidance on the scale of interest rate rises in 2027, and whether there are any signs of a shift from a hawkish to a dovish stance. Inflation figures: The CPI figures for the third quarter of 2026, released at the end of October, and in particularTruncated mean CPI Will there be a clear decline from 3.6 per cent towards 3.0 per cent? This is the decisive factor in whether the RBA will raise interest rates for the fifth time in December. Long-term interest rates and policy in China: China Bond 10-year valuation and whether there have been any changes to the 1-year and 5-year LPRs (more precise valuations can be verified on the China Bond website at a later date). Commodities: The Singapore Exchange (SGX) iron ore swap benchmark contract and the Platts 62% Index, to gauge whether iron ore prices have bottomed out and stabilised. The Australian labour market: The unemployment rate in the ABS Monthly Labour Force Survey: the threshold is 4.8 per cent; monitor whether the rise is accelerating.
