entry.title: Daily Briefing | 23 October 2026: Escalating conflict in the Middle East pushes Brent crude above US$110; Meta’s cash flow turns negative, sparking concerns over AI funding | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeOn 22 October, both the energy and technology sectors came under pressure simultaneously. In the Middle East, *The New York Times* reported that the US and Israel had drawn up plans to resume air strikes against Iran following the US mid-term elections; the Iranian Revolutionary Guard claimed that several vessels in the Persian Gulf had been struck or hit by mines; and the Houthi rebels launched another attack on Dammam Airport in Saudi Arabia. Brent crude rose to a high not seen in over five months, closing at around US$113 per barrel. On the technology front, Meta reported negative quarterly free cash flow for the first time in over a decade, fuelling market concerns that AI infrastructure is being sustained by debt and share issues; the Nasdaq fell 2.6 per cent on the day, whilst the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.7 per cent. Funds were withdrawn from technology stocks and redirected towards defensive sectors such as US Treasuries and consumer staples, with the yield on 10-year US Treasuries falling back to around 5 per cent. Separately, two high-risk vulnerabilities in PHP that allow remote code execution were disclosed, one of which was discovered with the assistance of AI; China’s National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) issued a new version of the ‘Measures for the Administration of Outward Investment’; and following Russia’s agreement to resume negotiations, large-scale mutual attacks broke out between Russia and Ukraine that same evening.
Key News1. The US is reportedly planning to resume air strikes against Iran following the mid-term elections; attacks in the Gulf have pushed Brent crude to a five-month highThe New York Times, citing US officials, reported that the US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans to resume strikes against Iran following the US mid-term elections on 3 November. The operation has been described as “short and intense”, with targets likely to include energy facilities, nuclear facilities, and stockpiles of missiles and drones. On the same day, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy stated that four vessels involved in “illegal oil transfers” in the northern Persian Gulf had been struck and set alight, whilst three other vessels had struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz; it warned that it would launch a wider-ranging response against US bases in the region. In Saudi Arabia, the authorities attributed the attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam to the Houthi rebels; the attack left two people dead and eight injured. Saudi Arabia also reported that an Aramco oil field had come under attack. US State Department spokesperson Pigott stated that the non-essential personnel evacuation order issued the previous day applied only to Saudi Arabia, citing an increase in attacks by the Houthi rebels on civilian targets. Oil prices rose sharply on the day. During the Asian trading session, Brent crude rose by around 2.5 per cent to US$111.5, climbing to around US$113 before the close—an increase of approximately 4 per cent and its highest level in more than five months; WTI rose by around 2.3 per cent to around US$99.4. Since the outbreak of the conflict in Iran in late February, Brent has risen by more than 50 per cent in total. Key points to watch going forward include whether the US will publicly respond to reports of airstrike plans, the passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz and insurance premiums, as well as whether the Houthi rebels will continue to target Saudi airports and oil fields. Source:CNBC Africa、Just Security News Round-up (including links to reports from Reuters, the BBC and The Wall Street Journal)、Investing.com Market Close Review 2. Meta is ‘burning through cash’ for the first time in over a decade, bringing the issue of funding for AI infrastructure to the foreMeta’s third-quarter results, released the previous day, showed that capital expenditure for the quarter was close to US$35 billion, whilst free cash flow stood at a negative US$2.12 billion, compared with a positive US$10.63 billion a year earlier. According to Reuters, this marks the first time in over a decade that Meta has recorded a quarterly net cash outflow. The company has also raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure guidance from US$130 billion to US$135 billion, and plans to issue non-voting Class C shares to fund its AI investments. On 22 October, Meta’s share price fell by approximately 7 per cent – its steepest decline since July – whilst the price of its credit default swaps (CDS) hit a record high. The sell-off quickly spread across the entire AI sector. Lam Research fell by around 12 per cent following its earnings report, Nvidia dropped by around 4 per cent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell by 6.7 per cent, with chip stocks recording their worst single-day performance since late June. Emerging cloud service providers were hit even harder: CoreWeave fell by around 10 per cent, with yields on its unsecured bonds having already risen to 15 per cent the previous week; Nebius fell by around 7 per cent despite announcing a $3.5 billion credit facility from Citigroup. Analysts at Bank of America believe CoreWeave requires approximately US$20 billion in funding to fulfil its customer contracts. Matthew Maley of Miller Tabak stated that the core question for the market is the return on these investments, noting that returns may materialise more slowly than expected; he also pointed out that large companies have no shortage of financing channels, and that the real pressure lies with small and medium-sized AI firms. The significance of this development lies in the fact that market focus has shifted from ‘how much is being invested in AI’ to ‘who is funding it and at what cost’. With US Treasury yields still hovering around 5 per cent, the model of expanding computing power through debt and equity financing will come under closer scrutiny. Key points to watch: capital expenditure guidance in next week’s earnings reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, as well as refinancing developments at companies such as CoreWeave. Source:Reuters (reprinted by Investing.com) 3. Two high-severity vulnerabilities in PHP that allow remote code execution have been disclosed; AI played a part in their discoveryThe PHP team released a security update on 21 October, addressing two vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both are classified as ‘Critical’, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2; an attacker could execute code remotely on the server without needing to log in. The former relates to the incomplete initialisation of request data when memory is insufficient, whilst the latter relates to the misuse of a released request state by the subsequent request. Deployment methods such as PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are all affected, with mod_php posing the highest risk; the PHP team has demonstrated an exploit that can be triggered before application code executes. The official recommendation is to upgrade to versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and it is stated that temporary mitigation measures can only reduce the risk; they do not provide complete protection. On the same day, OpenAI disclosed that the security firm Calif had discovered one of the vulnerabilities using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, whilst Wiz had independently discovered and reported two others; the relevant fixes were led by PHP maintainers, following approximately two months of prior coordination. According to the BBC, the Finnish government temporarily shut down some online services at one point, whilst Edinburgh City Council and the BBC also took some pages offline to apply patches. PHP underpins a vast number of websites and content management systems; this incident demonstrates that AI has begun to play a practical role in vulnerability discovery, which may consequently narrow the time gap between attackers and defenders. Points to watch: whether the vulnerabilities will be exploited on a large scale in the wild, and how users of older, end-of-life PHP versions will manage the situation. Source:Official PHP Security Advisory、OpenAI 4. The National Development and Reform Commission has issued a new version of the ‘Measures for the Administration of Outward Investment’, which will come into force on 1 December.On 22 October, the National Development and Reform Commission published the ‘Measures for the Administration of Outward Investment’, comprising six chapters and 76 articles, divided into General Provisions, Guidance and Services for Outward Investment, Supervision of Outward Investment, Protection of Outward Investment, Legal Liability and Supplementary Provisions. The Measures shall come into force on 1 December 2026, The “Measures for the Administration of Overseas Investment by Enterprises”, issued in 2017, are repealed simultaneously. The new Measures define the scope of investors as domestic enterprises, other organisations and resident individuals, and support the conduct of outward investment in accordance with market principles; investors may continue to invest in overseas financial markets through channels such as QDII, Stock Connect and the Cross-Border Wealth Management Connect. With regard to the protection of rights and interests, the Measures have refined the reporting system for material adverse events and established an annual reporting system for outbound investment information, in response to discriminatory measures imposed by certain countries and regions requiring Chinese enterprises to provide technology, data or dispose of equity interests and assets. With regard to risk prevention, the Measures refine the reporting system for overseas reinvestment and establish a reporting system on preliminary work for projects involving substantial sums or those affecting bilateral diplomatic relations. This document has been issued against the backdrop of Chinese enterprises accelerating their expansion into overseas markets, whilst some countries are tightening their scrutiny of Chinese investment. The new regulations provide institutional support for enterprises expanding overseas, whilst also strengthening prior oversight of large-scale and sensitive projects; they will have a significant impact on sectors with extensive overseas operations, such as new energy, automotive and mining. Key points to watch: the specific operational guidelines for approval and filing procedures; whether the catalogue of sensitive projects will be adjusted; and the supporting regulations to be issued by the Ministry of Commerce and the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. Source:21 Economic Network (reprinted from CCTV News) 5. Just hours after the Russian side agreed to resume negotiations, large-scale attacks broke out between Russia and UkraineKremlin adviser Ushakov stated on 21 October that, following Putin’s meeting with US Special Envoy Witkov in St Petersburg, Putin had agreed in principle to resume trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November; this would be the first round of US-mediated negotiations since February. Zelenskyy expressed his support, though he remained cautious, saying, “Let’s see how this goes.” However, that same evening, Russian forces launched 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv in three waves and deployed drones, resulting in one death and 22 injuries. At least four people were killed across Ukraine, including two who died when a market in Lozova, Kharkiv Oblast, was struck. The Russian Ministry of Defence claimed to have shot down 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, whilst Moscow Mayor Sobyanin stated that 630 of them were heading towards the capital; as a result, flights to and from Moscow’s airports were temporarily restricted. The fact that negotiations are taking place alongside large-scale air strikes suggests that both sides are stepping up military pressure ahead of the talks in order to secure a more favourable negotiating position. From a market perspective, the Russia-Ukraine negotiations could ease the risk premium on European energy and refined oil products; however, until a ceasefire framework is finalised, such expectations of an easing remain uncertain. Key points to watch: the specific date and venue of the trilateral talks; whether an agreement on a mutual moratorium on strikes against energy infrastructure can be reached first; and whether air traffic and refineries around Moscow will continue to be affected. Source:Associated Press (reprinted by ClickOnDetroit)、Associated Press (reprinted by Arab News) Market Correlation and Today's ObservationOn 22 October, US equities exhibited a typical flight-to-safety trend: the S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent to 7,664.99 points, the Nasdaq dropped 2.6 per cent to 26,008.86 points—its worst performance since 5 June—whilst the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely unchanged; During the session, the consumer staples and healthcare sectors performed strongly, whilst the technology sector fell by nearly 3 per cent. Funds flowed into US Treasuries, with the 10-year yield falling by around 12 basis points at one point to dip below 5 per cent, having stood at around 5.13 per cent the previous day; Gold fell by approximately 2 per cent, whilst Bitcoin dipped below US$82,000. Initial jobless claims for the week fell to 194,000, a three-month low, indicating that the labour market remains stable; the recent decline was driven more by AI funding and geopolitical risks than by weakening economic data. Looking at several news stories from today in conjunction: whilst the situation in the Middle East has pushed up oil prices—which should have boosted inflation expectations and yields—US Treasury yields have instead fallen sharply. This suggests that the market is currently more concerned about the valuations of risk assets and financing pressures than about inflation. For the AI industry chain, the combined effects of high oil prices, high interest rates and uncertainty regarding returns on capital expenditure are placing the greatest pressure on emerging cloud service providers and semiconductor equipment stocks, which carry higher levels of debt. China’s revised regulations on outbound investment and the Russia-Ukraine negotiations, meanwhile, represent medium-term variables with limited short-term impact on the market. Checklist:
Official responses from the US or Israel to reports of ‘air strikes resuming after the election’, as well as shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and oil tanker insurance premiums Will Brent hold steady at $110, and will the yield on 10-year US Treasuries continue to fall back below 5 per cent? Capital expenditure and AI revenue figures in next week’s earnings reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, as well as trends in yields on Meta CDS and CoreWeave bonds Interest rate forecasts ahead of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy meeting on 28 October Supplementary Rules to the ‘Measures for the Administration of Outward Investment’ Will the trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine take place as scheduled after 10 November?
Source:Investing.com Market Close Review、Benzinga、Yahoo Finance Cover image:Anatoly Maltsev / Unsplash

entry.title: Consumption is no longer the defining feature of the US economy: how AI capital expenditure has become the ‘backbone’ of US GDP | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original.
Introduction: For a long time, global investors have held a deeply ingrained consensus regarding the US economy: ‘Consumption is life; without it, the economy dies’. Personal consumption expenditure (PCE) accounts for nearly 70 per cent of US GDP; as long as ordinary Americans continue to use their credit cards, the economic engine will not stall. However, the latest macroeconomic data released in 2026 paints a new reality that completely overturns this conventional wisdom:Consumer spending has taken a back seat; instead, the US economy is now underpinned by the proliferation of AI data centres, expensive GPU clusters and extensive power grids. Wall Street estimates suggest that nearly half of US economic growth this year has been driven directly by AI capital expenditure (Capex); under the most aggressive projections, this figure has even been estimated at a staggering 74 per cent. Exactly how many percentage points has AI investment contributed to growth? What would happen to the US economy if this colossal computing-power money-spinner were to suddenly grind to a halt? Are we reliving the old dream of the 1990s ‘trillion-fibre’ Great Leap Forward?
Prologue: The Emergence of a Single-Engine EconomyLet us first turn our attention to several sets of macroeconomic data officially finalised this year by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA):
The fourth quarter of 2025: The annualised quarter-on-quarter growth rate of US real GDP was only a meagre +0.5%, almost slipping to the brink of stagnation; First quarter of 2026: GDP growth suddenly rebounded strongly to +2.1%(Third estimate revised to +2.5 per cent); The second quarter of 2026: The final GDP figure remains stable at +2.2% the moderate range.
AI Data Centre Construction and Macro Capital Expenditure Figure 1Schematic illustration of AI capital expenditure (trading terminals and data centre server rooms): AI capital expenditure has evolved from an isolated commercial activity undertaken by tech giants into the primary driver of US macroeconomic growth. (Image source: TFTC / Ghost CDN) On the surface, this appears to be a standard report card on the US economy’s ‘soft landing’. Yet behind the spotlight, the structural pillars have undergone a historic fracture and reorganisation:The contribution to economic growth from household consumption—which had previously been the dominant driver—has been significantly squeezed, whilst investment in residential property has acted as a drag on growth for several consecutive quarters due to high mortgage interest rates of 7.5 per cent.The only driving force that will prevent the US economy from plunging into recession in 2026 is the AI infrastructure development on which the tech giants are betting heavily, regardless of the cost. As Bridgewater asserted in its macroeconomic research report:The US economy is becoming a giant ship powered by a single engine—and that sole pillar of support is known as AI capital expenditure. 1. The ‘74 per cent’ controversy: How many percentage points has AI actually contributed to the US economy?In the debate between the financial community and macroeconomists, ‘Just how much has AI actually contributed to GDP growth?’ is currently the most contentious and revealing topic. The conclusions circulating in the market range from 30% to 74% or even higher, depending on the circumstances. How on earth did this vast range of figures come about? We must break it down into four distinctly different statistical methodologies: Scenario 1: TFTC’s ‘74 per cent’ – the broadest scenario (radical projection)This summer, the renowned macroeconomic analysis organisation TFTC calculated, based on the Bureau of Economic Analysis’ (BEA) National Income and Product Accounts for the first quarter of 2026 (NIPA Table 1.5.2), that:Investment in AI data centre construction and software accounted for nearly 74 per cent of US GDP growth in the first quarter. The algorithm is extremely straightforward and crude:In the first quarter, the annualised contribution to US real GDP growth was 2.1 percentage points. TFTC directly extracted two major sub-categories from fixed asset investment—Information processing equipment(including data centre servers, network hardware and GPU clusters) contributed approximately 0.65 percentage points, plusIntellectual Property Products(primarily in AI training and enterprise-level software development) contributed approximately 0.90 percentage points, with the two combined totalling 1.55 percentage points。1.55% ÷ 2.10% ≈ 73.8% ≈ 74%
Reasonableness: The St. Louis Fed also used the same sub-components as proxy variables for tracking AI in a special report published in January this year; this methodology has precedents at central bank level; Weak points: These two broad categories fall under the ‘broad IT basket’ and inevitably include traditional non-AI software and standard office equipment procurement; they represent the broadest possible upper limit in analysts’ projections.
Measure 2: The Federal Reserve’s (Fed) rigorous net contribution measure (30 per cent–50 per cent)On 17 July 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published a landmark research note entitled ‘AI Development and the Macroeconomy’ (The AI Buildout and the Economy). Economists at the Federal Reserve have developed a more sophisticated proxy model: one that tracks four major sub-sectors simultaneously—software, data centre construction, electricity infrastructure and computing equipment—butIt specifically excluded the negative impact of the sharp rise in imported components on net exports.。 Federal Reserve, FEDS Notes, Figure 7: Analysis of the quarterly contribution of key AI components to US GDP growth Figure 2The quarterly contribution of the Federal Reserve’s AI investment agent index (software + data centre construction + electricity infrastructure + IT computing equipment) to real GDP. The net effect (black line) shows a significant contribution, but this is subject to considerable volatility due to drag from net exports, such as server imports. (Data and chart: Federal Reserve Board / BEA, FEDS Notes 17 July 2026) The conclusion reached by the Federal Reserve is highly enlightening:The boost from gross investment in AI development has indeed been exceptionally strong; however, as a large proportion of server components rely on overseas supply chains, the surge in imports has, in some quarters, directly offset half of the total investment contribution. After adjusting for import leakage,The actual contribution of net investment in AI to US GDP growth falls within the range of approximately 30 per cent to 50 per cent。 More importantly, the Federal Reserve was quite forthright in its report:“As of 2026, no widespread signs of technological transformation have yet been observed in aggregate macroeconomic productivity data.” In other words, current GDP is purely the result of massive investment in ‘infrastructure construction’ using real money; the cost-saving and efficiency-boosting benefits of AI technology itself are still far from being realised at the macro level. Source 3: Bridgewater’s 1.4 percentage point median (approximately 50 per cent)Greg Jensen, Chief Investment Officer at Bridgewater, and others have calculated that:AI capital expenditure directly contributed to approximately 1.4 percentage points of US GDP growth in 2026; this accounted for a full half (50 per cent) of the projected annual growth of 2.8 per cent. They forecast that by 2027, this boost will have increased further to 1.5 percentage points. This level is now fully on a par with the intensity of business investment seen during the internet boom of the 1990s. Perspective 4: Goldman Sachs’ global trillion-dollar outlookJoseph Briggs, a macroeconomist at Goldman Sachs, has calculated this based on the total money supply:In 2026, total global investment in AI-related sectors is set to officially exceed US$1 trillion (>$1T), with the United States alone accounting for US$581 billion ($581B) of this figure.
Statistical and Analytical Criteria Calculated contribution percentage / amount Core Methodology and Features Key Limitations and Notes
TFTC Aggressive Upper Limit Calibre ~74%（Q1 2026） NIPA Table 1.5.2: Direct sum of the ‘software’ and ‘hardware’ sub-items (contributing 1.55 percentage points / 2.1 per cent) Includes non-AI traditional IT and software procurement; the scope is rather broad
Federal Reserve (Fed) – strict net basis 30% – 50%(Dynamic fluctuations) Based on a comprehensive analysis of four categories of factors, the negative impact of import leakage in servers and components on net exports has been excluded. The net effect is subject to significant quarterly fluctuations due to the trade deficit, indicating that productivity gains have yet to materialise
Bridgewater Headquarters ~50%(Contributing approximately 1.4 percentage points over the year) This includes profit distribution by chip giants and combined investment in software and hardware, which is expected to account for half of the full-year growth. The most widely cited benchmark in the market forecasts a figure of 1.5 percentage points by 2027
Goldman Sachs’ Macro Perspective United States $581B(Global > $1T) Global Top-Down Capital Expenditure Statistics Measuring the total stock of funds, rather than the marginal change in GDP for a single quarter
An objective conclusion for the general reader：As for the question ‘Exactly how many percentage points has AI contributed?’, the honest answer is oneInterval—Even using the Federal Reserve’s most conservative net measure, AI is driving between 30 per cent and 50 per cent of economic growth across the United States; according to the widely cited central estimate,This year, one in every two dollars of growth in the US is attributable to AI capital expenditure。 In peacetime—when there is no war and the government is not actively pursuing a massive 4 trillion infrastructure programme—the private sector’s capital expenditure in a single industry alone accounts for nearly half of a major economy’s growth; this is an extremely rare occurrence in modern economic history. II. The Microfoundations of the Trillion-Yuan Infrastructure Programme: From the Five Giants to the 100-Billion-Yuan Computing Power ChainThis colossal macro-level load-bearing pillar has been built, at the micro-level, by a succession of technology giants through a series of irrevocable, binding contracts. Federal Reserve (FED) Notes, Figure 4: Explosive rise in quarterly capital expenditure by major tech giants Figure 3Trends in quarterly capital expenditure among major tech giants (hyperscalers): from approximately US$3 billion to US$5 billion per quarter in 2019, soaring to the epic scale of tens of billions of US dollars per quarter per company today. (Data: SEC 10-Q filings / Federal Reserve Board) 1. The spending arms race amongst the five tech giantsAccording to the latest financial results and guidance disclosed by major technology companies:
Microsoft: The capital expenditure guidance for the 2026 calendar year has been raised directly to Approximately US$190 billion ($190B), a staggering 61 per cent year-on-year increase, with expenditure by a single company exceeding market expectations by US$35 billion; Amazon: Annualised capital expenditure is also surging towards Approximately US$200 billion ($200B) High; Statistics show that the total capital expenditure of the world’s five largest cloud giants, including Alphabet (Google) and Meta, for the year 2026 alone will amount to US$700 billion to US$725 billion ($700B–$725B) astronomical range.
Leading think tank A specialised study published by Epoch AI Further evidence of this dramatic change:At present, AI-related capital formation alone (data centre construction and hardware equipment) accounts for approximately 0.8 per cent of US GDP, driving the share of the entire computing infrastructure in GDP up to 1.5 per cent.— Compared with the historical average of just 0.7 per cent between 2015 and 2022, this represents a staggering ‘doubling surge’. 2. A follow-up to the previous instalment: The chain of computational debt among micro-entitiesThe microscopic foundation of this macro-level pillar is precisely those two cutting-edge large-model unicorns that we dissected in our previous two in-depth analyses:
Anthropic: The draft prospectus reveals that the company is burdened with debt spanning approximately 10 years and amounting to as much as US$518 billion ($518B) firm commitments to purchase computing power, of which nearly 80 per cent (US$413.7 billion) are fully irrevocable, binding contracts; OpenAI: In 2025 alone, expenditure on cloud computing power for Microsoft Azure is set to reach as much as US$17.2 billion, whilst the total budget for the long-term computing infrastructure plan up to 2030 is a staggering US$856 billion ($856B)… and have even joined forces to spearhead the US$500 billion ‘Stargate’ supercomputing project.
The total long-term computing power debt committed by the two companies alone has already surpassed the total annual investment in AI across the United States. This closed loop—where ‘buyers sign massive, irrevocable commitments ➔ cloud service providers frantically snap up land to build data centres ➔ chip manufacturers ramp up production to full capacity’—has directly endowed this capital expenditure with an extremely strong, unstoppable momentum: the arrow is on the string; no one can stop it now. III. Counterfactual analysis: What would happen if AI capital expenditure were to come to a halt?The simplest way to assess just how important a column is, is to carry out aCounterfactual Analysis: Assuming that the major players stop stepping up their investments tomorrow, and this pillar is removed or scaled back, what would happen to the US economy? Based on the verified data model, we can clearly deduce three levels of mechanical impact:
Impact Levels Assumptions Transmission mechanisms and economic consequences
Impact 1: Slowdown in growth Zero growth in capital expenditure (capex) or a 20 per cent contraction in the existing stock The 1.4pp increase projected by Bridgewater has effectively evaporated; nearly half of the US’s GDP growth for the quarter has been wiped out, and should it contract by 20 per cent, it would fall by more than 1 percentage point, bringing the economy to the brink of recession; the +0.5 per cent figure for Q4 2025 represents the true underlying trend once the impact of AI is factored out.
Impact 2: Employment and Regional Shock The investment slowdown is being felt across the real economy’s industrial chain Data centres are, by their very nature, a heavy industry: electrical installation, specialist electricians and heavy-duty HVAC systems are all under significant strain; the impact is concentrated in ‘computing corridors’ such as Northern Virginia, Texas and Arizona, where the retreat of capital-intensive industries has given rise to political pressure on local finances and employment.
Impact 3: The ratchet effect in factor prices Even if spending returns to normal The electricity grid connection quotas, industrial land and water prices—which were fiercely contested in the early stages—exhibit extremely high stickiness; the utility bills for households and the manufacturing sector, which have been driven up, are unlikely to fall rapidly; “stalling growth coupled with soaring costs” is leading to a slide into the quagmire of stagflation.
The impact is transmitted from top to bottom in three stages: the first stage is immediate (data for the current quarter); the second stage is delayed by 2–4 quarters (the project construction cycle); and the third stage is the most enduring (the ratchet effect of factor prices).
Growth halved in an instant：AI capital expenditure contributed 1.4 percentage points to the full-year growth rate.If AI capital expenditure were merely to ‘stop growing’ (with the growth rate falling to zero whilst absolute investment levels remained unchanged), the US GDP growth rate for that quarter would be wiped out by nearly half.; If tech giants were to cut their overall budgets by 20 per cent due to pressure on profits, US real GDP would contract by more than one percentage point, instantly pushing the economy to the brink of recession. That +0.5 per cent figure for the fourth quarter of 2025 – which narrowly avoided turning negative – represents the true underlying decline in the US real economy once the AI frenzy is factored out.
Heavy Industry and the Local Economic Shock：Contrary to the widespread belief that ‘AI is merely a virtual economy that writes code’, today’s data centres are, in essence, aA Celebration of Heavy Industry and Civil Engineering. The procurement of high-voltage substations, industrial chillers and standby diesel generator sets has sustained a large number of mid-to-high-end manufacturing and specialist construction teams across the United States. Should investment dry up, key hubs such as Northern Virginia’s ‘Data Centre Corridor’ would immediately face a wave of stalled projects and mass redundancies in the construction sector.
The ‘ratchet effect’ of factor costs：Austan Goolsbee, President of the Chicago Federal Reserve, recently issued an extremely sobering warning:Data centres are encroaching on the electricity, land and water resources essential to ordinary households and the manufacturing sector in every conceivable way. Even if tech giants were to suddenly cut back on spending in the future, the inflated peak-hour electricity prices, grid modernisation surcharges and industrial land rents are highly inelastic and would not fall in tandem. The real economy would be forced to bear the bitter consequences of rising input costs for the long term, without reaping the benefits of an AI boom.
IV. Echoes of History: A Fateful Comparison with the ‘Great Leap Forward’ in Telecommunications Fibre Optics in the 1990sToday’s AI frenzy is not the first time humanity has staked the macro-level fate of a nation on a high-stakes gamble involving communications and computing infrastructure. Thirty years ago, a similar scenario played out in an almost identical manner amidst the telecommunications and internet boom. ARK Invest: A comparison of AI capital expenditure as a proportion of GDP with the railway boom of 1873 Figure 4Historical comparison of capital expenditure on cutting-edge technology as a proportion of GDP: the current rate of growth in AI capital expenditure has surpassed that of the US railway construction cycle in 1873. (Source: ARK Invest via Fortune) 1. 1996–2001: The Sensational Story of the Fibre-Optic BubbleIn the mid-to-late 1990s, under the banner of the ‘Information Superhighway’:
Global telecoms operators and fibre-optic giants have collectively blown through Approximately 2 trillion US dollars ($2T) With its vast capital, it has laid more than 85 million miles advanced fibre-optic cables; The proportion of telecoms capital expenditure to GDP in the US peaked at 1.0 per cent to 1.2 per cent… which fuelled the economic boom of the latter part of the Clinton era.
However, when commercial demand failed to keep pace with the frenetic supply of technology, a brutal downturn ensued:
In 2002, what was then the largest case of financial fraud and bankruptcy in US history—WorldCom’s spectacular collapse… as giants such as Global Crossing collapsed one after another, the telecoms sector saw nearly US$2 trillion wiped off its market capitalisation; Exactly four years after the bubble burst, a survey revealed that of the fibre-optic cables laid across the United States that year,As many as 85 per cent to 95 per cent have never been activated or used, and have become ‘dark fibre’ lying dormant underground.。
But the most ironic twist in history is this:It was precisely this vast network of dark fibre—abandoned by bankrupt companies and virtually a free find—that provided an extremely cheap and ahead-of-its-time physical foundation for the rise, after 2005, of high-definition video streaming services (YouTube, Netflix), the mobile internet via smartphones, and the first generation of modern cloud computing services (AWS).The pioneers bled and went bankrupt, ultimately paving the way for the subsequent boom in innovation. 2. Similarities and differences this time round: why is AI more fragile than fibre optics?
Dimensions of comparison The Great Leap Forward in Telecommunications Fibre Optics in the 1990s Major Expansion of AI Data Centres in the 2020s Potential Risks and Differences in Mechanisms
Peak as a percentage of GDP Approx. 1.0% – 1.2% The current total is 1.4% – 1.5% Both are part of a ‘super technology cycle’ that is reshaping the national macro-investment structure.
Authenticity of underlying technology It’s true: the internet has completely transformed the world. Indeed, large language models are becoming a new form of productive capacity. Technology itself is not a scam; rather, it is the pace at which capital is being drawn down prematurely that is excessive.
Equipment manufacturer’s cycle amplifier Nortel, Lucent Nvidia, Broadcom Equipment suppliers, acting as monopolists, reap the largest profits in the entire industry, thereby amplifying the capital-chasing effect
Physical depreciation attributes of assets Extremely durable: As glass fibre buried underground is not subject to wear and tear, maintenance costs are virtually zero; we are waiting for demand to catch up. Rapid depreciation：The depreciation cycle for GPU chips is only 3 to 5 years, As the next-generation computing architecture evolves rapidly, hardware that has backed the wrong horse will face obsolescence and be phased out. ⚠️ The balance sheets of this round of AI infrastructure are far more vulnerable than those of fibre-optic networks
Financing Structure Models Telecom operators increased their leverage through large-scale corporate bond issues (which ultimately led to a collapse as they were forced to roll over their debt). In the early stages, it was underpinned by the tech giants’ abundant operating cash flow and cloud profits Rapid ‘debtification’ is underway: Anthropic and OpenAI are accumulating computing power liabilities running into tens of billions or even hundreds of billions
Macroeconomic Monetary Environment In the latter stages of the bubble, Federal Reserve Chairman Greenspan had ampleRoom for interest rate cuts The Federal Reserve is mired in the battle against inflation(With the base rate remaining high at 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent, and expectations of further rate rises still present) External financing costs are extremely high, and there is no low-interest safety net to rescue the market
The most crucial difference lies precisely inDepreciation period：Even though it took eight years for Netflix to arrive on the fibre-optic cables laid underground all those years ago, the cables remained in perfect condition; but today, the millions of state-of-the-art GPUs piled up in data centres,Within three years, depreciation costs will be whizzing past on the profit and loss account, and within five years, the next generation of manufacturing processes will ruthlessly render them obsolete in terms of computing power-to-energy efficiency ratio.. AI Capital does not have the luxury of patience to wait a full decade for demand to develop naturally. V. The Physical Ceiling and the Macroeconomic Closed Loop: The Thirst for Electricity is Driving Up InflationIf the slow pace of commercialisation in the software sector is a hidden concern from a business perspective, then the most brutal challenge currently facing AI capital expenditure is a series of ruthlessUpper limits in physics and engineering。 1. A 33-gigawatt grid bottleneck and transformer delivery schedules spanning nearly three yearsIn an in-depth special report published in October 2026, Morgan Stanley calculated a set of figures regarding the skills gap that left Silicon Valley engineers breathless:
It is estimated that by 2028, the additional electricity demand from data centres across the US will reach as high as 97 GW (gigawatts)； Even if all the accelerated schemes for on-site power generation (industrial gas turbines, solid oxide fuel cells, and even attempts to restart small nuclear reactors) were taken fully into account, the US power grid could, at best, barely muster an additional 24 GW; Data centres across the US face an insurmountable net power shortfall of between 32 and 33 GW (equivalent to 34 per cent of total demand being at risk of power cuts).。
Accompanying the power shortfall is a supply disruption and severe congestion in the global heavy electrical equipment supply chain:According to an authoritative industry survey by Wood Mackenzie, the current cost of purchasing a unit in North America isThe standard delivery lead time for large power transformers (LPTs) is as long as 128 weeks (nearly 2.5 years), whilst the generator step-up transformer is as long as 144 weeks (nearly 3 years)! Whereas in 2020, this lead time was just 6 to 12 weeks. Gartner’s research further predicts that, within the next year, there will be 40 per cent of new AI data centres are directly affected by the suspension of electricity supply quotas… as many as half of the planning projects are facing substantial delays. 2. The Federal Reserve’s closed-loop warning: ‘AI is driving up inflation’This scramble for physical resources is not only curbing the expansion of technology companies, but has also come directly to the attention of the Federal Reserve: In the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s September FOMC meeting, a single line was formally included in the record of the entire Monetary Policy Committee:“Geopolitical developments and the surge in AI-related investment are jointly driving up inflationary pressures (AI-related investments were pushing up inflationary pressures).” Public statements by Federal Reserve officials no longer conceal their concerns:
Beth Hammack, President of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, pointed out that, in order to secure access to the grid, tech giants are willing to ‘write any exorbitant cheque’ for even mediocre electrical switchgear; Austan Goolsbee, President of the Chicago Fed, went so far as to state outright that AI is causing inflation“It is breaking out of its original narrow technological niche”… leading to a classic case of overheating in macroeconomic demand across the cement, steel, specialised copper products, electricity and labour markets.
This creates an absurd and dangerousMacro-level infinite loop：
In order to maintain their competitive position, tech giants are pushing ahead with capital expenditure totalling hundreds of billions; The infrastructure boom and energy shortages have directly driven up electricity and input inflation; Inflationary stickiness is forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain high interest rates and even continue raising them (currently at 3.75 per cent–4.00 per cent); High interest rates, in turn, have driven up the cost of borrowing for tech giants and the cost of financing for the real economy; Ultimately, this high-cost pillar supporting GDP became an increasingly heavy burden and increasingly difficult to sustain.
VI. Future Scenarios: Three Possible Fates for AI-Powered Load-Bearing ColumnsIn light of the forthcoming third-quarter GDP figures and the technology giants’ capital guidance for the coming year, the trajectory of this pillar of support presents the following three probability distributions:
Role-play scenario Probability of occurrence Core trigger thresholds for macroeconomic and fundamental factors The Ultimate Significance of the Economy and Capital Markets
Scenario A(The load-bearing columns are sturdy) ~55%(Base case) • The Q3 GDP figures released on 29 October confirmed that fixed investment continues to show robust positive growth;• The five tech giants have maintained their capital expenditure guidance at the US$700 billion level in their November earnings reports, showing no sign of backing down;• On-site power generation and nuclear energy solutions are gradually being implemented, providing temporary relief from electricity shortages. Single-engine continuation: US GDP as a whole remains within the 2.0 per cent–2.5 per cent range, with AI capital expenditure continuing to account for nearly half of the growth. Concerns about a ‘coexistence of prosperity and overheating’ are lingering, but there is no risk of a systemic recession in the short term.
Scenario B(The engine suddenly cut out) ~25%(Risk scenarios) • Commercialisation and monetisation by large-scale model companies have fallen far short of expectations, forcing the industry giants to scale back their capital budgets in the second half of the year;• Delays in grid connection exceeding 50 per cent have resulted in a large number of projects being put on hold;• Persistently high interest rates have caused the highly leveraged computing power debt chain to collapse. Cliff-face landslide: With AI investment growth turning negative and US GDP growth rapidly falling below 1.0 per cent, the truth behind the economy’s decline has been laid bare. The Federal Reserve may be forced to swiftly adjust its monetary policy towards interest rate cuts, or even consider introducing liquidity support measures.
Scenario C(Productivity fully realised) ~20%(Better than expected) • Data from the Bureau of Labour Statistics (BLS) has, for the first time, shown that labour productivity growth in sectors with high exposure to AI—such as finance, software and biotechnology—has exceeded 2.0 per cent for several consecutive quarters;• Intelligent agents and enterprise workflows have fully realised a self-sustaining commercial ecosystem. A historic leap forward: The current trillion-scale capital expenditure has been officially recognised as laying the foundations for a great, forward-looking strategy; the ‘AI bubble’ theory has been thoroughly debunked, reviving the narrative of the ultimate boom seen in the fibre-optic and internet eras.
VII. Honest Explanation of Data Definitions (Key Delimitations and Prudential Statements)When reading through all the arguments presented in this report, readers are urged to exercise sound academic judgement:
The BEA does not have a separate ‘AI industry statistical category’: All references in the text to “AI contributing 74 per cent” or “contributing 1.4 percentage points” are analytical conclusions derived by leading financial institutions and think tanks using proxy variables from NIPA sub-categories and bottom-up supply chain decomposition models; they do not constitute official statistical definitions issued by the US government; Bridgewater’s research reports contain elements of commercial copyright paraphrasing: Key figures, such as its 1.4 percentage point contribution in 2026 and the $650 billion investment by Big Tech, are derived from cross-referenced and verified reports by authoritative financial media outlets and macroeconomists; Forward-looking and time-sensitive constraints: The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) will officially release the advance estimate of real GDP for the third quarter of 2026 to the global community on 29 October; at that time, the extent to which AI capital expenditure drives the economy in the second half of the year will undergo a fresh round of stress testing based on objective data.
Conclusion: Do not mistake the scaffolding for the building itselfReturning to the original question: is consumption no longer the driving force behind the US economy? Judging by the marginal increase in aggregate output, this is certainly the case. Over the past year and a half, it has been the trillion-yuan gambles taken by several tech giants that have single-handedly pulled the US economy back from the brink of a slowdown. In this sense, AI capital expenditure is indeed a well-deserved ‘pillar of support’. Yet every serious economist is well aware that:Capital expenditure is, in essence, merely the ‘scaffolding’ used when constructing a building; it can never replace the building itself.The ultimate aim behind companies’ willingness to splash out hundreds of billions of dollars annually on chips and power stations must be to achieve a genuine leap in purchasing power and efficiency across both the consumer and production sectors of society. If, three years from now, when this computing power edifice—built with a trillion dollars—is finally completed, there are still only a handful of companies paying for it from outside the door, whilst inside there is a pile of overheating silicon wafers facing a three-year obsolescence cycle, then this sturdy load-bearing pillar could, overnight, become the heaviest blow to the US economy. The two giants of the large-scale model sector are heading for the public capital markets, whilst tech giants are securing power contracts for the next decade. Is this trillion-dollar gamble a major industrial revolution set to reshape the world, or a fibre-optic-style tragedy-comedy for which American utilities will ultimately foot the bill? The answer lies in the bills over the next two years. Main Sources of Information and Verification Index Federal Reserve Official Economic Research Notes (FEDS Notes, 17 July 2026): The AI Buildout and the Economy TFTC In-depth Macroeconomic Survey Report: AI Capital Expenditure Drove 74 per cent of Q1 2026 GDP Growth (BEA Third Estimate Analysis) Epoch AI Think Tank Report (5 June 2026): AI data centres’ share of GDP Bridgewater’s Macro Analysis (verified via a repost from Edward Conard’s Macro Roundup): The Macro Implications of the AI Capex Boom Goldman Sachs Global Economic Research Report: Global AI Investment is Forecast to Exceed $1 Trillion in 2026 St. Louis Fed Macro Tracker: Tracking AI’s Contribution to GDP Growth Morgan Stanley Industry Report on Power Shortages (5 October 2026): AI Data Centre Power Grid Shortfall Fortune column (Liaquat Ahamed, 2 June 2026): A comparison between the 1873 railway boom bubble and the AI infrastructure boom (chart source: ARK Invest) Minutes of the Federal Reserve’s September FOMC Monetary Policy Meeting (published on 7 October 2026)

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 24 October 2026: Brent crude nears US$117; US expands technology investment restrictions on China; OpenAI plans to raise funds at a valuation of US$1.25 trillion | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeOver the past 48 hours, oil prices have remained the dominant theme in global markets. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard claimed that several more oil tankers had been struck in the Gulf, whilst Saudi Aramco evacuated staff from its Dammam headquarters and switched to remote working. On 23 October, Brent crude closed at around US$116.70 per barrel, up approximately 3 per cent on the day. Trump invoked the Defence Production Act to allocate up to US$150 million to expand refining capacity, but this failed to curb oil prices. US consumer confidence remained at a five-month low, whilst one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7 per cent; ahead of the Federal Reserve’s meeting next week, market bets on a further interest rate hike this year have not subsided. On the technology and geopolitical fronts, the US Treasury Department proposed expanding foreign investment review rules to include supercomputing, hypersonic technology and biotechnology within the scope of restrictions; OpenAI is reportedly in talks to raise up to US$30 billion at a valuation of US$1.25 trillion, with the valuation and funding issues of AI companies continuing to attract attention. Domestically, the State Council’s Executive Meeting examined population, economic and social development, and made arrangements to promote the expansion and quality improvement of the service sector.
Key News1. Amid a series of statements regarding attacks in the Gulf, Brent crude closed at around US$116.7, whilst the US invoked the Defence Production Act to boost fuel productionOn 22 October, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy stated that four oil tankers engaged in oil transhipment in the northern Persian Gulf had been struck, whilst three other vessels had struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz; The Associated Press was unable to verify these claims, whilst Mr Trump alleged that Iran was “fabricating attacks” ahead of the mid-term elections to drive up oil prices. According to CBS, citing Reuters, Saudi Aramco has instructed staff at its Dammam headquarters to evacuate and work remotely. The Houthi rebels claimed to have carried out four attacks within Saudi Arabia in 48 hours, including one on the Ministry of Defence building in Riyadh; the Saudi-led coalition stated that it had intercepted four drones over Riyadh and Medina. Furthermore, according to a report by TheStreet, Iran has warned that it will target energy infrastructure in the Gulf should it come under further attack. Against this backdrop, oil prices have risen consecutively. Brent crude closed at US$113.17 on 22 October and rose by a further 3.1 per cent on 23 October, closing at around US$116.7; according to the Associated Press, Brent crude was still trading below US$97 in early October. On 22 October, Mr Trump signed a presidential memorandum in Ohio, invoking the Defence Production Act to designate oil production, refining, transport and storage facilities as ‘essential to national security’, and allocated up to US$150 million to expand refining capacity and increase diesel and petrol output. This funding represents a very small proportion of the national fuel market and is unlikely to alter supply and demand in the short term. The buffer is also shrinking. According to Al Jazeera, citing data from the US Department of Energy, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to approximately 283 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982; analysts estimate that global available emergency reserves stand at only around 400 million barrels, nearly half of which are in Japan. Key points to watch: whether the Saudi East–West Pipeline (which Aramco says has increased its throughput from 2 million to 7 million barrels per day) can remain operational; the number of vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz; and whether the US will take action against Iran following the 3 November election. Source:Associated Press (reprinted by the Times Leader)、FinanceFeeds、Seoul Economic Daily、Al Jazeera 2. The US Treasury Department plans to extend restrictions on overseas investment, with biotechnology included for the first timeOn 22 October, the US Treasury Department issued proposed rules to expand the scope of the ‘Foreign Investment Security Programme’ in order to implement the Comprehensive Overseas Investment National Security Act (COINS Act), which comes into force in December 2025 alongside the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defence Authorisation Act. The proposed rules cover semiconductors and microelectronics, artificial intelligence (referred to in the rules as ‘super-intelligent systems’), quantum information technology, high-performance computing and supercomputing, and hypersonic systems; the Treasury has also invoked a separate authorisation to include biotechnology. “Countries of concern” include China (including Hong Kong and Macao), Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuela under the Maduro regime. Treasury Secretary Bessent stated that the rules are intended to prevent adversaries from exploiting US investment to develop critical technologies. The deadline for public comments is 7 December; until the final rules are issued, the current regulations will continue to apply. The provisions on biotechnology have provoked the strongest reaction. According to STAT, citing the research organisation Veda, the proposed rules would prohibit US companies from engaging in relevant financial transactions with Chinese biotechnology firms and their equipment and tool suppliers; however, US pharmaceutical companies would still be permitted to licence or purchase drug rights from China. Over the past two years, US pharmaceutical firms have imported a significant number of innovative medicines from China. If this rule is implemented in its current form, the channels for US dollar financing available to innovative Chinese pharmaceutical firms would be further restricted, and cross-border licensing deals may become the primary remaining form of cooperation. Key points to watch going forward include lobbying by the industry during the public consultation period, the effective date of the final rule, and the response from China’s Ministry of Commerce. Source:Unite.AI、STAT 3. OpenAI is reportedly in talks to raise up to US$30 billion at a valuation of US$1.25 trillionAccording to TechCrunch, citing CNBC, OpenAI is in talks for a new round of private funding of up to US$30 billion, with a pre-money valuation of US$1.25 trillion. The round is being led by Coatue, with participation from investors in the United Arab Emirates; the UAE funding may be linked to an agreement to provide OpenAI with additional computing power. OpenAI’s valuation stood at US$852 billion following its funding round in March this year. The company had quietly filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June but has now opted to pursue private funding first. The terms are still under negotiation, and OpenAI has declined to comment. A month ago, Bloomberg reported on a similar funding plan with a valuation of US$1.4 trillion; the figure this time is lower. According to CNBC, Anthropic—which raised US$65 billion in May at a valuation of US$965 billion—is seeking to go public at a valuation of between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion. This funding round comes during a week in which AI shares have come under pressure. Following Meta’s shift to negative free cash flow, the market has begun to question who will fund AI investments and how long it will take to see a return. Should OpenAI secure funding at a valuation exceeding US$1 trillion, it would become the highest-valued private company in history, demonstrating that demand in the private equity market for leading model developers remains strong; A valuation lower than the figure reported last month would suggest that investors are driving down the price. Key points to watch going forward include the final post-funding valuation, the specific details of the computing power agreement with the UAE, and the IPO timetables for OpenAI and Anthropic. Source:TechCrunch 4. Executive Meeting of the State Council: Coordinating population development with economic and social development, and promoting the expansion and quality improvement of the service sectorOn 23 October, Li Qiang, Premier of the State Council, presided over a meeting of the State Council Executive Meeting to examine work relating to the coordinated development of the population and the economy and society, and to hear a report on the implementation of the decisions made at the National Conference on the Service Sector. With regard to population matters, the meeting proposed leveraging the ‘comprehensive demographic dividend’ to underpin high-quality development. It called for enhancing the quality of the population, improving lifelong learning and skills training, and promoting high-quality and full employment. It also called for optimising the layout of infrastructure in accordance with population distribution, building a fertility-friendly society, and refining supporting policies on marriage, childbirth, child-rearing and education, with a view to stabilising the size of the newborn population. With regard to the service sector, the meeting called for strengthened support in areas such as financing, land use, talent and data; the steady advancement of price reforms in public utilities; the revitalisation of idle resources; the removal of market access barriers; and the elimination of hidden barriers to private investment. It also encouraged the expansion of investment in the service sector and the realisation of the potential for service consumption, supported eligible localities in piloting innovative measures, and called for the improvement of the statistical monitoring system for the service sector. This meeting continued the recent policy approach of prioritising consumption and the service sector. Total retail sales of consumer goods grew by only around 1.1 per cent in the first three quarters, with consumption of goods remaining weak; service consumption and population policy are being treated as long-term levers for stabilising domestic demand. “Public utility price reform” is worth noting, as it may involve price adjustments for water, electricity and gas, which will affect both household expenditure and the profitability of public utility companies. The meeting did not specify the scale of funding. Key points to watch in the coming period include specific measures to support childbirth, detailed rules on liberalising market access for the service sector, and consumption data for the fourth quarter. Source:China News Network、People’s Daily Online 5. US consumer confidence remains at a five-month low, whilst inflation expectations continue to riseThe final October consumer confidence index released by the University of Michigan on 23 October stood at 48.0, higher than the preliminary reading of 46.3 but slightly below September’s figure of 48.1, and remains the lowest in five months. One-year inflation expectations rose from 4.6 per cent to 4.7 per cent, whilst long-term inflation expectations rose from 3.4 per cent to 3.5 per cent. The current conditions index in the preliminary reading stood at 44.7, a record low; in the final reading, the sub-index for conditions for purchasing durable goods fell sharply by 18 per cent. The data suggests that rising oil prices are simultaneously dampening consumer sentiment and fuelling inflation expectations—a combination that poses the greatest challenge for the Federal Reserve. According to the Associated Press, US inflation remains well above 3 per cent. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates at its last meeting, and the market expects it to hold rates steady at the meeting on 28 October, though there is a stronger inclination towards a further rate rise in December. Key points to watch: the Fed’s statement next week regarding the impact of energy prices, and the inflation data to be released subsequently. Source:Trading Economics、Associated Press (reprinted by the Times Leader) Market Correlation and Today's ObservationOn 23 October, US shares continued to fall, with the main downward pressure this time coming from oil prices rather than technology shares. The S&P 500 index fell 0.5 per cent to 7,623.68 points, marking its second consecutive week of losses; the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent (652.82 points) to 52,215.16 points; and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.2 per cent to 25,955.34 points. Nearly three-quarters of S&P 500 constituents fell, with energy stocks leading the decline: ConocoPhillips rose 3.6 per cent and Chevron rose 2.9 per cent; following the previous day’s sharp fall, Micron, AMD and Intel rebounded slightly. Although American Express reported better-than-expected profits, it announced its first large-scale redundancies in around a decade, causing its share price to fall by 3.7 per cent. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose slightly from 4.96 per cent to 4.99 per cent. Looking at several news items together: rising oil prices affect interest rates via inflation expectations, and in turn affect demand via consumer confidence; it is difficult for the Federal Reserve to prop up the economy through interest rate cuts, and high interest rates will continue to drive up the cost of financing for AI infrastructure. OpenAI’s fundraising at a valuation exceeding US$1 trillion demonstrates that demand for leading AI companies in the primary market remains strong, whilst the secondary market has adopted a more cautious stance towards AI capital expenditure. The US has expanded its restrictions on outward investment; in the short term, the impact on A-shares and Hong Kong stocks will be concentrated primarily in the innovative pharmaceuticals and semiconductor sectors, whilst in the medium to long term, this will continue to reduce the flow of venture capital between China and the US. Checklist:
Whether Brent will break through the $120 mark, and the situation regarding the Saudi East-West Pipeline and passage through the Strait of Hormuz The statement from the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy meeting on 28 October and expectations of an interest rate rise in December, as well as whether the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds will rise above 5 per cent again Capital expenditure guidance in next week’s earnings reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon OpenAI’s final valuation following its funding round and the UAE computing power agreement China’s response to the US’s new regulations on outward investment, and the reaction of the innovative pharmaceuticals sector on the Hong Kong stock market Supporting Measures for Population and Service Sector Policies Adopted by the State Council Executive Meeting

entry.title: OpenAI vs Anthropic: Why is the larger behemoth actually going public later? | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original.
Introduction: InPrevious articleIn this article, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the accounting paradox and the turning point in Anthropic’s ability to generate cash flow, as revealed in its draft prospectus, which highlights a ‘huge book loss of 80.7 billion’. However, the emergence of this draft has brought to light an even more staggering capital drama—The rivalry between the two giants in the global AI sector is set to witness an extremely dramatic race to the IPO finish line. In terms of user recognition and scale, OpenAI—with 900 million weekly active users and 50 million subscribers—is undoubtedly the undisputed market leader; yet on the road to the Nasdaq, this colossus—valued at over 850 billion—has postponed its listing until 2027, allowing the smaller Anthropic to beat it to the punch and ring the bell this November. Why is the larger company trailing behind? What financial calculations and practical challenges lie behind this trillion-dollar IPO race?
Prologue: A Qualifying Session Defying Conventional WisdomIf you had asked tech analysts on Wall Street six months ago, ‘Who will be the first AI company to go public with the largest IPO in history?’, the vast majority would undoubtedly have answered: Sam Altman and his OpenAI. After all, by any publicly available measure, OpenAI is the undisputed leader in the world of large language models:
User base: Global weekly active users (WAU) officially surpassed the mark as early as the beginning of the year 900 million (900M+), and is set to reach the 1 billion mark by the summer; Paid chassis: With over 50 million There are over 7 million individual paid subscribers and corporate accounts; Commercialisation and profit-making: In the third quarter of 2026, net annualised recurring revenue (ARR) exceeded US$50 billion A major milestone.
By comparison, Anthropic—founded by the Amodei siblings, who left OpenAI—has always been regarded as a challenger, both in terms of user recognition and team size. However, in the autumn of 2026, the capital markets presented a truly baffling scenario:Anthropic, a smaller player, is pressing ahead with its underwriter roadshow at a remarkable pace and is expected to officially list on the Nasdaq in mid- to late November; meanwhile, OpenAI—with a valuation of US$852 billion and having secured the largest private funding round in history—has publicly announced that it is postponing its IPO until 2027. Why is it that the even larger behemoths are reluctant to go public first? To understand this scene, we must see through Wall Street’s fundamental mindset in the current cycle of high interest rates:Anthropic sells its corporate clients a solid ‘profit and loss account’, whilst OpenAI sells its global users a grand ‘super traffic gateway’—and in the current public market, the exacting mutual funds are, at this stage, only willing to pay for the former. I. An Industry Blunder: The Timing of the Secret S-1 FilingBefore we analyse this race, we need to first set the record straight regarding a ‘blunder’ that has been widely circulated in financial media circles. Earlier this year, Bloomberg, Fortune and Axios reported in succession that ‘OpenAI had secretly filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC on 22 May’, sending shockwaves through the global technology sector. However, subsequent official verification confirmed that:The so-called submission on 22 May was merely a misreport by the media to build anticipation; the actual date of the confidential submission is 8 June 2026. This date is extremely delicate:Anthropic filed its confidential S-1 on 1 June 2026, a full week ahead of OpenAI. On 8 June, the very day OpenAI formally filed its prospectus, a seismic event took place across the Atlantic at Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC): Apple announced a major partnership with Google, under which Siri would be integrated with the Gemini engine by default. OpenAI, which had previously been viewed by the outside world as deeply tied to Apple, effectively lost one of the most crucial distribution channels in the mobile ecosystem on the very day it filed its prospectus. With this one-week time lag, Anthropic’s valuation in the private market has even overtaken that of its peers (its post-Series H valuation on 28 May reached US$965 billion, Weisuo’s OpenAI Series C round in March’s US$852 billion). From that moment on, the ‘right of primogeniture’ in the AI capital markets quietly changed hands. II. OpenAI’s Dilemma: An Accounting Amplifier and a Genuine Money-Sucking Black HoleAs we noted in our previous analysis of Anthropic’s 80.7 billion loss, according to leaked audited financial statements disclosed by the UK’s *Financial Times* (FT) and *Fortune* magazine,OpenAI also has an extremely alarming ‘book loss amplifier’。 fig-openai-2025-loss-breakdown Figure 1Breakdown of OpenAI’s 2025 financial structure: booked revenue of $13.07B, actual operating loss of -$20.92B; Due to the revaluation of financial instruments associated with the transition to a Profit-Making Public Benefit Company (PBC), the accounts included a one-off non-cash entry of up to $41.55B, ultimately resulting in a net loss of -$38.5B on the balance sheet. (Data: Leaked audited financial statements from the Financial Times (FT) and Fortune) 1. 2025 Real Ledger: For every dollar earned, I’m still losing 1.60 dollarsJudging by the audited financial statements, OpenAI’s 2025 presents a starkly polarised picture:
Revenue side: Booked revenue for the full year stood at US$13.07 billion, demonstrating the exceptional monetisation potential of consumer-grade products; Cost side: Research and development (R&D) expenditure amounted to US$19.18 billion, selling and administrative expenses of US$5.73 billion, and cost of sales of US$7.50 billion; Operating loss: The actual operating loss amounted to -US$20.92 billion. This means that in 2025,For every dollar of revenue OpenAI generates, the business itself still incurs a net loss of 1.60 dollars.(Although there has been a marked improvement compared with the 2024 figure of a loss of $2.37 for every $1 earned, there is still no sign of a return to operating profitability.)
And the staggering figures in the report - a net loss of US$38.5 billion Among these, there are more than US$41.55 billion This relates to the revaluation of the fair value of equity and derivative financial instruments arising from the reorganisation into a Public Benefit Company (PBC). This mechanism is an accounting construct that stems entirely from the same source as Anthropic’s revaluation of 72 billion in debt. 2. The cash flow gap: moving into the black vs continuing to bleed cashHowever, the financial trajectories of the two companies took completely opposite turns as they entered 2026: Anthropic’s quarterly revenue trends Figure 2Anthropic’s quarterly revenue trend: Q1 $4.7B ➔ Q2 $11.6B ➔ Q3 $16.8B. Not only did it generate 3.7 times the full-year revenue for 2025 in Q3 alone, but it also achieved consecutive quarters of positive adjusted operating profit in Q2 and Q3 (Q3 operating profit margin: 11 per cent). (Data: Reuters / S-1 draft; Chart: SweetValueLab) Whilst Anthropic has been the first to cross the adjusted operating profit threshold by selling coding tools to businesses (generating $1.70 in revenue for every $1 of computing power), OpenAI’s rate of cash burn is heading towards an even greater unknown:
The single-supplier black hole: In 2025 alone, OpenAI’s spending went to a single supplierMicrosoft Azure’s cloud computing bill amounted to as much as US$17.2 billion… which directly exceeded its total annual revenue! Projected long-term blood loss: According to investor presentation materials for sovereign wealth funds, as reported by the FT, OpenAI predicts Cumulative free cash flow (FCF) for the period 2026 to 2030 is set to reach a staggering -$278 billion (–$278B)； The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), citing model estimates, reports that by 2028, OpenAI’s annual cash burn rate will soar to US$85 billion. Even the massive $122 billion funding round, which was only finalised in March this year, is expected to, given the frenetic pace of computing infrastructure development, The trough will be reached by the end of 2028。
III. 852 billion buyback programme stalls: the market casts a vote of no confidence with hard cashOn 31 March this year, OpenAI officially announced the completion of the largest single private funding round in the history of commercial enterprise—A total of US$122 billion ($122B), with the post-investment valuation set at US$852 billion ($852B)。 The line-up of investors in this funding round is nothing short of stellar:
Amazon an investment of US$50 billion; Nvidia An investment of US$30 billion; SoftBank An investment of US$30 billion (to be paid in instalments, representing a stake of approximately 13 per cent); approximately US$12 billion from traditional top-tier institutions; It even took the unprecedented step of opening up more than US$3 billion in investment quotas to high-net-worth retail investors via wealth management channels.
Yet behind all this revelry lies a little-known, strict clause:Of the US$50 billion invested by Amazon, a full US$35 billion constitutes ‘contingent capital’— —the contract explicitly stipulates that this sum will only actually be transferred once OpenAI has successfully completed an IPO by the end of 2028, or once an independent committee has determined that it has achieved a milestone in the development of artificial general intelligence (AGI). A scene of even greater symbolic significance took place on 10 August 2026:OpenAI has approved a funding round totalling US$7 billion ($7B) the employee shareholding tender offer. At the time, the latest market data showed that OpenAI’s annualised revenue had surged from US$25 billion in February to US$40 billion in August,Business volume surged by 60 per cent within five months。 According to standard valuation principles, this buyback should command a premium of at least 30 per cent to 50 per cent.However, the revelations by Bloomberg and CNBC took everyone by surprise:This US$7 billion share buyback was priced strictly at the original price of US$8,520 per share, without the slightest deviation. OpenAI’s ARR Trends for 2023–2026 and Breakthroughs During the Plateau Phase Figure 3OpenAI’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) growth trajectory for 2023–2026: after a five-month plateau at the $25 billion mark, growth has accelerated again to the $40 billion–$50 billion range, though valuation multiples have not expanded proportionally during this period. (Data: Bloomberg / FT / CNBC; Chart: ValueAddVC) This harsh commercial reality sends an extremely clear signal:Even the long-standing institutional shareholders participating in the buyback refused to pay even a single cent’s premium on top of the 852 billion figure. Sam Altman has repeatedly emphasised that OpenAI must, once it has reached 1 trillion dollars ($1T) only after reaching its valuation benchmark should a company consider entering the public market. If a company’s revenue has risen by 60 per cent but its valuation has remained stagnant, forcing it onto the US public market at this stage would almost certainly result in a valuation correction—with the share price falling below the issue price—immediately upon listing. IV. The Capital Structure Showdown: A Light-Footed Approach vs the Burden of the PastWhy has Anthropic been able to ‘move quickly in small steps’ towards a Nasdaq listing, whilst OpenAI has hit a snag?If we lay out and compare the shareholdings and governance structures of the two companies, the answer becomes immediately clear:
Key Governance and Capital Dimensions Anthropic (Light and Swift) OpenAI (burdened with a heavy load)
Top-level legal framework Public Benefit Company (PBC) + 5-tier equity isolation Public Benefit Company (PBC) + Non-profit Foundation Dual-tier Holding Structure
Founder control over voting rights Extremely tight and secure: Upon the establishment of Founder LLC, the seven founders held only approximately 14 per cent of the economic shares, but through Class F sharesHold a firm grip on 50.1 per cent of the absolute voting rights, supplemented by the LTBT Long-Term Trust Framework A stalemate between multiple interests: The non-profit foundation retains approximately 26 per cent of the economic interest (corresponding to a book value of over $130 billion) and holds exclusive control over the Class N board; management’s control is subject to institutional checks and balances.
Shareholdings in strategic technology giants Amazon (15–21 per cent stake) and Google (approximately 14 per cent stake) are passive strategic financial shareholders with no exclusivity clauses. Microsoft holds a stake of approximately 27 per cent (with a market capitalisation exceeding $135B); Early-stage deep integration; IP commercialisation and intellectual property licensing have been secured and extended until 2032
Computing Power and Supply Chain Agreement Commitments totalling approximately $518B for computing power procurement have been signed (47 per cent of revenue is routed via AWS/GCP cloud services) It pays Microsoft over 10 billion in computing power costs annually; it is also spearheading the $500 billion ‘Stargate’ infrastructure project, with a capital expenditure plan totalling $856 billion by 2030.
The biggest compliance hurdle to listing Largely cleared: Approximately $72 billion worth of convertible bonds were automatically converted into ordinary shares at the closing bell at a pre-set price, and the balance sheet was cleared in an instant. Intricately complex: How can one demonstrate to the SEC that a non-profit foundation holding 26 per cent of the voting rights does not conflict with the interests of public shareholders? How should Microsoft’s exceptionally large free float of 27 per cent be addressed? These issues remain entirely unresolved.
Anthropic’s US$518 billion computing power commitment, broken down by competitor Figure 4A breakdown of Anthropic’s computing power ecosystem: whereas OpenAI is deeply tied to Microsoft Azure, Anthropic’s commitment of 518 billion is spread across a diverse range of partners, including Broadcom, Google and Amazon, offering a clearer path for capital exit. (Data: Reuters / S-1 draft; Chart: SweetValueLab) As a former technology underwriting specialist at Morgan Stanley pointed out:Anthropic is a modern company that has been meticulously designed from day one with commercialisation and an IPO in mind; OpenAI, on the other hand, is an aircraft carrier that was converted from a non-profit research institute partway through its journey, its hull laden with unresolved ties to Microsoft, its non-profit board and early donors.
