entry.title: Daily Briefing | 28 October 2026: Neither of the two main blocs secures a majority in the Israeli general election; China’s industrial profits rise by 14.4 per cent in September; OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Terra | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThis edition covers Tuesday 27 October, with some technology news dating from 26 October. The main themes of the day were ‘voting and negotiations’. Israel held its first parliamentary election since the attacks of 7 October. Exit polls from three television stations all indicated that neither Netanyahu’s camp nor the opposition led by Eisenkot would secure a majority of 61 seats; Likud remains the largest party, and the process of forming a government is likely to drag on for several weeks. In Iran, Pezeshchiyan met with Putin and the Emir of Qatar in Moscow, whilst Tehran put forward ‘seven conditions’ for negotiations; however, the Houthi rebels continued to fire missiles at Saudi Arabia and claimed to have attacked the Rastanura refinery. The diplomatic developments caused Brent crude to fall by approximately $2 during trading, whilst WTI dipped below $100. Domestically, the National Bureau of Statistics reported that profits at industrial enterprises above a specified scale rose by 14.4 per cent year-on-year in September, an acceleration of around 10 percentage points compared with August, with the electronics and raw materials sectors providing the main support. In the technology sector, OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra, designed primarily for computer operations, at half the price of the previous generation of similar models. Brazilian assets rebounded slightly following the previous day’s sharp fall, with the Finance Minister pledging to uphold fiscal discipline.
Key News1. Exit polls from the Israeli general election: Likud remains the largest party, with neither bloc securing a majorityIsrael held parliamentary elections on 27 October, the first general election since the attacks of 7 October 2023. According to a compilation by *Israel Today*, exit poll results from three television stations were similar: Netanyahu’s Likud party secured 24 to 25 seats, remaining the largest party; Yashar!, led by former IDF Chief of Staff Eizenkot, secured between 21 and 23 seats, whilst Bennett’s B’Yachad secured between 12 and 14 seats. According to data from the Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, Eisenkot’s bloc is projected to win approximately 53 seats, Netanyahu’s bloc approximately 50, and Arab parties a combined total of approximately 17; neither side is expected to secure the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Knesset. The *Israel Times* summarised the situation as follows: “The anti-Netanyahu camp is in the lead, Likud remains the largest party, and neither side has a clear path to a majority.” Voter turnout was very high. According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, citing figures from the Central Elections Committee, by 8.00 pm approximately 74.3 per cent of voters had cast their ballots, compared with 66.3 per cent at the same stage in the 2022 general election—the highest figure in decades. The atmosphere during the election was tense: Netanyahu claimed that Arab voters were “rushing to the polling stations” and accused the Arab party Ra’am of “attempting to steal the election”; Eizenkot, meanwhile, accused Netanyahu of laying the groundwork for refusing to recognise the results. Prior to the election, Netanyahu also stated that, as long as he remained in power, Trump was willing to take action to “completely eliminate the Iranian threat”. Exit polls are only preliminary results. According to *Time* magazine, the final count is expected to be completed by 30 October, with the official results to be announced on 4 November. President Herzog will then consult with the various parties and authorise the most promising candidate to form a government within 42 days; Should multiple rounds of coalition-building efforts fail, the current Likud government will continue to govern as a caretaker government until the next election. Key points to watch: which side the Arab parties and Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party will align with; whether Netanyahu will contest the results; and the impact of the deadlock over forming a government on Israel’s decision-making regarding Iran. Source:Israel Today、The Israel Times、Jewish Telegraphic Agency、Time Magazine 2. The Iranian President met with Putin in Moscow, whilst Tehran put forward ‘seven conditions’ for negotiations; the Houthi rebels continued their attacks on Saudi ArabiaIranian President Pezeshigian met with Putin on 27 October whilst attending the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow. According to TASS, citing the Iranian President’s Office, the two sides discussed oil and gas cooperation and the expansion of economic and trade ties; publicly available information made no mention of the war or the Strait of Hormuz. On the same day, Pezeshizian also met with the Emir of Qatar, Tamim; according to *Gulf News*, Iranian state media merely stated that the two sides discussed bilateral relations, whilst the Qatari side claimed that the talks covered the war, the Strait of Hormuz and energy supplies. In Tehran, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met with security official Rezaei, emphasising the need to end the state of “neither war nor peace”. Iranian official Bagheri Kani stated that the US must first meet seven conditions before Iran would consider negotiations, and warned that the US might be seeking to reach a short-term agreement before the 3 November mid-term elections, only to resume military pressure afterwards. The conflict has shown no signs of abating. According to *Gulf News*, on 27 October, the Saudi-led coalition intercepted three ballistic missiles fired towards the eastern region and four drones fired towards the south, before subsequently intercepting two more ballistic missiles fired towards Riyadh; The Houthi rebels claimed to have launched a ballistic missile attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery in Ras Tanura, a claim that has not been confirmed by the Saudi authorities. The Egyptian parliament approved the provision of military support to Saudi Arabia, which Houthi officials described as tantamount to a declaration of war on Yemen. Both the United States and Australia have advised their citizens against travelling to Saudi Arabia. Regarding the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian military stated that an oil tanker struck a mine and caught fire outside the Iranian-authorised shipping lanes, adding that the strait was “completely closed” to vessels that did not comply with Iranian regulations. Key points to watch: the specific details of Iran’s ‘seven conditions’ and the US response; whether Qatar’s mediation efforts will make headway; whether the Houthi attacks on Rastanura are true; and whether the fighting will further draw in countries such as Egypt. Source:TASS、Gulf News、Reuters (reprinted by Euronext) 3. In September, profits at industrial enterprises above a specified scale rose by 14.4 per cent, an acceleration of approximately 10 percentage points compared with August.The National Bureau of Statistics announced on 27 October that from January to September, the total profits of industrial enterprises above designated size nationwide amounted to 6,033.74 billion yuan, representing a year-on-year increase of 15.5 per cent; operating revenue stood at 106.21 trillion yuan, up 6.6 per cent. Profits for the month of September alone rose by 14.4 per cent year-on-year, according to Caixin, an acceleration of 10.2 percentage points compared with the 4.2 per cent growth recorded in August. By sector, profits in the mining industry rose by 38.2 per cent, whilst those in the manufacturing sector increased by 17.0 per cent; however, the electricity, heat, gas and water production and supply sector saw a decline of 14.3 per cent. Growth came primarily from two sources. The first was the AI-related electronics sector: according to an interpretation by Yu Weining, Chief Statistician of the Industrial Department at the National Bureau of Statistics, profits in the manufacture of computers, communications and other electronic equipment increased by 1.0 times, driving the growth in total profits of industrial enterprises above designated size by 9.6 percentage points; profits in the high-tech manufacturing sector rose by 52.0 per cent, with their share of total profits rising to 25.5 per cent. The other driver was the raw materials sector, buoyed by oil and commodity prices: the non-ferrous metals sector grew by 79.7 per cent, the chemical industry by 49.2 per cent, coal mining by 57.0 per cent, whilst the petroleum processing sector returned to profitability. Downstream sectors came under significant pressure: profits in the automotive manufacturing sector fell by 22.8 per cent, ferrous metal smelting by 73.3 per cent, non-metallic mineral products by 46.9 per cent, and electricity and heat production and supply by 17.9 per cent, indicating that rising upstream costs are squeezing the mid- and downstream sectors. Profits for foreign-invested enterprises rose by just 0.5 per cent, whilst those for private enterprises increased by 8.7 per cent; both figures were below the overall average. The operating profit margin stood at 5.68 per cent, up 0.44 percentage points year-on-year; however, Caixin noted that the growth rate of accounts receivable reached a three-year high, indicating increasing pressure on enterprises to recover payments. Key points to watch: the October PMI, the further squeeze on mid- and downstream profits from oil prices in the fourth quarter, and whether the strong growth in the AI-related electronics sector can be sustained. Source:National Bureau of Statistics、Xinhua News Agency (Analysis by Yu Weining)、Caixin 4. OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra: designed for computer operations, with prices halvedOn 26 October, OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, positioned as a fast, low-cost mid-range model primarily intended for computer operations, visual reasoning, programming and everyday office tasks, such as filling in forms, editing videos, interpreting technical drawings and automating repetitive desktop tasks. According to BleepingComputer, OpenAI states that it completes tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol; the API pricing is set at US$1 per million input tokens and US$5 per million output tokens, which is 50 per cent lower than that of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol. In terms of test results, on the Agents’ Last Exam, Terra scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at medium reasoning intensity, at approximately one-third of the latter’s cost; its score on Terminal-Bench 4.0 was 50.3 per cent, more than double that of the previous generation. OpenAI also notes that GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra are still recommended for the most complex programming tasks. The model is now available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Education users, and has been launched on Codex and via the API. The focus of this launch is on price and speed. Last week, Moon’s Dark Side launched the Kimi K3.1 Pro at approximately half the price of Claude Opus 5.5; now, OpenAI has slashed the price of its mid-range model by half, indicating that competition amongst AI agents is shifting from a focus on capability to a focus on cost per task. For Anthropic, which is preparing for its IPO, this will also dampen market expectations regarding its pricing power. Key points to watch going forward include: third-party evaluation results for Terra; whether Anthropic and Google will follow suit with price cuts; and whether more affordable computer-operated models can drive large-scale adoption in the enterprise sector. Source:BleepingComputer、9to5Mac 5. Brazilian assets rebounded slightly following a sharp fall; the Finance Minister stated that “it is not a fundamental issue”Following the sharp fall in Brazilian markets triggered by Lula’s re-election, Brazilian assets rebounded somewhat on 27 October. According to Reuters, the Ibovespa index rose by around 1 per cent, having fallen by 13.9 per cent the previous trading day; the real appreciated by nearly 2 per cent against the US dollar to around 5.31, whilst interest rate futures retreated. Finance Minister Durigan stated that the previous day’s sell-off reflected investors’ prior betting positions and “was not a reaction to fundamentals”, adding that the government would continue to uphold fiscal responsibility. Market views remain widely divided. According to Reuters, JPMorgan believes the market has not yet formed a clear view of Lula’s new government and expects investors to reassess the situation in the coming weeks; investors at Armor Capital, however, view this sharp fall as a buying opportunity. The previous day, the Brazilian Ministry of Finance had cancelled the government bond auction scheduled for 27–29 October and repurchased a portion of its government bonds in an effort to stabilise the market. Key points to watch: whether Lula’s team can swiftly announce a credible fiscal framework and the appointments to his economic team; the stance of the Central Bank of Brazil; and any legal challenges to the election result from Flávio Bolsonaro’s camp. Source:Reuters (reprinted by Investing.com) Market Correlation and Today's ObservationOn 27 October, US shares continued to rise. According to TheStreet, the S&P 500 rose by 0.60 per cent to 7,722.60 points, whilst the Nasdaq rose by 1.18 per cent to 26,477.81 points, whilst the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely unchanged, closing at 52,377.57 points; the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note stood at around 4.99 per cent. Tech stocks led the gains for the second consecutive day, with optimism stemming from Anthropic’s prospectus continuing to prevail; the prospectus also revealed that Anthropic expects to pay SpaceX up to US$120.5 billion for computing power by 2029, further illustrating the scale of expenditure on AI infrastructure. In terms of earnings reports, Boeing fell by around 10 per cent after reporting results that fell short of expectations and revising down its full-year delivery targets, whilst UPS reported better-than-expected results and raised its full-year guidance. Regarding oil prices, according to Reuters, diplomatic activity in Tehran and Moscow caused Brent crude to fall by approximately $2 during trading to around $113.7, whilst WTI fell below $100; however, attacks by Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia and a mine strike in the Strait of Hormuz limited the decline, with UBS raising its year-end forecast for Brent crude to around $110. Looking at several news stories together: the deadlock over the formation of a government in Israel and Iran’s negotiating conditions have made the situation in the Middle East even harder to assess ahead of the US mid-term elections, with oil prices set to fluctuate between the prospects of ‘negotiation’ and ‘conflict’. High oil prices have already been reflected in China’s industrial profits, with profits surging in the upstream mining and raw materials sectors whilst declining in the downstream automotive, steel and power sectors. In the AI sector, falling model prices are occurring alongside rising expenditure on computing power; this week’s earnings reports from tech giants will reveal whether AI investment can be translated into revenue. Checklist:
Did the Federal Reserve’s 28 October monetary policy statement and Wash’s press conference signal an interest rate rise? Capital expenditure and cloud business growth in the financial reports of Microsoft, Alphabet (28 October) and Amazon (29 October) Final election results in Israel and the outlook for government formation The details of Iran’s ‘seven conditions’ and the US response, as well as whether Brent crude can hold above $110 Third-party reviews of GPT-6.1 Terra and competitors’ pricing responses China’s October PMI, Brazil’s fiscal framework and the trend in the real
Source:TheStreet、TipRanks、Reuters (reprinted by Euronext) Cover image:Dmitrii Vaccinium / Unsplash

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 29 October 2026: Fed holds rates steady but two members vote for a hike; mixed results from Microsoft and Google; SK Hynix says memory chips are sold out until 2029 | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThis edition covers Wednesday 28 October. The main themes for the day were ‘interest rates and AI ledgers’. The Federal Reserve kept interest rates at 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent, though two members, Cook and Hammack, voted in favour of a further 25 basis point hike; the futures market now prices in a more than 80 per cent probability of a rate rise in December. In after-hours trading, Microsoft and Alphabet delivered contrasting results: Microsoft’s Azure business grew by 48 per cent and capital expenditure came in below expectations, with the share price rising by around 4 per cent after the close; Alphabet’s cloud revenue doubled, but earnings per share fell significantly short of expectations due to investment losses, whilst free cash flow was negative, leading to a fall of around 8 per cent in after-hours trading. Further upstream, the memory chip sector remained red-hot, with SK Hynix posting a record quarterly operating profit and stating that its DRAM and HBM production capacity is virtually fully booked through to 2029. In the Middle East, vote counts in Israel showed Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats and the opposition with 48, neither of which secured a majority; The Wall Street Journal reported that the US has asked Gulf states to prepare for a possible resumption of military action against Iran following the mid-term elections, with Brent crude rebounding to around US$115. Domestically, the China Development Bank announced the completion of the deployment of 365 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments, whilst the ChiNext Index on the A-share market surged by 3.4 per cent.
Key News1. The Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged, whilst Cook and Hamak voted in favour of a rate riseOn 28 October, the Federal Reserve announced that it would maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent. According to Yahoo Finance, this was the second monetary policy meeting since the first interest rate rise in over three years in September; the vote was 10 to 2, with Governor Cook and Cleveland Fed President Hamack both advocating a further 25 basis point increase; This was Hamack’s second vote in favour of a rate rise since July, and the first time Cook had cast a dissenting vote during his tenure. The statement noted that uncertainty remained high due to factors such as geopolitical tensions, whilst domestic spending remained resilient and productivity and capital investment were strong; it added that “the accumulation of further information” would assist the Committee in determining its policy stance. Inflation is at the heart of the disagreement. The CPI rose by 3.7 per cent year-on-year in September, up from 3.4 per cent in August; the core CPI stood at 2.6 per cent. The core PCE, which the Federal Reserve places greater emphasis on, is due to be released on 29 October, and the market expects it to exceed 3 per cent. At a press conference, Governor Wash stated that, following the September rate rise, financial conditions for some businesses and households had already tightened, and that high interest rates were also affecting AI infrastructure, with some credit spreads widening; however, he noted that capital expenditure was “not only robust but also spreading to more sectors”. He added that there had been no discussion of politics or the mid-term elections amongst his colleagues, and that politics had not influenced this decision. Wash also announced that, from 2027, one of the eight annual meetings will be dedicated to discussing monetary policy strategy, with no vote on interest rates and, it is expected, no policy statement issued. According to TheStreet, following the announcement of the decision, the futures market priced in a probability of approximately 83 per cent for a rate rise in December. Key points to watch going forward include the core PCE figures on 29 October, Trump’s stance towards the Fed following the mid-term elections on 3 November, and whether there will be another rate rise at the December meeting. Source:Yahoo Finance、Traders Agency (Key points from the Wash press conference)、TheStreet 2. Microsoft and Alphabet’s earnings reports: one rose by 4 per cent in after-hours trading, the other fell by 8 per centMicrosoft announced its results for the first quarter of the 2027 financial year (ending 30 September) after the market closed on 28 October. According to the company’s announcement, revenue stood at US$92.3 billion, up 19 per cent year-on-year; operating profit was US$45.9 billion, up 21 per cent; Microsoft’s cloud revenue totalled US$63.9 billion, up 30 per cent; Azure revenue grew by 48 per cent, exceeding the company’s previous guidance of 44 per cent to 45 per cent. GAAP net profit rose by 32 per cent, including the impact of the investment in OpenAI; excluding this, adjusted earnings per share stood at $4.89, which, according to FinanceFeeds, exceeded market expectations of $4.73. The most closely watched figure, capital expenditure (including finance leases), stood at approximately US$39.4 billion, below market expectations of around US$45.9 billion; however, adjustments to the lease accounting treatment may affect comparability. Microsoft’s share price rose by nearly 4 per cent in after-hours trading. Alphabet announced its third-quarter results on the same day, reporting revenue of US$127.6 billion, up 25 per cent year-on-year, which was slightly below expectations of approximately US$127.9 billion; earnings per share stood at US$2.12, well below expectations of around US$3, primarily due to a book loss of US$8.7 billion on equity investments, which reduced earnings per share by approximately US$0.55. According to XTB, Google Cloud generated revenue of US$30.7 billion, up 103 per cent year-on-year, whilst operating profit rose from US$3.6 billion to US$11.1 billion, representing a margin of 36.2 per cent; however, search revenue stood at US$63.4 billion, growing by only 12 per cent, and YouTube advertising revenue reached US$11.2 billion, up 9 per cent. Capital expenditure in the third quarter reached a record US$51.4 billion, up 114 per cent year-on-year, whilst free cash flow stood at a negative US$9.1 billion. According to CNBC, the company has maintained its capital expenditure guidance for the year at between US$195 billion and US$205 billion, and expects a significant increase in 2027. Alphabet’s share price fell by approximately 8 per cent in after-hours trading. The difference between the two sets of financial results lies in the pace of investment and returns: Microsoft’s cloud revenue growth and cost control have demonstrated returns to the market, whilst Alphabet’s cloud business is equally robust; however, with core advertising growth slowing and cash flow turning negative, investors’ tolerance for continued capital expenditure is waning. Key points to watch: AWS growth and capital expenditure in Amazon’s 29 October earnings report, and specific comments regarding expenditure in 2027 during Alphabet’s earnings call. Source:Microsoft Announcement、FinanceFeeds、XTB、Wealth、CNBC 3. SK Hynix posts record quarterly operating profit, stating that DRAM and HBM will be virtually sold out by 2029SK Hynix announced its third-quarter results on 28 October. According to the *Seoul Economic Daily*, revenue stood at 104.6 trillion won, a year-on-year increase of 327.9 per cent; operating profit was 83.3 trillion won, up 632 per cent, with an operating profit margin of 79.7 per cent, setting a record for the sixth consecutive quarter. According to the *JoongAng Ilbo*, operating profit exceeded market expectations of 76.96 trillion won as compiled by FnGuide, driven primarily by strong shipments of HBM4, growing demand for server memory and NAND sales fuelled by data centre solid-state drives; however, net profit stood at 39.78 trillion won, falling short of expectations. Park Jun-deok, the company’s Executive Vice President of DRAM Marketing, responded to market concerns that demand for memory had peaked by stating that the company’s DRAM and HBM production for the next three years, up to 2029, was “effectively sold out”. The company also announced a new 60 trillion won shareholder return programme; combined with the recently completed 40 trillion won share buyback and cancellation, total shareholder returns this year will reach 100 trillion won, of which cash dividends will exceed 30 trillion won. According to TheStreet, SK Hynix closed 10.9 per cent higher in Seoul that day, whilst Samsung Electronics rose by approximately 9 per cent and the KOSPI index gained 6.6 per cent; US chip stocks also strengthened as a result. This financial report indicates that spending on AI infrastructure is flowing heavily into upstream sectors such as storage; even as downstream cloud providers face pressure on their cash flow, order visibility remains high in the upstream sector. Key points to watch: Samsung Electronics’ quarterly results; whether memory prices can remain at high levels; and whether the ‘sold out until 2029’ situation will trigger a new round of capacity expansion. Source:Seoul Economic Daily、The JoongAng Ilbo、TheStreet 4. Israeli vote count: Netanyahu’s camp secures 53 seats but still falls short of a majority; *The Wall Street Journal* reports that the US is asking Gulf states to prepare for action against IranThe results announced by Israel’s Central Elections Committee on 28 October showed that Netanyahu’s camp secured 53 seats, an increase on the exit polls, but still eight seats short of the 61-seat majority; the opposition camp led by Eizenkot secured 48 seats, whilst Arab parties collectively won 19 seats, a historic high. According to Ynet, Likud won 26 seats and remains the largest party, whilst Eisenkot’s Yashar! secured 21 seats and Bennett’s Beyachad won 12 seats. There are still over 500,000 double-envelope ballots (mainly from military personnel and others) that will not be counted until the evening of 29 October, which may alter the distribution of seats. Statements from all sides suggest that forming a government will be a difficult task. Netanyahu celebrated the Likud’s victory as the largest party and called for unity within the “Zionist camp”; Eizenkot stated that “the public has chosen change”, demanded Netanyahu’s resignation, and refused to serve under him, including in a rotating premiership arrangement. Democratic Party leader Goren has advocated for the opposition bloc to form a government with the support of Arab parties; the Joint List and Ra’am have also expressed their willingness to support this, but there remain divisions within the opposition bloc regarding reliance on Arab parties. According to the *Jerusalem Post*, the deadlock could lead to a prolonged caretaker government or even a repeat election. As for Iran, according to *The National*, citing *The Wall Street Journal*, Washington has warned several Arab Gulf states to prepare for the possibility that the US may resume military operations against Iran following the mid-term elections on 3 November; Meanwhile, Qatari mediators have submitted a new draft agreement to Iran to end the war, and Iran is expected to respond by the end of this week. The conflict continues: the Saudi-led coalition claims to have intercepted a Houthi missile fired at Taif, whilst the Houthi rebels claim to have carried out a drone attack on Abha International Airport, a claim not confirmed by Saudi Arabia. Key developments to watch: the final seat allocation following the counting of the double-envelope ballots; Iran’s response to the Qatari draft; and US military decisions following the mid-term elections. Source:Ynet、The Jerusalem Post、The National (citing The Wall Street Journal) 5. The China Development Bank has disbursed 365 billion yuan through new policy-based financial instruments, with nearly half of this amount directed towards sectors such as AI and the digital economy.According to a Xinhua News Agency report on 27 October, the China Development Bank has completed the disbursement of 365 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments, with the funds entirely used to supplement project equity capital, corresponding to a total project investment of approximately 5.5 trillion yuan. In terms of allocation, 127.99 billion yuan was channelled to projects involving private investment and private capital, accounting for 35.1 per cent; 277.86 billion yuan was allocated to 11 major economic provinces, including Anhui, Zhejiang and Sichuan, accounting for 76.1 per cent; 179.01 billion yuan was allocated to projects in sectors such as artificial intelligence, the digital economy, green and low-carbon development, biopharmaceuticals and consumer goods, accounting for 49 per cent. The China Development Bank stated that it will next provide supporting project loans, strengthen post-investment management and work to ensure that tangible progress is made as soon as possible. The background to this is that this year’s Government Work Report proposed the issuance of 800 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments to leverage more social investment; At the end of August, the National Development and Reform Commission convened a national conference on investment promotion, calling for the accelerated disbursement of funds. These instruments are intended to supplement project equity capital, thereby amplifying matching bank loans and private capital, and provide direct support for investment in infrastructure and emerging industries during the fourth quarter. On the market front, according to Sina Finance, A-shares staged a sharp rebound on 28 October: the Shanghai Composite Index rose by 0.91 per cent to close at 3,681.47 points; the Shenzhen Component Index rose by 2.02 per cent; the ChiNext Index rose by 3.40 per cent; trading volume across both markets totalled 1.63 trillion yuan, an increase of 167.5 billion yuan compared with the previous trading day, with over 4,100 individual stocks rising, led by the memory chip, CPO and humanoid robot sectors. Key points to watch: the pace of deployment of the remaining new policy-based financial instruments, the October PMI, and whether supporting loans will drive a rebound in investment during the fourth quarter. Source:Xinhua News Agency、Sina Finance Market Correlation and Today's ObservationOn 28 October, US shares traded within a narrow range. According to Tech Insider, citing Reuters, the S&P 500 rose 0.22 per cent to 7,739.58 points, whilst the Nasdaq gained 0.02 per cent to 26,482.16 points. Chip stocks strengthened on the back of SK Hynix’s earnings report, but blue-chip stocks such as Tesla and Apple traded lower. The market showed little change following the announcement of the Federal Reserve’s decision, though the probability of a rate rise in December was priced in further. On the data front, according to TheStreet, the US goods trade deficit widened to US$134.9 billion in September, primarily as imports of capital goods hit a record high, driven by AI infrastructure. As for oil prices, according to *The National*, at 2.00 pm UAE time, Brent crude rose by 0.87 per cent to US$114.87, whilst WTI climbed by 1.59 per cent to US$101.49; UBS expects Brent to remain around US$110 by the end of the year. Looking at several news items together: profits in the AI industry chain are becoming concentrated upstream; the financial results of SK Hynix and Microsoft demonstrate that genuine demand exists, but Alphabet’s negative free cash flow indicates that not every company is able to cover its investments with current revenue. Against a backdrop where the Federal Reserve is likely to continue raising interest rates and the 10-year US Treasury yield has already hovered around 5 per cent this week, the market will place greater emphasis on cash flow rather than merely growth. The situation in the Middle East and oil prices remain the primary external drivers of inflation, which is also one of the reasons for the emergence of ‘hike votes’ within the Federal Reserve. Domestically, policy-driven financial instruments and the rebound in the A-share market indicate that domestic policy is focused on stabilising investment, whilst technology stocks on the A-share market are being driven more by the overseas memory chip market. Checklist:
US core PCE on 29 October, and the monetary policy decisions of the European Central Bank (29 October) and the Bank of Japan (30 October) AWS growth and capital expenditure in Amazon’s (29 October) financial results: can Alphabet’s share price hold above $300? Final seat allocation and prospects for government formation following the counting of Israel’s double-envelope ballots Iran’s response to the draft agreement on Qatar, and whether the US will take military action against Iran following the mid-term elections Samsung Electronics’ Financial Results and Trends in Memory Chip Prices China’s October PMI and the subsequent roll-out of new policy-based financial instruments
Source:Tech Insider (citing Reuters)、TheStreet、The National Cover image:He Junhui / Unsplash

entry.title: Serbia’s Economic Crossroads Amid Political Upheaval: Lithium Mines, Russian Gas and ‘Ironclad Friendship’ | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original.
Introduction: In our post last week on‘The Synchrony of the Wave of Protests in Europe’In our in-depth analysis, we examined how high interest rates and energy inflation had sparked protests amongst young people in Southern Europe and France. Just a few days later, this wave of youth protests sweeping across Europe reached the Balkans, where it entered its ‘second phase, focusing on governance issues’: On 25 October 2026, Serbia’s snap parliamentary election produced a historic upset: the ‘Students’ List’, a party with no prior governing experience, secured an absolute majority, bringing an end to the Vucic camp’s 14-year rule. However, once the euphoria of the election had subsided, what lay before this young team were not abstract political slogans, but three weighty volumes of transnational economic figures, each with far-reaching implications:Will Rio Tinto’s lithium mine in Europe—valued at nearly US$3 billion—be kept open or shut down? How can a smooth transition be achieved between the cheap Russian gas, the supply of which is renewed every three months, and the state-owned refinery that has just changed hands? And what will become of the China-Serbia infrastructure investment project, which provides vital support for the nation’s industrial lifeline and tens of thousands of jobs?
Introduction: The counter-intuitive ‘vote of confidence’ cast by bond tradersLate on the night of 25 October 2026, the atmosphere in the vote-counting hall in Belgrade was electric. Just two hours after the polls closed, Vucic—the strongman who had dominated Serbian politics for 14 years (and who had previously resigned as president to stand for prime minister)—took to the podium ahead of schedule to concede defeat. Formed by university students and young academics,“Student List – Students Win”The Alliance secured approximately 2.2 million votes, winning seats in the 250-seat parliament 135 to 140 seats (exit polls put the figure at 138 seats), surpassing the threshold of 126 seats to achieveA majority on its own; whilst the ruling coalition secured only around 105 seats. The turnout across the country was close to 69 per cent, reaching a historic high not seen for decades. In a subsequent column, Bloomberg characterised this dramatic upheaval as ‘a group of faceless young people taking control of the state’. However, on the first trading day following the announcement of the election results, the reaction of the capital markets took everyone by surprise: The first to make their position clear were not Brussels, nor Moscow, but international sovereign bond traders. Initial reaction in the Serbian capital markets following the general election Figure 1Post-election market movements in Serbia: yields on US dollar-denominated bonds maturing in 2036 fell to 6.42 per cent (a one-month low), whilst 10-year euro-denominated bonds fell by 17 basis points; S&P maintained its BBB- investment-grade rating, reflecting an initial positive response from the capital markets to the easing of political risks. On 27 October, yields on Serbia’s benchmark US dollar-denominated sovereign bonds maturing in 2036 fell rather than rose, dropping by 12–13 basis points to 6.42%, hitting a new low in nearly a month; the yield on 10-year offshore euro-denominated sovereign bonds also fell sharply by 17 basis points to 5.19%. Rather than witnessing a panic-driven flight of capital, the market responded by investing real money in sovereign bonds, thereby casting its first vote of confidence in this young team with absolutely no track record in government. However, in stark contrast to the buoyancy in the bond market, Belgrade’s local share index, the Belex15, rose only slightly throughout the day +0.23%; Strickland Metals, a mining company listed in Australia and with gold exploration projects in Serbia, saw its share price brieflyA sharp fall, with the share price dropping by as much as 33 per cent during the session。 Behind the cautious approach to ‘debt-driven’ stocks lies an extremely complex dual mindset in the capital markets： International creditors welcomed the peaceful resolution of the long-standing political deadlock and public opposition; however, in a commentary issued on 28 October, the international credit rating agency Fitch sounded a warning—Although electoral uncertainty has diminished, the new administration’s economic agenda, policy priorities and cabinet formation remain a mystery.。 The 90-day countdown to forming a government, as stipulated by the Constitution, is about to begin. The young elected representatives will soon discover that in this landlocked nation situated on the geopolitical fault line between East and West,Taking a political stance is an extremely cheap exercise, whilst the hard realities of capital and energy leave no room for black-and-white thinking.。 I. The Life and Death of Europe’s Largest Lithium Mine: The 20-Year Struggle at JadarIf there is one asset capable of simultaneously influencing Brussels’ green ambitions, the balance sheets of international mining giants and street politics in Serbia, it must surely be the one located in the west of the country:The Jadar lithium-boron deposit。 A timeline of the twenty-year struggle over the Yadarl lithium mine Figure 2A 20-year timeline for the Jadar lithium mine: Rio Tinto’s investment commitment was increased from $2.4B to $2.95B (put on hold in November 2025); the EU designated it a strategic project under the CRMA; and, following a change in government after the general election, the project faces a licence expiry deadline in 2027. 1. Europe’s ‘white gold’, dormant for 20 yearsIn 2004, geologists working for the global mining giant Rio Tinto discovered a unique lithium-bearing borate mineral in the Jadar Valley in Serbia, which was subsequently officially named ‘Jadarite’. Following nearly twenty years of exploration and feasibility studies, this mineral deposit has been confirmed asThe largest and highest-grade undeveloped lithium deposit on the European continent：
Resource reserves: Proven ore reserves amount to 118 million tonnes, with an average lithium oxide (Li₂O) grade of up to 1.8%； Design capacity: Estimated annual output once full production is achieved 58,000 metric tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate, 160,000 metric tonnes of boric acid and 255,000 metric tonnes of sodium sulphate; Industry standing: According to estimates by the industry think tank AlphaBriefing, the mine’s production capacity alone is sufficient to meet10 per cent to 15 per cent of total demand for electric vehicle batteries in Europe... Over its entire life cycle (40 years), it is expected to produce 2.3 million metric tonnes of lithium carbonate, which would be sufficient to propel Serbia directly into the ranks of the world’s top ten lithium-producing countries.
Rio Tinto’s Yadarl Lithium Mine: Key Financial Statements and Constraints Figure 3Rio Tinto’s Yadal lithium mine accounts: cumulative investment of approximately 640 million euros (€640M), the project’s total budget has been reassessed at US$2.95 billion ($2.95B), with the licence due to expire in 2027; an annual output of 58,000 metric tonnes of lithium carbonate is sufficient to reshape Europe’s electric vehicle supply chain. 2. Abolition, Revival and Tying to Transnational StrategiesThe political tug-of-war surrounding this mega-mine has been almost the most intense domestic political storm to hit Serbia over the past five years:
July 2021: Rio Tinto has formally approved up to US$2.4 billion ($2.4B) commitments to investment in the construction of; 20 January 2022: Following months of roadblock protests in more than 40 towns and cities across the country, the Burnačić government, under pressure from the general election, announced the revocation of the spatial planning order for the project (the Constitutional Court subsequently ruled that this revocation order was unconstitutional); July 2024: The Vučić government issued a new decree in accordance with a ruling by the Constitutional Court, reviving the project at short notice, prompting tens of thousands of people in the capital to take to the streets for a mass environmental rally; 4 June 2025: The European Commission, keen to reduce its reliance on key raw materials from overseas, has officially included Jadar among the first 13 entities outside the EUStrategic Projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), linking it directly to the security of Europe’s electric vehicle strategy.
3. Rio Tinto’s retreat and the sword of Damocles hanging over 2027However, on 13 November 2025, Bloomberg reported that Rio Tinto had officially placed the project into ‘care and maintenance’ status, with the total budget for the project being reassessed and adjusted to US$2.95 billion ($2.95B)。 It must be pointed out that,Rio Tinto’s decision to put the project on hold at the time was not entirely due to local political protests： A more crucial commercial factor is that, against the backdrop of a global slump in lithium prices, Rio Tinto’s new management has implemented strict capital discipline and cost-cutting measures, with Jadar becoming one of the key projects targeted for active downsizing. By the end of 2025, Rio Tinto will have invested Approximately 640 million euros (€640M) the actual sunk costs. Rio Tinto’s current statutory exploration and mining licences are due to expire on Due to expire in 2027. There is now just over a year left for the various parties to engage in mediation. 4. The new government’s dilemma: anti-mining allies versus the EU’s strategic carrotFor the newly elected ‘student list’, the Yadar lithium mine is a deeply divisive political issue that cannot be avoided:
The Shackles of Public Opinion: According to reports from several Balkan media outlets, Zlatko Kokanović, the most prominent local environmental activist and leader of the anti-mining movement in the Jadral Valley, is himself a key figure within the ‘Students’ List’ coalition. Should the new government give the green light to the project, it would amount to a direct betrayal of its grassroots support base; Pressure from the EU: Whilst congratulating the country on the success of the election, the EU has made no secret of its expectations regarding the CRMA strategic project. The conditions offered by Brussels are extremely attractive—integrating Jadar into the European battery supply chain would not only secure billions of euros in infrastructure funding but would also provide the quickest route to opening substantive accession negotiations.
It must be made absolutely clear that, to date, the newly elected team has not issued any official statement regarding the Jadar lithium mine project. Any assertion that the new government will ‘inevitably impose a total ban’ or ‘immediately and comprehensively reopen’ is premature from both a commercial and political perspective. Based on verified data and political and economic constraints, the future of the Jadar project is characterised by the following three probability distributions:
Evolutionary scenarios Probability Analysis Core Trigger Thresholds and Game Theory Pathways Economic and Industrial Chain Impacts
Maintain the suspension(Continuation of the benchmark) ~50% • Following the formation of the new government, it adopted a ‘wait-and-see’ approach, refraining from introducing new policies;• The environmentalist faction within the alliance exercises an effective veto;• No extension of the planning permission has been granted by 2027. Rio Tinto was forced to take a further write-down of €640 million on historical investments in its financial report; its strategy for lithium mines outside the EU has suffered a setback, forcing it to diversify its supply chain towards Africa or South America.
Conditional resurrection(Restart after compromise) ~30% • The EU is using a substantial green transition fund and an accelerated accession process as bargaining chips;• The new government may introduce a top-tier international environmental audit conducted by a third party, or put the matter to a nationwide referendum;• Global lithium carbonate prices have stabilised and are on the rise. With US$2.95 billion in investment gradually being released, Serbia has established itself as a key hub for the European battery industry; however, the ruling coalition is set to face a severe test of political division from within.
A formal legislative ban(Completely terminated) ~20% • Parliament has delivered on its radical environmental campaign pledges by passing legislation to permanently ban lithium mining;• Street-level environmental campaigns act as a powerful deterrent against any signs of a resurgence. Rio Tinto’s asset project has come to a complete standstill, and an International Investment Dispute Settlement (ISDS) arbitration may be initiated; Europe’s strategy for battery self-sufficiency has fallen through, further deepening its reliance on existing import chains.
(Note: The probabilities set out above are analytical estimates based on the current macroeconomic situation and the dynamics of the various parties’ interactions; they are not definitive forecasts.) II. The Russian gas bill, renewed every three months: the hidden oil time bomb that Vučić defused ahead of scheduleIf lithium mines are crucial to Serbia’s future, then natural gas and oil are what directly hold the entire country by the throat. For a long time, the vast majority of Serbia’s natural gas supplies have come from Gazprom. In the geopolitical context following the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the Vučić government has leveraged its special relationship with Moscow to secure highly favourable energy terms for Serbia:
Short-term lock-up of shares: Throughout 2026, the gas supply agreement signed by Serbia and Russia remained in forceA rolling extension model involving ‘renewal every three months’(The contracts were renewed in March and June respectively until the end of September, and subsequently extended again until the end of 2026). Moscow categorically refused to sign a new long-term gas supply agreement, instead using frequent contract renewals to turn the gas tap into a political lever with which to exert pressure on Belgrade at any time; Unbeatable price differences: According to figures disclosed by Vučić in September, the price of pipeline gas purchased by Serbia from Russia is approximately 318 euros per 1,000 cubic metres (€318/1,000 m³), which was slightly below the benchmark price on the European TTF spot market at the time. This relatively favourable price has kept thousands of factories in Serbia running and ensured that ordinary residents’ winter heating bills remain low.
Compared with the outstanding short-term natural gas contracts,In the oil refining sector, Vučić played an extremely astute move to hedge his risks on the eve of his election defeat： As Serbia’s only modern oil refinery,The National Petroleum Industry of Serbia (NIS) supplies approximately 80 per cent of the country’s refined oil products. However, as Gazprom Neft and its affiliates have long held a majority stake in NIS (approximately 56 per cent), the company has, since In January 2025, the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added Gazprom Neft to the list of entities subject to sanctions relating to Russia.From the outset, it has been living under the shadow of sanctions; for over a year now, the entire island’s fuel supply has been teetering on a knife-edge, relying solely on rolling exemptions granted by the US. 20 October 2026 — Just five days before the general election, Serbia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, Siniša Mali, suddenly made an official announcement： The Russian shareholders have signed a binding share transfer agreement with the Hungarian multinational energy giant MOL Group, under which MOL will acquire the majority stake held by the Russian side; at the same time, the Serbian state’s shareholding has been increased to 35 per cent. The transaction is currently pending approval by the competition regulators in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. This agreement, reached at the eleventh hour on the eve of the election, is of great practical significance: Before leaving office, Vučić decisively defused this ‘secondary sanctions’ time bomb—which could have triggered a nationwide fuel shortage at any moment—for his successor. Bringing in a controlling stake from a company based in an EU Member State (Hungary’s MOL) whilst increasing the domestic public shareholding—should the transaction be successfully approved—would remove the main basis for US sanctions against NIS and ensure the continued operation of the Pančevo refinery during the transition of power. The energy challenge facing the new government has thus been greatly simplified: the oil supply chain has largely been stabilised, whilst the real test will come this winter—when the short-term contract with Gazprom expires once again on 31 December— whether the new cabinet will embrace the EU’s common foreign policy in exchange for Brussels’ expensive and limited-capacity liquefied natural gas (LNG), or continue to hold its nose and head to the negotiating table in Moscow to secure a renewal at €318? III. The Foundation of the ‘Rock-Solid Friendship’ between China and Serbia: A Concrete List Linking Industrialisation and EmploymentFollowing the announcement of the election results, some Western media outlets raised the speculative question of whether ‘the ironclad friendship between China and Serbia might be undermined’. However, a close examination of Serbia’s macroeconomic fundamentals reveals an inescapable truth:Chinese investment is not an abstract political slogan, but a tangible presence that has long been deeply embedded in the very backbone of Serbia’s industrialisation. Unlike the speculative capital circulating in financial markets, Chinese investment in Serbia is heavily concentrated in the manufacturing sector, the primary mining industry and strategic transport corridors, forming the bedrock of the country’s foreign trade exports and local tax revenue:
Key Strategic Partnership Projects Investors and Contractors Business scale, standing and current operational status Key economic and social impacts
Smederevo Steelworks(Železara Smederevo) Hebei Iron and Steel Group(HBIS Group) • The acquisition was completed in 2016 for 46 million euros (according to Xinhua News Agency);• Through the ongoing implementation of environmental protection measures and production line upgrades, the company has ranked among Serbia’s largest exporters for many years (according to Xinhua News Agency). It averted the crisis of closure and bankruptcy facing the century-old steelworks, safeguarding thousands of direct jobs (according to Xinhua News Agency, more than 5,000 workers), whilst also stimulating further employment across the upstream and downstream sectors.
The Bor Copper-Gold Mine and the Ciucaru-Pegi Copper-Gold Mine(Bor / Čukaru Peki) Zijin Mining(Zijin Mining) • Implement investment in technical upgrades and capacity expansion at mines (with a cumulative value running into hundreds of millions of US dollars);• A major expansion project is currently underway at the Jama Bor underground mine, with plans to increase the annual ore processing capacity to18 million tonnes(Serbia-Energy reporting standards). This has made Bor one of the cities with the highest average wages in Serbia (according to media reports), whilst Serbia has become one of Europe’s leading producers of refined copper and gold.
Hungary–Serbia Railway (Serbian section)(Belgrade–Subotica) Chinese companies involved in the construction(Joint construction of multiple contract sections) • The Bei-Nuo section (approximately 75 kilometres) is already in commercial operation at a speed of 200 kilometres per hour;• Total capital expenditure (CAPEX) for the 183-kilometre section of the projectOver 2 billion euros(Serbia-Business statistical criteria). It has reduced the journey time between the capital, Belgrade, and Novi Sad from around 90 minutes to just over 30 minutes, becoming part of the Central European land transport corridor.
Tyre and Automotive Components Manufacturing Chinese manufacturing companies such as Linglong Tyres • Linglong Tyre is investing in the construction of a smart tyre manufacturing base in Zrenjanin (with a planned investment of approximately US$1 billion, according to the company’s announcement). Attracting the supply chains of major European car manufacturers to the region, and providing employment for local industrial workers.
When analysing the aforementioned economic and trade cooperation, we must not only take an objective view of the narrative of Sino-Serbian friendship constructed by official media outlets such as Xinhua News Agency, but also draw rational conclusions based purely on commercial and employment considerations: Based on reports from Chinese sources such as Xinhua News Agency and local media outlets such as serbia-business.eu,The number of jobs created locally by various medium- and large-scale investment projects from China runs into the “tens of thousands”(As reported). From this, a relatively cautious business conclusion can be drawn: The newly elected student movement may be closer to European values, but in the absence of any viable alternative, it would be difficult for any pragmatic government to single-handedly shut down a modern steelworks that supports the livelihoods of thousands of families, or to halt the expansion of a copper mine that is generating a stable cash flow. Chinese projects offer Serbia not abstract slogans, but tangible industrial assets and jobs. In view of the current status of the project:The foundation of China–Serbia economic and trade relations is rooted more in the complementary nature of their real economies than in the personal will of any individual politician. In the foreseeable future, this cooperative framework is highly unlikely to change significantly, and is likely to become a key pillar supporting the new government’s efforts to stabilise domestic employment and public finances. IV. The Macroeconomic Foundation and the 90-Day Test: The First Lesson in Governance for a Leaderless TeamIn accordance with Serbian constitutional procedures, once the Electoral Commission has announced the official results and the new parliament has been convened, the winning coalition must, within The formation of the government will be formally completed within 90 days, otherwise the country will be forced to hold new general elections. This youth and student movement, known as the ‘Faceless Group’, is about to face its first major test of real-world governance since its inception:
The macroeconomic fundamentals still provide a safety net：In its latest assessment in mid-September 2026, the leading international credit rating agency S&P Global affirmed Serbia’s Long-term sovereign credit rating of BBB-(In October 2024, it was officially upgraded from speculative-grade BB+ to the lowest investment-grade category). Although real GDP growth for 2026 has been revised down slightly due to global geopolitical turmoil to 3.2%, and relaxed the deficit target to 3.5 per cent of GDP, but S&P explicitly pointed out that Serbia’s foreign exchange reserves are ample, its total government debt-to-GDP ratio is manageable (remaining below the 50 per cent safety threshold), and the social relief packages distributed prior to the election (accounting for approximately 1 per cent of GDP) have not undermined the country’s fiscal foundations; The Shift from the ‘Political Risk Discount’ to the ‘Policy Uncertainty Discount’：Why did sovereign bond yields hit a one-month low (6.42 per cent) following the election victory?This is because, in the secondary market, the years-long street standoffs, road blockades, school strikes and potential political instability have been factored in as an extremely high risk premium. The Students’ Alliance secured power with an absolute majority of more than half the seats, thereby averting a protracted ‘hung parliament’ crisis,Instantly wiped out the largest political risk premium in the short term； The real challenge will come once the policy has been introduced：However, as the applause dies down, the capital markets’ focus will shift seamlessly from ‘who takes office’ to ‘how they will govern’.As Fitch has warned:A young team with no clear cabinet line-up and no experienced Minister for Economic Affairs is highly likely to become bogged down in factional infighting and decision-making paralysis at an early stage.. Faced with the expiry of Rio Tinto’s lithium mining concession in 2027, the negotiations on natural gas supply guarantees that must be extended by the end of the year, and the massive infrastructure capital expenditure required for EXPO 2027, whether these young leaders can maintain an investment-grade credit rating amidst bureaucratic hurdles and external pressures will directly determine the sustainability of the current bond market rally.
Conclusion: Between idealism and the pull of realityAt the rally celebrating the election victory, young demonstrators sang the national anthem at the top of their voices, marking the end of an era. It was a moving moment in which the younger generation exercised their democratic voice through the ballot box. But outside the building, the economic machine never stops turning: Beneath the ground lies the Yadar lithium mine, in which Lituo has invested some 640 million euros and which has been included in the EU’s strategy on critical raw materials; through the pipelines flows Russian gas, which keeps industry running but whose supply is choked by short-term contracts renewed every three months; and on the banks of the Danube stand steelworks and mines revitalised by Chinese investment, which support the livelihoods of thousands of families. Serbia’s national fortunes have never depended on whether it can make a decisive, either/or choice between East and West, but rather on whether it can, amidst the intricate web of major powers, carefully and shrewdly safeguard every last bit of its own development dividends. For young people about to take up positions in government offices, their rite of passage into idealism begins with picking up these three heavy ledgers. Main Sources of Information and Verification Index Reuters on-the-ground report (Reuters, 25 October 2026): Serbia votes as students seek to unseat Vučić in a snap election Balkan Insight (26 October 2026): Student List wins an outright majority in the Serbian parliamentary elections Bloomberg Financial Markets Column (Bloomberg, 27 October 2026): Bond Market Gives Initial Nod to Serbia’s Untested Election Winner Fitch Ratings Sovereign Rating Update (28 October 2026): Serbia’s Election Result Shifts Focus to Policy Uncertainty S&P Global Sovereign Credit Report (S&P Global Ratings, 16 September 2026): Research Update: Serbia’s ‘BBB-/A-3’ Ratings Affirmed; Outlook Stable MrEast In-Depth Analysis of Lithium Mine Data (August 2026): By the Numbers – Serbia’s Lithium Standoff Rio Tinto Group’s official Jadar operations page (Rio Tinto Operations): Jadar Lithium-Borate Project Reuters Energy Exclusive (28 August 2026): Serbia secures further sanctions waiver for Russian-owned oil firm NIS Xinhua Overseas Special Report (Xinhua 2026-05): Steel Mill Revival Underlines Thriving China-Serbia Ties Serbia Energy Industry Investment Update: Zijin plans massive expansion of the Bor copper mine to 18 million tonnes
Explanation of Data Definitions and Scope Following the election victory, the student list expressed support for both the Jadar lithium mine and cooperation with ChinaThere has been no official policy statement as yet, All the projections in this paper are analytical estimates and do not constitute forecasts; The figures “Rio Tinto has invested a total of €640 million” and “licences expiring in 2027” are based on media and industry sources; the figure “accounting for 10–15 per cent of European battery demand” is based on estimates by alphabriefing; none of these are official figures; The gas price of €318 per thousand cubic metres is based on information disclosed unilaterally by Vučić; the terms of the current contract have not been made public; the transaction value of the NIS-MOL deal has not been disclosed, and completion is subject to regulatory approval; Bond yields are based on market readings for the first week following the election (Bloomberg/Yatırım Masası, etc.); these are unofficial pricing figures.
