entry.title: Daily Briefing | 30 October 2026: Alphabet plummets 12.6 per cent in a single day; US Q3 GDP grows by 3.4 per cent; PCE inflation rises to 3.6 per cent; Iran rejects Qatar’s ceasefire proposal | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThis issue covers Thursday 29 October; the section on Chinese policy includes news from 26 to 29 October. The main theme of the day was ‘growth is strong, but money is being spent too quickly’. US third-quarter GDP grew by 3.4 per cent year-on-year, driven primarily by AI-related capital expenditure; however, PCE inflation rose to 3.6 per cent in September, with core PCE inflation rising to 3.1 per cent, whilst the futures market continues to price in an approximately 80 per cent probability of a Fed rate rise in December. In the stock market, investors began to scrutinise the cash flow statements relating to AI investment: Alphabet fell 12.6 per cent after its free cash flow turned negative, marking its largest single-day decline since its IPO in 2004; in after-hours trading, although Amazon’s AWS division reported 39 per cent growth, its free cash flow for the past 12 months turned negative at US$42.4 billion, causing its share price to fall by around 10 per cent at one point; Intel fell by approximately 17 per cent in after-hours trading due to weaker fourth-quarter guidance. The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5 per cent, warning that the energy shock would push up inflation and weigh on growth. In the Middle East, Iranian officials described Qatar’s proposal as merely an “unacceptable idea”, whilst news that US Vice President Vance had written to Iranian security officials caused oil prices to fall slightly. Domestically, the 800 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments has been fully deployed, and the central bank had previously introduced new tools to stabilise the bond market.
Key News1. US GDP grew by 3.4 per cent on an annualised basis in the third quarter, whilst PCE inflation rose to 3.6 per cent in SeptemberThe US Department of Commerce announced on 29 October that preliminary figures for real GDP in the third quarter showed an annualised growth rate of 3.4 per cent, higher than the 2.2 per cent recorded in the second quarter and also above market expectations. According to data cited by the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), consumer spending rose by 3.8 per cent; business investment, excluding housing, grew by 12.7 per cent, with investment in information processing equipment rising by 37.4 per cent, software investment by 9.6 per cent and research and development investment by 7.5 per cent, with AI infrastructure being the primary driver. Residential investment fell by 3.3 per cent, marking the sixth decline in the last seven quarters, with high mortgage rates continuing to weigh on the property market. Inflation figures released on the same day came in on the high side. According to Fox Business, the PCE price index rose by 3.6 per cent year-on-year in September, up from 3.4 per cent in August, and by 0.5 per cent month-on-month; the core PCE index, excluding food and energy, rose by 3.1 per cent year-on-year, up from 3.0 per cent in August, and by 0.3 per cent month-on-month, both in line with market expectations. Goods prices rose by 3.9 per cent year-on-year, whilst service prices rose by 3.5 per cent. The personal savings rate fell to 3.8 per cent, indicating that households are relying on fewer savings to sustain their consumption. Taken together, these two sets of data indicate that the US economy remains robust despite high oil prices and high interest rates, but there are no signs that inflation is easing. According to Fox Business, citing CME FedWatch, the market is pricing in a probability of around 80 per cent for a 25-basis-point rate rise in December. When the Federal Reserve kept interest rates on hold the previous day, there were already two votes in favour of a rate rise; this data will give the hawks greater confidence. Key developments to watch: the October non-farm payrolls figures due in early November, political pressure following the mid-term elections on 3 November, and the October CPI figures ahead of the December monetary policy meeting. Source:Public Broadcasting Service (PBS)、Fox Business 2. Alphabet closed down 12.6 per cent, marking its biggest one-day fall since going public, whilst Amazon and Intel plummeted in after-hours tradingAlphabet, which had released its financial results after the market closed the previous day, saw its share price fall sharply during regular trading on 29 October. According to StockTitan, Alphabet’s share price fell from US$324.89 to US$283.82, a drop of 12.64 per cent; According to Yahoo Finance, this was the largest single-day fall since its IPO in 2004, wiping nearly $500 billion off its market capitalisation. Investor concerns centred on cash flow: Alphabet’s capital expenditure for the third quarter stood at $51.4 billion, whilst free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, and growth in both search and YouTube advertising was slowing. Microsoft, by contrast, fell only marginally by 0.16 per cent on the same day, with the market clearly distinguishing between companies where ‘investments are paying off’ and those where ‘investments are still burning through cash’. Software shares also came under selling pressure; according to Yahoo Finance, ServiceNow fell by approximately 25 per cent following its earnings report, Fortinet fell by approximately 21 per cent, and the software ETF (IGV) fell by 4 per cent. Amazon announced its third-quarter results after the market closed. According to the company’s announcement, revenue stood at US$201.9 billion, representing a year-on-year increase of 12 per cent (the company stated that bringing forward Prime Day to the second quarter had reduced third-quarter growth by approximately four percentage points); operating profit stood at US$28.1 billion, with an operating margin of 13.9 per cent—a record high; earnings per share were US$1.89, down from US$1.95 in the same period last year, primarily due to a US$9.5 billion gain on the investment in Anthropic recorded in the corresponding period last year. AWS revenue totalled $46.0 billion, up 39 per cent—the fastest growth in the past five years—with an operating profit of $17.8 billion. However, free cash flow for the past 12 months stood at negative $42.4 billion, compared with a positive $14.8 billion in the same period last year, due to a net increase of $94.8 billion in capital expenditure; The company is maintaining its capital expenditure plan of approximately $220 billion for this year. CEO Jassy stated that AWS is expected to grow by over 40 per cent in both 2027 and 2028. According to Yahoo Finance, Amazon’s share price fell by around 10 per cent in after-hours trading before the decline narrowed. Intel announced after the market closed on the same day that its third-quarter revenue stood at US$16.5 billion, up 21 per cent year-on-year, with revenue from its data centre and AI business totalling US$7.3 billion, a rise of 78 per cent; however, its revenue guidance for the fourth quarter was set at between US$15.0 billion and US$16.0 billion, below market expectations of approximately US$17.0 billion. CFO Zinsner stated that the slowdown in the PC market would continue at least until the first half of next year. According to Yahoo Finance, Intel’s share price fell by approximately 17 per cent in after-hours trading. This week’s earnings reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon have shifted the market’s focus from ‘Is demand for AI strong enough?’ to ‘Who can sustain their investment with cash flow?’. Key points to watch going forward include: the upcoming earnings reports from Apple and other companies; whether Alphabet and Amazon will adjust their capital expenditure plans for 2027; and whether more companies will turn to equity financing. Source:StockTitan、Yahoo Finance、Amazon Announcement、Intel Filing (SEC) 3. The European Central Bank has kept interest rates unchanged, stating that the energy shock will push up inflation and weigh on growthOn 29 October, the European Central Bank announced that it was keeping its three key policy interest rates unchanged: the deposit facility rate at 2.50 per cent, the main refinancing rate at 2.65 per cent and the marginal lending rate at 2.90 per cent. The statement accompanying the decision noted that the continued rise in energy prices poses an upside risk to inflation and a downside risk to growth, and that these effects are still being felt; whilst core inflation remains broadly stable and wages have not yet shown a significant reaction, a larger and more persistent energy shock, along with its indirect and second-round effects, is expected to push up inflation and weigh on growth. The statement also noted that financial conditions have tightened since the last meeting, which will dampen both inflation and growth. The European Central Bank reiterated that it would make decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis in line with the data, without committing in advance to a specific interest rate path, and emphasised that it stands ready to adjust all instruments within its remit and, where necessary, to deploy the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) to counter disorderly market volatility. Holdings under the asset purchase programmes (APP and PEPP) continue to be reduced as planned. Compared with the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank faces a more classic ‘stagflationary’ dilemma: the eurozone is more reliant on energy imports, and high oil prices have a more direct impact on growth; consequently, it has opted to adopt a wait-and-see approach for the time being, rather than considering interest rate rises as the Federal Reserve has done. Key points to watch: the preliminary eurozone inflation figures for November; whether energy prices will fall; and whether the latest round of economic forecasts at the December meeting will see inflation revised upwards and growth revised downwards. The Bank of Japan will announce the outcome of its monetary policy meeting on 30 October. Source:European Central Bank 4. Iranian officials have described the Qatari proposal as “unacceptable”; Vance has written to Iranian security officialsAccording to Reuters (as reported by Iran International), on 25 October, Qatari mediators presented Iran with a draft agreement to end the war in Tehran. The proposal outlines a seven-day process in which both sides would take daily confidence-building measures, guaranteed by several countries, with the process set to begin as early as next week. However, according to Israel’s Kan News, a senior Iranian official directly involved in the negotiations stated that what Qatar had proposed was merely “an unacceptable idea, not a proposal”; Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi did not reject it outright, stating that Iran was maintaining close contact with the mediators and that Iran’s own seven-day plan could be implemented within a week. The disagreement centres on the sequence of events: Iran is demanding that the blockade of its ports and sanctions on oil exports be lifted first, whilst the US insists on addressing the nuclear issue from the outset. Signals from the US have also been mixed. According to *The National*, citing *The Wall Street Journal*, Vice-President Vance wrote to Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, expressing a desire to resume peace talks; Trump subsequently stated that he had not instructed Vance to contact Iran, claiming the letter concerned humanitarian aid. Speaking at a rally in Texas, Trump said he would ‘absolutely’ strike Iran again, and that the war would end ‘when I want it to end’. The *Wall Street Journal* had previously reported that the US had warned Gulf states to prepare for possible short-term, intensive military operations following the mid-term elections. In Israel, according to *Israel Today*, the Central Elections Committee has completed the count of the double-envelope ballots, with Netanyahu’s camp securing 53 seats, the opposition 48 and Arab parties 19. The political landscape remains unchanged, with Likud retaining its position as the largest party with 27 seats; the official results are expected to be announced next Wednesday. Likud has accused Arab parties of ‘stealing the election’, to which the police have responded that there is no evidence to support this claim. Key developments to watch include Iran’s formal response to the Qatar draft resolution, US military decisions following the mid-term elections, and the mandate granted to Israeli President Herzog to form a government. Source:Iran International (citing Reuters)、Israel National News、The National、Israel Today 5. The full 800 billion yuan of new policy-based financial instruments has been fully deployed, and the central bank has introduced a ‘redemption swap facility’ for the bond marketAccording to a report in the Shanghai Securities News on 29 October, as of 28 October, the 800 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments had been fully disbursed, taking less than two months from the time the first tranche of funds was released in September. Of this, the China Development Bank (CDB) disbursed 365 billion yuan, corresponding to a total project investment of approximately 5.5 trillion yuan; the Export-Import Bank of China disbursed 120 billion yuan, stimulating total investment of over 1.7 trillion yuan; and the Agricultural Development Bank of China disbursed 315 billion yuan, corresponding to a total project investment of approximately 4.39 trillion yuan. Ming Ming, Chief Economist at CITIC Securities, estimates that this batch of instruments is expected to drive investment exceeding 11 trillion yuan. Liao Bo, an analyst at Northeast Securities, pointed out that new loans to enterprises and public institutions totalled 70 billion yuan in September, reversing the negative growth seen since June, which may be linked to the commencement of the funding programme. With regard to financial stability, according to a report republished by East Money, the central bank announced on 26 October the establishment of the ‘Bond Market Non-Bank Large-Scale Redemption Swap Facility’ (BNSF). When asset management products face concentrated redemptions and systemic pressure arises in the bond market, eligible bank wealth management subsidiaries, public mutual funds and their parent companies may borrow central bank bills from the central bank, raise funds through repurchase agreements in the market, and use these to acquire eligible bonds from the redeemed products, which are then pledged as collateral to the central bank. Together with the equity market swap facility launched in 2024, this tool forms an emergency liquidity mechanism for non-bank institutions covering both the equity and bond markets. Market participants emphasise that this is a tool designed to address extreme situations, aimed at breaking the ‘redemption–sell-off’ cycle; it is not intended as routine liquidity injection. Institutions must bear their own profits and losses, and it does not constitute a guarantee of principal repayment; specific limits and rates are yet to be announced. On the consumption front, the Ministry of Commerce convened a national meeting on 29 October to advance the ‘trade-in’ scheme for consumer goods, stating that the scheme had driven sales of relevant product categories to over 2 trillion yuan so far this year, and calling for the acceleration of subsidy payments. Taken together, these measures indicate that the policy focus is on using policy-based funds to stabilise investment in the fourth quarter and on stabilising consumption through the ‘trade-in’ scheme, whilst simultaneously preparing tools in advance to address potential redemption shocks in the bond market. Key points to watch going forward include: the October PMI figures due to be released on 31 October; whether supporting loans will stimulate the commencement of projects; and the detailed rules regarding the BNSF scheme. Source:Sina Finance (Shanghai Securities News)、East Money、Sina Finance (Xinhua Finance Morning Report) Market Correlation and Today's ObservationUS shares fell on 29 October. According to Yahoo Finance, the S&P 500 fell by 0.30 per cent to 7,720.39 points, ending a three-day winning streak; the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 0.25 per cent to 52,342.56 points; the Nasdaq fell by 1.38 per cent to 26,184.73 points, with Alphabet and software stocks proving the main drags. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note fell by approximately 5.6 basis points to 4.989 per cent. Regarding oil prices, according to *The National*, Brent crude closed at US$115.32 on 28 October and retreated to around US$114 during early Asian trading on 29 October; News of Vance’s letter to Iran raised hopes for negotiations, but attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia and Iran’s lukewarm response to the Qatar proposal limited the extent of the decline. According to HDFC SKY, citing data from the US Energy Information Administration, US crude oil stocks fell by 1.9 million barrels last week, whilst petrol stocks rose by 3.9 million barrels. Looking at several news stories together: the strength of the US economy stems largely from investment in AI, with capital expenditure accounting for nearly 40 per cent of GDP growth; however, this very investment is pushing Alphabet and Amazon’s free cash flow into negative territory, and the stock market’s tolerance for this has clearly diminished. On the inflation front, high oil prices are making it difficult for both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank to ease policy; the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates, whilst the European Central Bank is weighing up the balance between growth and inflation. For China, with the deployment of policy-based financial instruments now complete and the renminbi strengthening, the focus of domestic policy is on stabilising investment and consumption; the technology sector on the A-share market will continue to be affected by the AI valuation adjustments in the US stock market. Checklist:
The Bank of Japan’s monetary policy decision on 30 October, and the yen exchange rate Upcoming financial results from Apple and others, and whether Alphabet and Amazon’s share prices can stabilise China’s October PMI (31 October), as well as the BNSF guidelines and progress on the associated loans Iran’s formal response to the Qatar draft; decisions regarding Iran following the US mid-term elections US October non-farm payrolls and expectations for a December interest rate rise Official Israeli election results and mandate to form a government
Source:Yahoo Finance、The National、HDFC SKY Cover image:İsmail Enes Ayhan / Unsplash

entry.title: Daily Briefing | 31 October 2026: Intel posts its biggest fall since 1974; Nasdaq closes October with a sharp drop; Bank of Japan says inflation target has been met; Binance suffers the largest-ever hack, totalling US$6.3 billion | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original. Today's main themeThis edition covers Friday 30 October, which was also the final trading day of October. The main theme of the day was ‘a concentrated unwinding of risk’. US tech stocks continued to be weighed down by cash flow issues related to AI investments. Intel closed down by approximately 29 per cent following weak fourth-quarter guidance, marking its largest single-day fall since 1974, whilst the Nasdaq fell by 2.84 per cent on the day, bringing its cumulative decline for October to over 5 per cent. The cryptocurrency market suffered another heavy blow, with Binance reporting that approximately US$6.3 billion in assets had been stolen – the largest cryptocurrency theft on record – which a blockchain analytics firm attributed to North Korean hackers. The Bank of Japan kept interest rates unchanged at 1.25 per cent, but for the first time assessed that core inflation had largely reached the 2 per cent target; one committee member advocated a rate rise, leading the market to anticipate the next rate hike in December. Another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, whilst a Qatari mediator returned to Tehran with a revised proposal; Brent crude rose by approximately 2.5 per cent. Domestically, the central bank announced that, with effect from 2 November, overnight reverse repurchase agreements would serve as the primary open market operation tool; the ChiNext Index and the STAR Market Composite Index both fell by more than 4 per cent on the day.
Key News1. Intel closed down by around 29 per cent; the Nasdaq fell by 2.84 per cent in a single day, and has fallen by more than 5 per cent in OctoberOn 30 October, US shares fell across the board. According to TheStreet, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 1.06 per cent to 51,785.82 points, the S&P 500 fell 1.83 per cent to 7,578.97 points, the Nasdaq fell 2.84 per cent to 25,442.31 points, and the Russell 2000 fell 2.03 per cent; the S&P 500 technology sector fell by nearly 5 per cent, with nearly 70 per cent of stocks declining, whilst the VIX volatility index rose by approximately 32 per cent at one point. Intel led the decline. The company had issued fourth-quarter revenue guidance of US$15.0 billion to US$16.0 billion after the market closed the previous day, down from US$16.5 billion in the third quarter; According to StockTitan, the guidance for adjusted gross margin was 38.0 per cent, down from 44.1 per cent in the third quarter, whilst the guidance for adjusted earnings per share was US$0.25, below analysts’ expectations of US$0.43. The CFO stated that the slowdown in the PC market would continue at least until the first half of next year. According to TheStreet, Intel closed down by approximately 29 per cent that day, marking its worst single-day performance since 1974. The social media platform Reddit also plummeted by around 29 per cent; According to reports compiled by The Neuron, Reddit’s traffic from Google searches fell by an average of more than one million visits per week in October. CEO Huffman attributed this to Google’s AI model and plans to shift the site towards a login-based model to reduce data scraping. Amazon fell slightly by around 2 per cent following its earnings report. On a monthly basis, according to Yahoo Finance, the Nasdaq fell by approximately 5.2 per cent in October, marking its worst month since March 2025; the S&P 500 fell by around 1.2 per cent, whilst the Dow Jones Industrial Average actually rose by approximately 1.5 per cent. This week, Alphabet and Amazon reported negative free cash flow, Intel issued weak guidance, and Reddit’s traffic was hit by the impact of AI-powered search, with market concerns regarding AI expanding from ‘over-investment’ to ‘who will be replaced by AI’. Key events to watch: Apple’s earnings report on 2 November, the October non-farm payrolls figures due in early November, and whether major tech firms will cut their capital expenditure forecasts for 2027. Source:TheStreet、StockTitan、Yahoo Finance、The Neuron 2. The Bank of Japan has kept interest rates at 1.25 per cent and, for the first time, assessed that underlying inflation has broadly reached the 2 per cent target.The Bank of Japan concluded its monetary policy meeting on 30 October, keeping the policy rate at 1.25 per cent. This was the first meeting since the rate was raised from 1.00 per cent in September, and the rate remains at its highest level since 1995. According to the *Seoul Economic Daily*, the vote was 8 to 1, with committee member Hajime Takada advocating a rate hike to 1.5 per cent, a proposal rejected by the majority. In its outlook report, the Bank of Japan assessed for the first time that core inflation was ‘broadly in line’ with the 2 per cent target; this is the first time this has been stated since the 2 per cent target was introduced in 2013; At the same time, it raised its inflation forecast for the next financial year from 2.4 per cent to 2.6 per cent, whilst the core inflation forecast—excluding fresh food and energy—was revised upwards from 2.6 per cent to 2.7 per cent. High oil prices and the depreciation of the yen have been the main drivers of inflation this year. The central bank has also decided to accelerate the sale of its ETF holdings, selling approximately 860 billion yen annually at book value. According to Reuters’ calculations, at this rate it would take around 43 years to liquidate the entire portfolio, compared with 112 years under the previous plan. At a press conference, Governor Kazuo Ueda stated that core inflation had reached a level consistent with the target, but that vigilance was required regarding the risk of inflation exceeding the target; going forward, the focus would be on monitoring whether medium- to long-term inflation expectations stabilised around 2 per cent. According to Reuters’ analysis, the next interest rate hike could come as early as December. The market has widely characterised this decision as a ‘hawkish hold’. According to the Seoul Economic Daily, the US dollar fell against the yen from the previous day’s level of 157.79 to around 157.12. Key points to watch: whether interest rates will be raised to 1.5 per cent at the December meeting, whether the yen will continue to strengthen, and the reaction of Japanese government bond yields. Source:Seoul Economic Daily、Reuters (reprinted by Investing.com)、Bank of Japan Outlook Report 3. Binance says approximately US$6.3 billion has been stolen, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in historyBinance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, confirmed on 30 October that an attack on Thursday evening had resulted in the theft of approximately US$6.3 billion in assets. According to Al Jazeera, the attack was carried out in around 20 minutes, with the attackers instructing Binance’s wallets to transfer assets to addresses under their control – a method similar to the February 2025 incident in which Bybit lost US$1.5 billion; Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs stated that approximately US$6.36 billion was transferred out of Binance’s wallets across 10 blockchains. Binance said the figure “may still rise”. Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis believe that the attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group linked to the Lazarus Group; Binance co-CEO Teng Bin stated that the investigation has not yet identified the party responsible. Binance stated that it has frozen approximately US$3 billion, of which over US$2.3 billion has been frozen by the two stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle; the amount stolen is more than six times the size of its US$1 billion User Security Asset Fund (SAFU), but Binance has pledged to cover the full loss and expects to resume withdrawals within approximately 45 hours. In the markets, according to Al Jazeera, Bitcoin fell as low as US$76,368—a six-week low—whilst Ethereum dropped by more than 3 per cent to around US$2,178; Coinbase stated it had not been affected, but its share price fell by 4.8 per cent. The crypto market had previously been under pressure from rising US interest rates and weakening demand for ETFs. Key points to watch: whether Binance will be able to resume withdrawals on schedule, the fate of the remaining approximately US$3.3 billion, and the regulators’ response to custody security at major exchanges. Source:Al Jazeera、TheStreet 4. Another oil tanker attacked in the Strait of Hormuz; Qatar returns to Tehran with a revised proposalAccording to Euronews, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that on the evening of 29 October, a small boat placed two explosive devices above the waterline of an oil tanker; the explosions caused a fire in the engine room, and the vessel temporarily lost power; The incident took place approximately 25 nautical miles north-east of Hasab, Oman. The fire has been extinguished, the crew are safe, and the vessel has resumed its voyage. The Financial Times reported that the tanker was named Louise 1, and this may be the first reported successful ‘sticky mine’ attack in the Strait since the outbreak of hostilities in February. On 30 October, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard claimed that two oil tankers had encountered incidents whilst on “unauthorised” routes; Oman stated that its navy had evacuated 25 crew members from a burning Panamanian-flagged vessel. US Central Command stated that Iranian mines had been cleared from the main shipping lanes. On the diplomatic front, the Qatari mediator returned to Tehran on 30 October with a revised proposal. According to Euronews, citing CBS, there have been some signs of progress in the negotiations, and Iran is expected to respond by the end of this week; Axios reported that the mediators are seeking common ground on the inspection of nuclear facilities and the lifting of sanctions, but differences remain regarding the conditions for formally commencing negotiations. Axios and the Associated Press simultaneously reported that the US and Israel are considering launching a large-scale strike after the mid-term elections on 3 November, though Trump has not yet made a final decision. Speaking in a radio interview that day, Trump said a war with Iran would end “quickly”, but did not specify whether this would be through a deal or military action. According to TheStreet, following reports of attacks on oil tankers, Brent crude rose by around 2.5 per cent to around $117.8, whilst WTI rose by around 2.2 per cent to around $104.2. Key points to watch: Iran’s response to the revised proposal, US military decisions following the mid-term elections, and the reaction of the shipping and insurance markets to this new form of attack. Source:Europe News Channel、TheStreet 5. From 2 November, the central bank switched to using overnight reverse repurchase agreements as its primary operational tool, whilst the A-share market closed October with a sharp fallThe People’s Bank of China issued an announcement on 30 October stating that, with effect from 2 November, it will conduct overnight reverse repo operations on every working day, using a fixed-rate, quantity-based tender; the current operation rate is 1.25 per cent; The 7-day reverse repo will be converted to a fixed-volume, interest-rate tender with multiple winning prices, and will primarily be conducted during tax periods and at month-end. Tools such as ad hoc reverse and reverse repurchase agreements, and repurchase agreements with overseas central bank-type institutions, which were previously benchmarked against the 7-day reverse repurchase rate with basis points added or subtracted, will henceforth be benchmarked against the overnight reverse repurchase rate, with the range of basis points remaining unchanged. On 19 October, Governor Pan Gongsheng stated that the interbank overnight repurchase rate (DR001) had effectively become the central bank’s target rate for monetary policy, but that the maturity of the main open market instruments and policy rates remained at seven days, creating a discrepancy between the two. He therefore indicated that consideration should be given to switching the maturity of the main operations to overnight. According to Sina Finance, overnight transactions now account for more than 90 per cent of the average daily trading volume in the money market. Since October, the DR001 has generally fluctuated between 1.25 per cent and 1.30 per cent, with the 1.25 per cent rate broadly aligning with the central tendency of market interest rates. Several experts have emphasised that this constitutes a reform of the interest rate control framework; it is not an interest rate cut, nor does it signify a change in the stance of monetary policy. It will be worth monitoring whether the Loan Prime Rate (LPR) and bond pricing will gradually shift to be anchored by the overnight rate. In the markets, according to the 21st Century Business Herald, on 30 October, the Shanghai Composite Index fell by 1.44 per cent to 3,599.02 points, the Shenzhen Component Index fell by 2.73 per cent, the ChiNext Index fell by 4.13 per cent, and the STAR Market Composite Index fell by 4.66 per cent; Trading volume across both markets totalled 1.67 trillion yuan, an increase of 117.9 billion yuan compared with the previous day. The baijiu and banking sectors bucked the trend to rise, whilst the film and television, gaming and semiconductor sectors led the decline. According to data compiled by Sina Finance, the Shanghai Composite Index fell by 6.33 per cent in October, whilst the ChiNext Index dropped by approximately 23 per cent and the STAR 50 Index by approximately 24 per cent; the SSE 50 Index, however, fell by only 2.88 per cent, indicating a clear shift in capital from high-valuation technology stocks towards large-cap blue-chips. Key points to watch: the October PMI figures to be released on 31 October; the trend in overnight interest rates during the first week under the new framework; and whether technology stocks can stabilise amidst the overseas AI valuation correction. Source:The Paper、Sina Finance、21st Century Business Herald、Sina Finance (Hot Topics Hourly Report) Market Correlation and Today's ObservationThe sell-off on 30 October was seen simultaneously in the US stock market, the A-share market and the cryptocurrency market. According to TheStreet, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds fell by approximately 7 basis points to 4.917 per cent, as safe-haven capital flowed into the bond market; Bitcoin fell by around 3 per cent to around US$77,000. In Europe, according to Eunews citing preliminary figures from Eurostat, eurozone GDP grew by 0.4 per cent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter, outperforming expectations, though this was primarily driven by Ireland’s 5.5 per cent growth; excluding Ireland, growth stood at only around 0.2 per cent; France contracted by 0.1 per cent quarter-on-quarter, whilst Germany grew by 0.2 per cent and Italy remained flat. The US Bureau of Labour Statistics reported that the Employment Cost Index rose by 0.8 per cent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter. Looking at several news items together: this week, the books on AI investment have been scrutinised repeatedly; the sell-off on the last day of October saw both the Nasdaq and Chinese tech stocks post significant monthly declines, whilst energy stocks and defensive sectors proved relatively resilient. High oil prices continue to drive up inflation; the Bank of Japan has deemed its inflation target to have been met and is prepared to continue raising interest rates, whilst expectations are also high for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. The global interest rate environment remains unfavourable for highly valued assets. The People’s Bank of China has adjusted its operational framework rather than interest rate levels on this occasion; whilst the impact on liquidity will be limited in the short term, the more significant aim is to align policy rates with market rates. Checklist:
China’s October PMI (31 October) and the performance of overnight interest rates under the new framework Apple’s Earnings Report (2 November) and Whether the Big Tech Stocks Can Stabilise Progress on Binance’s resumption of withdrawals and liquidity in the cryptocurrency market Iran’s response to Qatar’s revised proposal, and the US’s decision regarding Iran following the mid-term elections on 3 November US October non-farm payrolls and expectations for a Fed rate rise in December Whether the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates in December, and whether the US dollar will fall below 155 against the yen
Source:TheStreet、Eunews、IndexBox、StockTitan Cover image:Maxim Hopman / Unsplash

entry.title: In the same week, macro and micro perspectives delivered conflicting assessments of AI capital expenditure | Aden’s Space
entry.content:
Automatically translated. Read the Chinese original.
Introduction: At our meeting on 24 October,‘AI: The Mainstay of Capital Expenditure’In a previous article, we analysed in depth how the tech giants’ investments of hundreds of billions of dollars in computing power single-handedly prop up half of the US economy; subsequently, in*The Year AI Agents Went Haywire*In this piece, we explored the dark side of governance amidst the rapid advance of cutting-edge technologies. However, in the final days of late October 2026, the global financial markets were the scene of a highly dramatic ‘split’:At the macro level, the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) and the Federal Reserve (Fed) have concluded that ‘the economy is exceptionally strong’.—Real GDP in the third quarter jumped to an annualised rate of +3.4%, and the Federal Reserve even went so far as to explicitly state in its policy statement—in black and white—that ‘productivity is strong and capital investment is robust’;However, at the micro level, the tech giants on the secondary market have faced a brutal, storm-like reckoning.—Alphabet plummeted by 12.6 per cent in a single day (according to StockTitan, marking its largest single-day fall since its IPO in 2004), with its market capitalisation evaporating by approximately US$500 billion; Amazon suffered a sharp after-hours slump due to capital expenditure of 100 billion and deteriorating free cash flow, with major media outlets exclaiming that “a trillion dollars in market capitalisation has evaporated”. The macro picture is celebrating, whilst the micro picture is bleeding. Why has the same AI-driven boom received such diametrically opposed verdicts within the same week?
Prologue: The Divided Pendulum and the Illusory ConsensusThe week of 28 to 30 October 2026 is destined to go down in the history of fintech as a ‘week of misalignment’ that will be analysed time and again. If one were to look only at the headlines of macroeconomic news, everyone would conclude that ‘the US economy is enjoying a golden age’:
Real GDP growth exceeds three per cent: The preliminary figure for US real GDP in the third quarter, released on 29 October, showed an annualised quarter-on-quarter increase of +3.4%, marking a sharp acceleration compared with the +2.2 per cent recorded in the second quarter; Endorsement from the highest levels of the government: In its statement following the monetary policy meeting on 28 October, the Federal Reserve explicitly characterised the macroeconomy as ‘expanding at a strong pace’ and specifically endorsed ‘strong productivity growth and robust capital investment’.
However, on the trading floor of Wall Street the previous night, an indiscriminate valuation bloodbath awaited the tech giants:
Alphabet Although cloud business revenue more than doubled, the share price plummeted on 29 October as search revenue fell slightly short of expectations and free cash flow remained negative for the second consecutive quarter. 12.6%(According to StockTitan statistics, this marked the largest single-day fall in the company’s history since its listing in 2004), wiping out approximately US$500 billion； Amazon Following hot on its heels, the company released its financial results; although its cloud computing division, AWS, recorded its fastest growth in nearly five years (+39.3 per cent), it suffered a severe cash drain due to maintaining capital expenditure of as much as US$220 billion for 2026, leading to a sharp fall in after-hours trading. 5 per cent to 8 per cent； Panic spread rapidly, and on 30 October (the last trading day of the month), the Nasdaq Composite Index closed lower 2.86% to 25,437 points; the S&P 500 closed lower 1.82% to 7,580.07 points, with both posting their worst single-day performance since June.
Many financial media outlets have simplistically and bluntly attributed this development to the ‘bursting of the AI bubble’. But if you look beyond the underlying ledger, you will arrive at a completely different, yet more profound conclusion: Neither the macro nor the micro perspective is wrong; they simply offer different perspectives on this capital expenditure—the largest in human history—at the same moment in time. I. Understanding the current ‘divergence in judgements’ in three sentencesBefore undertaking a detailed analysis of the official data, we can first distil the essence of this misalignment into three key facts:
In the grand scheme of things, AI isn’t quite as mysterious as people imagine：Of the 3.4 per cent GDP growth in the third quarter, the gross contribution from investment in capital goods—primarily information processing equipment—was only approximately 1.16 percentage points (accounting for approximately 34 per cent of the growth, and this represents the upper limit of AI’s contribution); more importantly, the original BEA text explicitly states that this batch of computing hardware is ‘primarily based on imported data’—The money comes from US tech giants, but a large proportion of the added value remains in the overseas chip manufacturing locations., after deducting the reduction in imports, the net boost to the US economy is far lower than the widely circulated claim that it accounts for ‘more than half’. What actually drove growth from 2.2 per cent to 3.4 per cent were two factors entirely unrelated to AI：Consumption (+2.52 percentage points) remains the largest component, whilst the main driver of the acceleration in the third quarter compared with the second quarter was, in fact,A significant restocking of private inventories (contributing +1.61 percentage points)withExpansion of federal government expenditure (contribution: +0.90 percentage points). This round of acceleration is essentially a combination of a traditional inventory cycle rebound and a fiscal stimulus. The market has never been concerned with whether there is ‘demand for AI’, but rather with ‘when this investment will generate cash flow’.：Google Cloud’s doubling (+103 per cent) and AWS’s fastest growth in five years (+39.3 per cent) provide irrefutable evidence that demand for AI is exceptionally strong; The reason the stock market has dealt such a heavy blow is to punish the tech giants for their reckless over-spending, which has “burned through the quarter’s free cash flow to a massive negative figure simply to secure contracts”.The equity market is pricing in which cash flows will run out first, whilst the bond market is pricing in that the 3.4 per cent growth floor has not been breached.。
II. A Detailed Breakdown of GDP: The True Composition of the 3.4 per cent FigureTo gain a clear understanding of the underlying context of the macroeconomic assessment, one must consult the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA Table 1.1.2) for third-quarter real GDP, published by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on 29 October 2026:
Key components of GDP Contribution in Q2 2026 Q3 2026 Contribution Official breakdown and reasons for changes
Annualised quarter-on-quarter real GDP +2.2% +3.4% Nominal (current) GDP: annualised growth for the same period +5.6%, with sales ultimately rising by +4.9 per cent
Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) +2.51 pp +2.52 pp Performance remained stable, with consumer spending on services acting as a driving force +1.89 pp(Primarily driven by healthcare, catering and accommodation)
Private fixed investment (Fixed) +1.35 pp +1.66 pp A mixed picture: driven by investment in equipment +1.16 pp, with residential investment continuing to weigh on -0.12 pp
Changes in Private Inventories (Inventories) -0.53 pp +1.61 pp A surge of 2.14 percentage points! There has been a strong technical rebound in inventories of non-durable goods in the wholesale and manufacturing sectors
Government consumption and investment (Gov) -0.01 pp +0.90 pp Contribution from federal expenditure: +0.90 percentage points (defence: +0.41 percentage points; non-defence: +0.49 percentage points, including the accounting item for oil sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve)
Exports of Goods and Services (Exports) +0.56 pp -0.68 pp Weaker exports of energy and petroleum products constituted a net drag
Total imports (Imports, net) -1.66 pp -2.64 pp The deduction has increased by nearly 1 percentage point! Imports of capital goods (excluding motor vehicles) surged, directly offsetting domestic value added
Total on the investment side +0.82 pp +3.27 pp Including inventory restocking (+1.61 pp) and investment in fixed assets (+1.66 pp)
Breakdown of Contributions to US GDP Growth in the Third Quarter of 2026 Figure 1A breakdown of the 3.4 per cent real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026 in the United States: inventories (+1.61 percentage points) and consumption (+2.52 percentage points) accounted for the bulk of the growth, whilst investment in equipment—primarily information processing equipment—contributed only 1.16 percentage points, with the net contribution largely offset by imports. Source: BEA NIPA Table 1.1.2. A Substantive Revision to Our Previous Argument on ‘Load-bearing Columns’In our article ‘AI Capital Expenditure: The Mainstay’, published on 24 October, we noted that Bridgewater estimated AI capital expenditure would contribute approximately 1.4 percentage points to full-year 2026 growth (accounting for half of that growth), and pointed out that the preliminary third-quarter GDP figures due on 29 October would serve as a stress test for the extent to which AI drives growth. Today, the official preliminary figures have provided the final verdict:
Mao’s contribution accounted for only 34 per cent：Of the 3.4 per cent overall growth, investment in equipment—primarily information processing equipment—contributed +1.16 percentage points(1.16 ÷ 3.40 ≈ 34 per cent). This figure falls far short of the widely publicised claim that ‘AI alone accounted for over half the growth’, and is certainly not comparable to the ‘74 per cent’ recorded in the first quarter under the aggressive algorithm; The growth in equipment “is mainly attributable to imports”：In the official text of its press release, BEA specifically stated in black and white: the surge in investment in computers and peripheral equipment,“Based primarily on import data”。In macroeconomic national accounts, high-end chips and assembled servers procured from TSMC or overseas are first included once in ‘domestic fixed investment’ (+1.16 pp), but are then immediately deducted by the same amount from ‘total imports’ (–2.64 pp; capital goods account for the lion’s share of import deductions).The conclusion is clear and stark: the vast majority of the money spent by these giants has gone towards the profits and output of overseas supply chains, whilst the net value added that actually contributes to the US domestic GDP is extremely meagre. The key lies in the micro level, not in the marginal change in GDP：This calculation constitutes a significant revision to our previous statement:AI capital expenditure is indeed an absolute mainstay of the balance sheets of companies such as Microsoft and Amazon, but in terms of the marginal net increase in US GDP, it is not as indispensable as is often claimed.
The September shortfall masked by the quarterly averageThird-quarter GDP figures appear to paint a rosy picture, even bringing the annualised increase in the PCE price index down from 5.0 per cent in the second quarter to 2.1%(Core PCE stood at 2.5 per cent). However, a breakdown of the high-frequency data for September alone reveals that the real economy was already showing signs of strain at the end of the quarter:
Prices have edged up month-on-month: The price index for personal consumption expenditure rose month-on-month in September 0.5%, rebounding year-on-year to 3.6%(Core year-on-year: 3.1 per cent); The real drivers of consumption have stalled: In September, real personal consumption expenditure, adjusted for inflation, rose by a mere US$2.6 billion month-on-month, remaining almost atzero-growth state； Residents’ water tanks have run dry: Real personal disposable income fell month-on-month -0.3%, the personal savings rate has fallen to 3.8% a historic low.
A consumer economy fuelled by drawing down savings has, coupled with monthly inflation resurging at the end of the quarter, forced the Federal Reserve into an unprecedented institutional impasse. III. The Federal Reserve’s Statement: Strong Official Endorsement, Yet a Split Among Voting MembersOn 28 October, the day before the GDP figures were released, the Federal Reserve concluded its two-day FOMC monetary policy meeting. The final decision was to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% Unchanged (following a 25-basis-point rate rise in September). However, behind the calm tone regarding the base rate, the entire official statement was rife with an extremely rare exchange of sharp retorts: 1. Three strong statements in the resolution’s preambleIn the body of the statement, the Federal Reserve, in a rare move, employed highly definitive language:
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace”— has completely eliminated the risk of a short-term recession; “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment remains robust”— The Federal Reserve has officially characterised the development of AI infrastructure as a core, positive force underpinning the economy in its official statement; Yet immediately afterwards, he still insisted:“Inflation remains elevated”。
2. A 10-to-2 split vote and undercurrents regarding interest rate risesAt the final vote, the Federal Reserve was split into two camps: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, President of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank Both cast votes against the decision, with both voting members explicitly advocating for a further interest rate rise of 25 basis points at that meeting.。 At the post-meeting press conference, the new Chair of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, demonstrated an extremely skilful balancing act: On the one hand, he reassured the markets by stating that the macroeconomy was ‘pointing in the right direction’, that he did not believe there was currently any uncontrollable overheating, and that the Federal Reserve’s role ‘is not to throw sand in the gears’ of the economic engine; However, on the other hand, upon closer examination of his remarks and the broader context, this journal’s analysis suggests that the underlying message is extremely clear:With GDP growth at 3.4 per cent, AI investment in full swing and September’s inflation rebounding to 3.6 per cent, the Federal Reserve has no grounds whatsoever to support a rate cut, yet there are at least two compelling reasons to resume rate rises in December. Just one day after the meeting (30 October), two more Federal Reserve members publicly stated that ‘interest rates need to be higher’ (as recorded in Yahoo Finance’s live closing market coverage) — the division has spread from the voting benches in the boardroom to the public arena. AI capital expenditure is becoming the Federal Reserve’s most vexing underlying variable—it not only provides growth at the macro level that prevents an economic downturn, but also competes for electricity and commodities at the physical level, thereby firmly blocking the path to interest rate cuts. IV. Financial Results Season Review: Four Major Companies, Four Distinctly Different CausesIf macroeconomic data suggests that capital continues to flow steadily into data centres, why did secondary market investors unleash a wave of selling targeting tech blue-chips on 28–29 October? To dismiss this round of market turbulence as merely the ‘bursting of the AI bubble’ is the laziest approach one can take in technology reporting. In fact, a closer examination of the four sets of financial statements released during this round reveals that the four tech giants are facing four entirely distinct underlying issues: Financial Results of the Big Four: A Comparative Analysis in a Four-Panel Grid Figure 2Q3 2026 ‘Big Tech’ earnings round-up: Google Cloud doubles revenue, whilst AWS accelerates to 39.3 per cent—its fastest growth in nearly five years—confirming robust underlying demand; The root cause of the sell-off is severe cash outflow (Amazon’s TTM FCF: -$42.4 billion; Google’s quarterly FCF: -$9.07 billion), rather than the businesses themselves. 1. Alphabet (Google’s parent company): Revenue slightly below expectations + cash flow negative once again Business Update: Total revenue amounted to US$127.58 billion ($127.58B), up 25 per cent year-on-year, as traditional search advertising (US$63.35 billion, $63.35B) fell slightly short of Wall Street’s forecast of $64.96 billion (64.96B), resulting in overall revenue missing the mark by a narrow margin; however, on the AI front, Google Cloud’s revenue year-on-yearSoared by 103 per cent to US$30.7 billion, achieving a remarkable ‘doubling in a single quarter’; The true cause of the illness: A precipitous drop in net profit and cash flow. The company reported earnings per share (EPS) of US$2.12 (significantly below the expected US$3.01; CNBC reported an adjusted figure of US$2.67, with the discrepancy primarily attributable to substantial non-operating book losses on equity investments); What shocked long-term investors even more was that, in a single quarter,Free cash flow (FCF) stood at US$9.07 billion, having deteriorated further following its first-ever dip into negative territory in the second quarter。 Clarifying Misunderstandings: There were rumours in the market at one point that a sharp fall had been triggered by out-of-control capital expenditure, but CNBC’s earnings verification clearly stated:Alphabet has left its full-year capital expenditure guidance for 2026 unchanged… merely suggesting that there may be an increase in 2027. Market Verdict: Sharp fall at the close on 29 October 12.6%(According to StockTitan’s statistics, this marks the largest single-day fall since the company’s listing in 2004), with its market capitalisation falling by approximately US$500 billion. The market is penalising the company because ‘the slowdown in its cash cow search business, coupled with the fact that the doubling of its cloud business is not yet sufficient to plug the massive hole in free cash flow’.
2. Amazon: Uncontrolled spending + free cash flow continues to take a heavy hit Business Update: Total revenue amounted to US$201.9 billion ($201.9B), up 12 per cent year-on-year, slightly below Wall Street’s expectations; AWS, the cloud computing leader, saw its revenue surge year-on-year +39.3 per cent to US$46 billion, marking the highest growth rate in the past five years; CEO Andy Jassy even predicted during the conference call that AWS’s growth is expected to consistently exceed the 40 per cent mark between 2027 and 2028; operating profit reached a record high of US$28.1 billion (with a profit margin of 13.9 per cent); The true cause of the illness: Astronomical capital expenditure is causing cash to drain away. In its financial report, Amazon not only maintained its full-year 2026 forecast of as much as US$220 billion ($220B) Its capital expenditure guidance, as further confirmed in its official 8-K filing:Over the past 12 months (TTM), Amazon’s net free cash flow stood at a staggering -$42.4 billion。 The latest signs of the debt relay: The latest quarterly filing, disclosed on the same day as the financial results, reveals that Amazon has established a supplier financing arrangement—allowing it to borrow up to US$80 billion ($80B), with withdrawals possible from the first quarter of 2027 (Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance). This marks Amazon’s second foray into the debt market this year: in June, it secured a $17.5 billion credit facility (Reuters). As Bloomberg put it, this is the latest move to “maintain financial flexibility” amidst hundreds of billions of dollars in AI spending;In other words, once their free cash flow has run dry, the tech giants begin to use money from the debt market to keep their computing power afloat.。 Market Verdict: Sharp post-market fall 5 per cent to 8 per cent. The logic of Wall Street is utterly ruthless—even though AWS has posted its fastest growth in five years, investors find it hard to accept that all the hard-earned cash generated by the entire company is being poured into data centres and a computing power black hole, and that the company is even having to fork out an additional $40 billion or more in liquidity.
3. Microsoft · Winner control group: Revenue and profits exceeded expectations + business cycle materialised Business Update: Revenue for the first quarter of the 2027 financial year reached a record high of US$92.3 billion ($92.3B), up 19 per cent year-on-year; net profit reached US$33.6 billion ($33.6B), representing a year-on-year increase of 32 per cent; Key breakthrough: Microsoft has, for the first time, disclosed the specific revenue figures in US dollars for its intelligent cloud, Azure – generating US$33.2 billion, a sharp rise compared with the same period last year 48%, far exceeding Wall Street’s consensus forecasts; Verification of the循环 mechanism: The financial report confirmed for the first time that revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI for the quarter amounted to Approximately US$10 billion (representing 11 per cent of total revenue for the quarter). Although, from an analytical perspective, this revenue of ten billion includes nested revenue flows arising from OpenAI’s procurement of Azure cloud computing power and revenue-sharing arrangements, it has successfully demonstrated to the market that ‘Microsoft is currently the only tech giant capable of converting computing expenditure into direct profit at a double-digit rate’; Market Verdict: Share price rose against the market trend following the release of the financial results +4.0%。
4. Intel: A casualty of the traditional business cycle – a grim outlook unrelated to AI Business Update: Intel’s guidance for fourth-quarter gross profit margin has fallen sharply compared with the third quarter 6.1 percentage points, management has issued a clear warning that traditional business operations are under pressure; Market Verdict: It closed at US$92.07 on 29 October, before plummeting in after-hours trading -23.0%; The following day (30 October), the panic in the markets continued, with shares closing sharply lower -28.6% to around US$65.8, marking its largest single-day fall since 1974 (Yahoo Finance). This is essentially a double blow resulting from the bottoming out of the traditional consumer electronics cycle and depreciation in contract manufacturing; attributing it solely to AI capital expenditure is a complete misinterpretation at the industry level.
V. Market Structure: Who is setting the price for growth, and who is setting the price for cash flow?Amidst this earnings season storm, the financial markets have exhibited a textbook example of a split in sentiment:
Precision Targeting of Technology Growth Stocks：On 29 October, the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.38 per cent, whilst the S&P 500 edged down by 0.31 per cent; by 30 October, the final trading day of the month, the sell-off reached its peak: the Nasdaq Composite closed lower 2.86% to 25,437 points; the S&P 500 closed lower 1.82% Reaching 7,580.07 points, both indices recorded their worst single-day performance since June, with the Nasdaq having fallen by around 8 per cent from its recent high (CNBC). The widely circulated claim that “tech stocks lost a trillion dollars in market capitalisation in a single day” is essentially a media estimate, but the core of the story is highly accurate—The sell-off has been concentrated specifically on heavyweight market leaders facing massive capital expenditure and deteriorating free cash flow (Alphabet alone accounts for 500 billion).； Safe-haven capital is flooding into the government bond market：In stark contrast to the turmoil in the stock market, the US Treasury market saw strong buying support during the same week. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note fell to its lowest level in nearly two months.
These diametrically opposed capital flows reveal the true pricing models currently employed by professional institutions:
Stock traders are pricing in the ‘risk of a disruption to micro-cash flows’: When tech giants are willing to pour as much as US$40 billion of their free cash flow into the race for computing power, big-tech shares—which were once regarded as defensive assets—lose their cash flow safety cushion and are downgraded to high-risk investments; Bond traders are pricing in ‘a solid foundation for GDP growth of 3.4 per cent’: Regardless of whether the tech giants make a profit this quarter, as long as they cash their 200 billion Capex cheques, the entire real economy and construction supply chain will continue to function, and there is absolutely no risk of a cliff-edge recession in the short term.
VI. Historical Comparison: The Chronological Reversal of the Telecoms Fibre-Optics Bubble of the 1990sIn our earlier macroeconomic research, we have on several occasions drawn parallels between the current expansion of AI data centres and the global telecoms fibre-optic boom of 1996 to 2001: back then, the global industry spent Approximately 2 trillion US dollars ($2T), laid more than 80 million miles of advanced fibre-optic cable, with telecoms capital expenditure accounting for up to 1.0%–1.2%, but four years after the bubble burst, there are still Between 85 per cent and 95 per cent of optical cables end up as dark fibre that has never carried any light.。 However, having reviewed this week’s market movements, we can distil a highly forward-looking macroeconomic hypothesis—The timing of the correction in this AI cycle is likely to be the exact opposite of that in the 1990s：
The dimension of the grand historical cycle 1996–2001: The Great Leap Forward in Telecommunications Fibre Optics 2024–2026: The Current AI Capital Expenditure Cycle Differences in Core Mechanisms and Implications
Cycle Start Logic The Internet took its first steps, and policies encouraged the roll-out of the information superhighway Breakthroughs in large-scale models spark a computing power arms race amongst tech giants All of these represent a depletion of forward-looking investment triggered by genuine technological breakthroughs
Capital expenditure intensity At its peak, it accounted for approximately 1.0% – 1.2% According to Epoch AI’s calculations, investment in computing infrastructure as a proportion of GDP has reached Approximately 1.5 per cent The concentration of capital and the intensity of capital expenditure in this round have even surpassed those of that year
Timeline of the Liquidation Process Micro trends peak first ➔ Macro trends confirm later：1. Nasdaq technology shares were the first to peak and plummet in March 2000;2. It was only in the following quarters that telecoms expenditure gradually began to decline and eventually peaked;3. It was not until after 2001 that the macroeconomic GDP recession was officially recognised in the statistics. Confirm the macro picture first ➔ Settle the micro details first：1. Macroeconomic data was the first to confirm spending (GDP for Q3 2026 recorded growth of 3.4 per cent);2. During the earnings season, the micro-level stock market was the first to react to the deterioration in free cash flow;3. Macroeconomic value added is not fully retained within the country due to import leakage. ⚠️ Macroeconomic indicators lag behind expenditure, whilst the stock market leads returns。The macro view records ‘how money has been spent over the past three months’, whilst the micro view scrutines ‘whether the money can be recouped over the next three years’.
The most critical reality lies in the intergenerational differences in the depreciation patterns of assets: Even though the fibre-optic cables buried in the ground all those years ago had lain dormant for eight years, the glass fibres remained intact and were ultimately snapped up by Netflix and YouTube as the foundation for the streaming boom; But the millions of advanced GPUs currently piled up in the server room,Within three years, depreciation costs will be ruthlessly reflected in the financial statements, and within five years, the equipment will face physical obsolescence in terms of energy efficiency.. The tech giants have not had the luxury of waiting a full decade for demand to develop naturally; every day, they are racing against the physical ageing of silicon wafers. VII. Macroeconomic Scenario Update: A Rational Reassessment of the Probability of Load-bearing ColumnsTaking into account this week’s release of the BEA’s GDP real component breakdown and the latest developments surrounding the ‘Big Tech’ earnings reports, we are publicly revising the probabilities of the macroeconomic scenarios set out in our 24 October article, ‘AI Capital Expenditure: The Cornerstone’.Prudent iterative refinement： Comparison of Probability Adjustments for AI Capital Expenditure Scenarios Figure 3The Evolution of the Macro Narrative on AI Capital Expenditure: A Comparison of Iterative Revisions to Scenario Probabilities. The market has shifted from a simple ‘spending frenzy’ to a ‘rigorous scrutiny of cash flow’; the probability of the baseline scenario continuing has been revised downwards, whilst the probability of growth peaking and slowing has risen significantly.
Classification of evolutionary scenarios 24 October: Original Probability 31 October: Correction probability Key trigger thresholds and macroeconomic conditions Determination of the Meaning of ‘Market’ and ‘Asset’
Scenario A(To be continued after digestion) 55% 45%(▼ Down 10pp) • Subsequent technology sector financial reports from November to December confirmed that growth in the enterprise cloud business remained at over 35 per cent;• Industry giants have narrowed or turned their quarterly free cash flow into a positive figure by raising prices or scaling back traditional non-core businesses;• At its December meeting, the Federal Reserve clarified its policy path, dispelling doubts about an interest rate rise exceeding market expectations. Volatility following a valuation reset: AI capital expenditure remains a key expenditure item, but the valuation multiples offered by the market are contracting systematically; share prices have shifted from a one-way surge to being driven by the delivery of results.
Scenario B(Growth has peaked and is slowing) 25% 40%(▲ Up 15 percentage points) • Two consecutive quarters of deteriorating free cash flow have raised concerns amongst the board, prompting some major companies to cautiously revise their guidance for incremental expenditure downwards in 2027;• The expansion of the scope of power grid delays has led to new projects being postponed involuntarily;• As interest rates rise, the cost of debt financing is beginning to erode net profit. Kinetic Shift: The marginal contribution of AI capital expenditure to US GDP has fallen back to the 0.5 percentage point range, and the macroeconomic outlook for 2027 is subject to a modest downward revision.
Scenario C(Hard-landing fracture) 20% 15%(▼ Slight decline, remaining at a low level) • The commercialisation of large-scale model applications has been systematically discredited, leading to widespread order cancellations by cloud service providers;• A major debt default involving highly leveraged computing power forced a drastic cut in expenditure. Hedging against extreme risks: Although individual shares have come under heavy selling pressure, the 40 per cent to 100 per cent real growth rate in the cloud business demonstrates that underlying demand has not collapsed, and the probability of a hard landing remains low and within a manageable range.
(Note: The probabilities set out above are analytical projections based on the evolution of macroeconomic variables and the current state of the strategic interplay between various parties; they do not constitute investment forecasts or definitive advice.) VIII. Honest Explanation of Data Definitions and Factual BoundariesWhen reading this report, readers are asked to maintain a clear understanding of the boundaries:
The accuracy of AI-driven investment contributions: In the official BEA press release, ‘information processing equipment’ is listed as the main sub-category driving investment in equipment (+1.16 pp); however, due to delays in format consolidation of the NIPA’s comprehensive multi-dimensional interactive data tables during the initial release of preliminary figures, the 1.16 percentage points represents the upper limit of the contribution to overall equipment investment; the precise contribution attributable solely to AI computing power, once isolated, may be slightly lower; Regarding media reports of ‘a trillion dollars wiped off in a single day’: This figure is a rough estimate by financial media outlets and overseas news sources (such as Intellectia and NBC commentary) based on post-market fluctuations in market capitalisation, the main text of this report is based on the official closing data showing that Alphabet lost approximately US$500 billion in market capitalisation in a single day (varying slightly across sources to around US$480 billion based on closing prices) and that the Nasdaq Composite Index closed down 2.86 per cent on 30 October; Regarding Alphabet’s earnings per share (EPS) metrics: The figure of US$2.12 disclosed includes unrealised gains or losses on changes in the fair value of equity investments recognised in accordance with accounting standards; CNBC’s adjusted operating figure is approximately US$2.67, and this should be viewed objectively in the context of non-cash distortions when analysing the figures; The Commercial Nature of Microsoft’s 10 Billion Revenue: The US$10 billion in revenue from the OpenAI arrangement disclosed in the financial statements essentially comprises offsets for Azure cloud resources and a revenue-sharing agreement; this constitutes a special model involving a deep strategic partnership and cannot be directly equated with standard enterprise-grade SaaS revenue; A Comparison of Timelines from the 1990s: The application of a time-reversed simulation—comparing the historical telecommunications bubble with current AI investment—forms part of the author’s macro-historical analytical framework, which aims to reveal the tension between macro-statistical lags and micro-level leading indicators; it does not constitute an absolute, mechanical repetition of history.
Conclusion: Computing power is strong, but cash flow is even strongerLooking back on this dramatic week, the clash between macro and micro factors has, in fact, served as a timely wake-up call. What macroeconomists see is the most spectacular wave of machinery installation in human history—hundreds of terawatts of transformers being hoisted into place, tens of thousands of state-of-the-art silicon wafers emitting a low rumble within server rooms, with 3.4 per cent of GDP faithfully recording every instance of capital extravagance that takes place on this land. But from the sidelines of the stock market, investors finally posed that most basic—and most devastating—question of business common sense: If annual capital expenditure of US$220 billion results in a net outflow of free cash flow exceeding US$40 billion over the past 12 months (Amazon TTM), how much longer can this frenzy possibly last? The latest development this week is that Amazon has disclosed a supplier financing arrangement of up to US$80 billion in its quarterly filings, using the hardware in its data centres as collateral for the debt—Where cash flow ends, the debt market begins。 There is no doubt about the demand for AI, no doubt about the explosive growth of cloud services, and certainly no doubt about the long-term vision of technology transforming the world. But as the ironclad rule of the capital markets states: Computing power may be robust, but free cash flow is always more robust than computing power. Whilst the tech giants raise their glasses at the macro-level banquet to celebrate growth exceeding 3.4 per cent, the micro-level reckoning has already begun in cold-blooded fashion. Only those who can be the first to truly transform red-hot computing power into cold, abundant free cash flow will survive the ebb of the next capital cycle.
